docs.title: Linux Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Most people learn Linux as a list of commands: chmod 755, systemctl restart, ps aux, iptables -A. That gets you through a day of sysadmin work, but it leaves the "why" as a black box — why does a chmod on a directory not do what you'd guess from the file case, why does killing a process sometimes leave a zombie behind, why does a service that starts fine by hand fail under systemd, why does ping work but curl time out on the same host. This course is about the layer underneath the commands: the kernel data structures, the on-disk formats, and the OS mechanisms that make the commands behave the way they do.

It's scoped deliberately narrow: this is Linux-the-operating-system, not Linux-the-shell-scripting-language (see Shell/Bash Mastery Path for that) and not Linux-in-production (see Server Ops Mastery Path for reverse proxies, deployments, HA and on-call). Here you'll find the filesystem's actual on-disk model, how permissions and processes really work under the hood, what systemd units and cgroups are doing, how the network stack resolves a name and routes a packet, and the security modules and kernel tools that sit underneath everyday commands.

It assumes basic command-line comfort (you can cd, ls, and edit a file) but no prior systems knowledge. Every lesson that can run on a real Linux kernel does — either directly (this course was written and verified on a real Linux virtual machine, not guessed from documentation) or noted plainly where a mechanism (a specific systemd target, a particular distro's package internals) couldn't be reproduced in the lab environment used to write it.

docs.title: Level 1 · The Kernel, Filesystem & Permissions
docs.text:
Level 1 builds the mental model everything else sits on: what the kernel actually is, how a machine gets from power-on to a login prompt, how the filesystem is laid out and how it really stores a file (not "in a folder" but as an inode with data blocks), what a permission bit actually gates, what a process is before it's even run anything, and how a package manager tracks what's installed. Every command in this level was run against a real Linux kernel, not guessed from documentation.

What was run, and what wasn't

This course was written and verified on a Debian/Ubuntu Linux virtual machine (an ARM64 VM running under Lima/QEMU on macOS, with the same kernel and userland you'd get from a cloud VM). Every ls, stat, ps, ps -ef --forest, ls -i, ln, chmod, useradd, dpkg -L, and boot-log excerpt shown was actually run and its real output is shown, trimmed for length where noted. Where a lesson talks about a different distro's package manager (RPM/DNF) or a mechanism the lab VM's provisioning didn't expose (actual UEFI firmware, a non-systemd init), it says so and draws on the vendor documentation instead of a fabricated run.

Prerequisites: comfort typing commands in a terminal (cd, ls, editing a file). No prior Linux internals knowledge assumed. If you want the shell scripting language itself — variables, loops, sed/awk — that's the Shell/Bash Mastery Path; this course treats the shell only as the window you're typing commands into.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. What Linux Actually Is: kernel vs distro vs userland, the Unix philosophy, monolithic vs microkernel, why "Linux" means dozens of different operating systems.
  2. The Boot Process: firmware (BIOS/UEFI), the bootloader, the kernel and initramfs, switching root, and the first userspace process.
  3. The Filesystem Hierarchy & Virtual Filesystems: the FHS layout (/etc, /var, /usr...), and the kernel-generated filesystems /proc and /sys that aren't really files at all.
  4. Files, Inodes & Links: what an inode holds, how a directory is just a name-to-inode table, and the real difference between a hard link and a symlink.
  5. Users, Groups & the Permission Model: UIDs/GIDs, rwx on files vs directories, umask, and why a directory's execute bit means something different from a file's.
  6. Advanced Permissions: SUID, SGID, Sticky Bit & ACLs: how passwd lets you change your own password, the sticky bit on /tmp, and POSIX ACLs for when owner/group/other isn't enough.
  7. Processes 101: PIDs and PPIDs, fork/exec, the process tree, and what PID 1 actually does.
  8. Standard Streams, File Descriptors & Pipes: fd 0/1/2 as kernel-level file table entries, what a pipe actually is, and why redirection order matters.
  9. Package Management Internals: what dpkg/APT and rpm/DNF actually track, dependency resolution, and what a package "install" really writes to disk.
  10. Project: Build and Boot a Minimal Root Filesystem: assemble a bare root filesystem by hand with debootstrap and chroot into it, so "what does an OS actually need to boot" stops being abstract.

docs.title: After Level 1
docs.text: Level 2 moves from reading the system to managing it while it's running: signals and process states, the scheduler, virtual memory and the OOM killer, disks and LVM, and systemd — units, services, timers and logs.

docs.title: 01 · What Linux Actually Is: Kernel, Distros & the Unix Philosophy
docs.text: If you've only ever heard "Linux" used as a single word for "the operating system on my server," the first useful thing to do is split it into three separate layers, because almost every confusing moment later in this course traces back to mixing them up.

docs.title: The three layers
docs.text:
The kernel is a single program: a few tens of megabytes of compiled C code that starts running the instant the bootloader hands it control, and that never stops running until you shut the machine off. It is the only piece of software that talks directly to the CPU in privileged ("kernel") mode. Its job is narrow but absolute: schedule processes onto CPUs, manage memory, talk to hardware through drivers, and implement a filesystem abstraction. Every other program on the system — including bash, systemd, and ls — runs in unprivileged ("user") mode and can only touch hardware or other processes by asking the kernel to do it on their behalf, through a system call. "Linux" in the strictest sense is just this kernel. You can check which exact kernel build you're running with uname -r.

The distro (distribution) is everything built around that kernel to make it a usable operating system: a package manager, an init system, a standard set of directories, default configuration, and a curated set of packages. Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch, and Alpine all ship the same kernel source (with different configuration and sometimes different patches), but they disagree about almost everything above it — how you install software, how services start, whether /bin is a real directory or a symlink into /usr/bin. When someone says "Linux behaves differently on my machine," what's usually different is the distro, not the kernel.

The userland is the actual programs you run: the shell, coreutils (ls, cp, mv...), compilers, editors, servers. Confusingly, most of the core userland on a typical Linux system comes from the GNU project, which is why old-timers insist on calling the whole stack "GNU/Linux" — the kernel is Linux, but a large share of the command-line tools you use every day are GNU tools, not part of the kernel at all. Alpine Linux swaps GNU's coreutils and C library for smaller ones (BusyBox and musl), and that single substitution is why some scripts that work everywhere else quietly break on Alpine (a point the Project in Level 1 and later lessons on package internals will come back to).

docs.title: Worked example: identifying all three layers on a running machine
docs.text:
$ uname -a
Linux lima-linuxlab 7.0.0-34-generic #34-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Wed Sep  2 14:34:54 UTC 2026 aarch64 GNU/Linux

$ cat /etc/os-release
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS"
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="26.04"
VERSION="26.04.1 LTS (Resolute Raccoon)"
ID=ubuntu
ID_LIKE=debian

$ ldd --version | head -n1
ldd (Ubuntu GLIBC 2.43-2ubuntu2.4) 2.43

$ ls -l /bin
lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 7 Apr 20  2026 /bin -> usr/bin

(Output above is from a real Ubuntu 26.04 LTS "Resolute Raccoon" VM used throughout this course; your own numbers will differ by kernel build and install date, but the layers you're reading won't.) Four commands, three layers: uname -a reports the kernel version (7.0.0-34-generic, Ubuntu's build, aarch64 architecture). /etc/os-release identifies the distro (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS) — note the ID_LIKE=debian line, itself a clue that Ubuntu is a Debian derivative sharing much of its packaging approach; this file is a distro convention, not a kernel feature, and the kernel has no idea what distro it's running inside. ldd --version shows which C library the userland is linked against (glibc here, not musl — this matters because statically-linked or musl-linked binaries behave slightly differently around DNS resolution and locale handling). And /bin -> usr/bin shows a distro-level filesystem layout decision (the "usrmerge"): on modern Debian/Ubuntu/Fedora, /bin, /sbin, and /lib are just symlinks into their /usr equivalents, a cleanup that took over a decade to roll out across distros and still surprises people who learned Linux from an older book.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The kernel's core design is monolithic: the scheduler, memory manager, filesystem code, network stack, and device drivers all run as one body of code sharing one address space in kernel mode, rather than as separate services that message each other (the microkernel approach used by, e.g., QNX or seL4). This is a real design tradeoff. A monolithic kernel is fast — a filesystem read doesn't need to hop between isolated services — but a bug in one driver can, in principle, crash the whole kernel, because there's no memory boundary between subsystems once you're inside it. Linux hedges this with loadable kernel modules (covered in Level 4): drivers can be compiled separately and loaded/unloaded at runtime without rebooting, which gives some of a microkernel's modularity without giving up the monolithic performance model.

The boundary between kernel and userland isn't a style convention — it's enforced by the CPU itself. Modern processors have hardware privilege levels (x86 calls them "rings," ARM calls them "exception levels"). The kernel runs at the most privileged level and user programs run at a restricted one; a user program literally cannot execute an instruction that reconfigures memory protection or talks to a disk controller — the CPU will refuse. The only door between the two is the syscall instruction, which the CPU treats as a controlled, well-defined jump into kernel code at an address the kernel itself chose in advance. This is why strace (Level 4) is such a powerful tool: every single interaction a process has with the outside world — opening a file, reading network data, creating another process — is a syscall, and tracing them traces everything that program actually does to the system.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating "Linux" and "Ubuntu" (or any distro) as synonyms. They aren't, and the gap matters the moment you work across two distros: a command, package name, default config path, or init system can differ while the kernel underneath stays conceptually the same.
  • Assuming GNU tool behavior is universal. Scripts relying on GNU-specific flags (sed -i without a backup suffix, certain date format strings) can fail silently or differently on BusyBox/musl systems like Alpine or embedded distros. If you only ever test on Ubuntu, you will eventually ship a script that breaks somewhere else.
  • Confusing "the kernel crashed" with "a userland program crashed." A segfaulting application is normal and recoverable — the kernel killed one process and everything else keeps running. An actual kernel panic is rare, system-wide, and (outside of dmesg/serial consoles) usually ends the session; conflating the two leads to over- or under-reacting to the wrong kind of failure.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Predict, then run, each of these four commands on any Linux machine (a VM, WSL, or a cheap cloud instance — not required to be the same distro as this lesson's examples) and write down, for each, which of the three layers (kernel / distro / userland) it's telling you about: uname -r, cat /etc/os-release, which bash followed by file $(which bash), and ls -l /lib64 (or /lib, if /lib64 doesn't exist on your system — note which one your distro uses, and whether it's a real directory or a symlink).

docs.title: 02 · The Boot Process: Firmware, Bootloader & initramfs
docs.text: Every troubleshooting guide for "my server won't start" assumes you know roughly where in the boot sequence things went wrong. This lesson walks that sequence in order, because each stage fails in a different, recognizable way — a firmware problem looks nothing like a bootloader problem, which looks nothing like a kernel panic, which looks nothing like a failed service after boot.

docs.title: The stages, in order
docs.text:
1. Firmware (BIOS on older/legacy machines, UEFI on essentially everything made since the early 2010s) runs the instant the machine powers on. It initializes just enough hardware to find a boot device, then hands control to a bootloader. UEFI firmware reads boot entries from an EFI System Partition (a small FAT32 partition you can see with fdisk -l or lsblk -f) rather than scanning a disk's first sector the way legacy BIOS did.
  2. The bootloader (GRUB, on most Linux distros) loads next. Its job is simple on paper — load a kernel image and an initramfs into memory and jump to the kernel — but it's also where you pick a kernel version, pass boot parameters (the famous GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX you edit when debugging), or boot into a rescue/recovery target.
  3. The kernel decompresses itself (kernel images are compressed to save disk space) and starts executing. At this point there is no filesystem, no process table, no /. The kernel's very first job is to mount a temporary root filesystem that lives entirely in RAM.
  4. initramfs is that temporary root filesystem — a small compressed cpio archive, unpacked into RAM, containing just enough tools (udev, disk/RAID/LUKS drivers, busybox-style utilities) to find and mount the real root filesystem, which might be on an encrypted LVM volume the kernel can't reach without extra driver support that isn't worth compiling into every kernel permanently.
  5. switch_root replaces the temporary initramfs root with the real root filesystem and execs the init system (systemd on most modern distros) as PID 1 — the point where this lesson hands off to Level 2's systemd lessons.

docs.title: Worked example: reading your own boot timeline
docs.text:
$ systemd-analyze
Startup finished in 317ms (kernel) + 1.336s (initrd) + 2min 45.052s (userspace) = 2min 46.706s
graphical.target reached after 2min 7.329s in userspace.

$ systemd-analyze blame | head -n5
2min 2.688s cloud-init-network.service
   2min 147ms systemd-networkd-wait-online.service
       37.719s cloud-final.service
        1.946s snapd.seeded.service
        1.589s sys-devices-virtual-misc-rfkill.device

$ ls -la /boot/initrd.img-7.0.0-34-generic
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root 91123407 Sep 27 21:59 /boot/initrd.img-7.0.0-34-generic

$ lsinitramfs /boot/initrd.img-7.0.0-34-generic 2>/dev/null | grep -E "^usr/sbin/(lvm|cryptsetup)$|cryptsetup\.so"
usr/sbin/cryptsetup
usr/sbin/lvm
usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libcryptsetup.so.12

(Real output from this course's Ubuntu 26.04 lab VM.) systemd-analyze's three-way split — kernel, initrd, and userspace — is exactly stages 3–4–5: kernel self-init, then the initramfs running as its own timed phase, then everything systemd orchestrates after switch_root. systemd-analyze blame tells you which unit took longest once systemd was in control, and this VM's own numbers make a real teaching point: cloud-init-network.service and systemd-networkd-wait-online.service dominate the boot at over two minutes each, because this is a cloud image — it's built to wait for network configuration from a cloud provider's metadata service before continuing, a cost a normal desktop or bare-metal install wouldn't pay. That's a genuinely useful "blame" result: it correctly points at cloud-init's network wait, not at anything actually broken. lsinitramfs lets you look inside the initramfs cpio archive without unpacking it by hand, and seeing real lvm and cryptsetup binaries in there explains why an initramfs exists at all: the real root filesystem might be on an LVM volume inside a LUKS-encrypted partition, and none of that can be assembled until drivers and tools for it are available — which is exactly what the temporary RAM-based root provides before the real one is reachable.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The reason there are two root filesystems in sequence (initramfs, then the real root) instead of one is a genuine chicken-and-egg problem. To mount your real root filesystem, the kernel might need: a driver for your disk controller, LVM's user-space tools to assemble logical volumes, cryptsetup to unlock an encrypted volume, and udev to create the right device nodes in the right order as hardware is detected asynchronously. All of that is substantial, versioned, and distro-specific — you don't want to compile it permanently into every kernel image, and you don't want to hunt for it on a filesystem you haven't mounted yet. The initramfs solves this by being a tiny, self-contained environment built specifically for this machine's hardware and storage layout at the time the kernel package was installed (which is why update-initramfs or dracut reruns automatically after certain package updates) — it carries exactly the drivers and tools needed to get from "nothing mounted" to "real root mounted," then gets discarded.

switch_root (as opposed to a simple chroot) is also doing real work: chroot only changes what path a process treats as /, but the initramfs environment has kernel filesystems like /proc, /sys, and /dev mounted, plus possibly running processes (udev daemons) that need to be moved to the new root or killed cleanly. switch_root handles unmounting the old root's special filesystems, remounting them under the new root, and killing anything still running from the old one — a chroot alone would leave you with a half-torn-down environment.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Editing /boot/grub/grub.cfg directly. This file is auto-generated by grub-mkconfig/update-grub from /etc/default/grub and the scripts in /etc/grub.d/; a manual edit survives exactly until the next kernel update regenerates the file and silently discards your change.
  • Assuming a "boot hang" always means a bootloader or firmware problem. A hang after GRUB's menu but before a login prompt is very often a userspace problem — a systemd unit that's blocking on a dependency, a broken fstab entry the real root mount depends on — not a kernel or bootloader fault at all; systemd-analyze blame and the rescue/recovery boot target (Level 4) are the right next step, not reinstalling GRUB.
  • Forgetting to regenerate the initramfs after changing storage configuration. Adding a new encrypted volume, switching RAID levels, or moving root onto LVM, and then not running update-initramfs -u (Debian/Ubuntu) or dracut -f (Fedora/RHEL), leaves you with an initramfs that doesn't know how to find your new root — the system boots the old initramfs successfully, then fails to find the real root and drops to an emergency shell.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run systemd-analyze and systemd-analyze blame on any Linux machine you have access to. Identify: (1) whether kernel time or userspace time dominates your boot, and (2) the single slowest unit in the blame list — then look up (systemctl cat <that-unit>) what that unit actually does, and form a hypothesis for why it's slow (network wait, disk wait, or genuine startup work).

docs.title: 03 · The Filesystem Hierarchy & Virtual Filesystems (/proc, /sys)
docs.text: Everything on a Linux system lives under one single tree rooted at / — there's no concept of a "C: drive," and a second disk doesn't get its own letter, it gets mounted somewhere inside the existing tree (Level 2 covers mounting in depth). The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) is the convention that says what belongs where, and once you know it, an unfamiliar Linux system stops being a maze.

docs.title: The layout that matters day to day
docs.text:
• /etc — system-wide configuration, almost always plain text. If you're hunting for "where is X configured," it's under here unless the program is very unusual.
  • /var — data that changes while the system runs: logs (/var/log), package manager caches (/var/cache), spool files, and databases that expect to live on the root filesystem rather than user storage.
  • /usr — the bulk of installed software: /usr/bin for programs, /usr/lib for libraries, /usr/share for architecture-independent data (man pages, icons, locale files). On a modern "usrmerge" system (Lesson 1), /bin and /lib are symlinks into here.
  • /home — personal directories for regular users; /root is the superuser's home, kept separate on purpose so it's never accidentally on a separate, possibly-unavailable mount.
  • /opt — self-contained third-party software that doesn't want to spread its files across /usr.
  • /tmp — world-writable temporary storage, usually cleared on reboot and sometimes backed by RAM (tmpfs).
  • /dev — device files (Level 2's udev lesson), /proc and /sys — covered below.

docs.title: Worked example: /proc and /sys are not files on disk
docs.text:
$ stat -f /proc
  File: "/proc"
    ID: 1a00000000 Namelen: 255     Type: proc
Block Size: 4096       Fundamental block size: 4096
Blocks: Total: 0          Free: 0          Available: 0

$ cat /proc/version
Linux version 7.0.0-34-generic (buildd@bos03-arm64-067) (aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc ...) #34-Ubuntu SMP ...

$ cat /proc/cpuinfo | head -n7
processor   : 0
BogoMIPS    : 48.00
Features    : fp asimd evtstrm aes pmull sha1 sha2 crc32 atomics ...
CPU implementer : 0x61
CPU architecture: 8
CPU variant : 0x0
CPU part    : 0x000

$ echo $$
10106
$ ls /proc/10106 | head -n8
attr  autogroup  auxv  cgroup  clear_refs  cmdline  comm  coredump_filter

$ cat /proc/10106/status | grep -E "^(Name|State|VmRSS)"
Name:   bash
State:  S (sleeping)
VmRSS:      5292 kB

$ ls /sys/class/net
eth0  lo

$ cat /sys/class/net/eth0/mtu
1500

(Real output, captured on this course's Ubuntu 26.04 ARM64 lab VM — note that ARM's /proc/cpuinfo has no model name field at all; that's an x86-specific convention, and ARM instead reports CPU implementer/CPU part codes, which is itself a small reminder that /proc reflects whatever the kernel's arch-specific code chooses to report, not a fixed universal schema.) stat -f reports /proc's filesystem type as literally proc, not ext4 or tmpfs, with zero blocks total — it isn't backed by a block device at all. Reading /proc/version or /proc/cpuinfo doesn't read bytes off a disk; it triggers kernel code that formats live information into text on demand, the moment you open the file. /proc/<pid>/ exists only as long as that process does — ls /proc/10106 after that process exits gives "No such file or directory," because there's nothing backing it once the kernel's internal process-table entry is gone. /sys works the same way but is organized by device and driver rather than by process, and — unlike most of /proc — many files under /sys are genuinely writable: writing a new value to certain files there changes live kernel/driver state immediately (Level 3's sysctl lesson uses this directly).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
/proc and /sys are virtual filesystems (procfs and sysfs): the kernel implements the standard file-operations interface (open, read, write, readdir) for them, but instead of looking up bytes on a disk, each read calls into kernel code that generates the content at that instant from live, in-memory data structures. This is a deliberate, elegant design choice: rather than inventing a new API (ioctls, netlink sockets, special syscalls) for every piece of kernel state someone might want to inspect, the kernel exposes huge amounts of itself through the one interface every program and script already knows how to use — open(), read(), cat, a shell redirect. It's why a two-line shell script can read CPU temperature, process memory, or network interface statistics without linking against any special library.

The split between the two exists mostly for history and API cleanliness. /proc is older (the name literally means process information filesystem) and over the decades accumulated system-wide information too (/proc/cpuinfo, /proc/meminfo) that has nothing to do with any one process, which the kernel developers eventually considered a design mistake. /sysfs was introduced later specifically to give devices and drivers a clean, consistently structured place to expose state (and increasingly, tunable parameters you write to, not just read), without further bloating /proc. Both are still around because too much existing software (monitoring tools, container runtimes reading /proc/<pid>/cgroup, top itself) depends on /proc's existing layout to ever remove it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating /tmp as a reliable place to store anything you care about. systemd-tmpfiles and many distros' defaults clear /tmp on every boot, and on some systems /tmp is a tmpfs mount — data there vanishes not just on reboot but is also capped by available RAM.
  • Trying to cp or rsync /proc or /sys like normal directories. File sizes reported for files under /proc are frequently 0 or wrong (the kernel doesn't know the content's length until it generates it), which breaks tools that pre-allocate based on stat() size; this is also why you can't meaningfully back up /proc.
  • Confusing /usr/local with /usr. /usr is owned by the package manager — hand-editing files there is exactly as fragile as hand-editing grub.cfg (Lesson 2) and will be overwritten by the next package update. /usr/local exists specifically for software you install outside the package manager, so it survives updates.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: On any Linux machine, find your shell's own process ID with echo $$, then explore /proc/<that-pid>/ — read status, cmdline, and list fd (open file descriptors; this previews Lesson 8). Separately, run cat /sys/class/net/*/operstate for every network interface on the machine and match the result (up/down) to what ip link reports for the same interfaces.

docs.title: 04 · Files, Inodes & Links: How Linux Actually Stores Data
docs.text: "A file is stored in a folder" is the mental model most people carry from other operating systems, and it's close enough for daily use but wrong in a way that makes hard links, rm while a program is still reading a file, and df vs du disagreements all look like bugs instead of the direct, predictable consequences of how Linux filesystems actually work.

docs.title: What's really there: inodes and directory entries
docs.text:
Every file and directory on a filesystem like ext4 or xfs is represented by an inode — a fixed-size on-disk structure holding the file's metadata: owner (UID/GID), permission bits, size, timestamps, and pointers to the data blocks that actually hold the file's content. Critically, the inode does not store the filename. The filename lives in a directory entry — an entry in the parent directory's data, which is itself just a list of (filename, inode number) pairs. A directory is a special kind of file whose content is this list; ls reads that list and, for each name, looks up the corresponding inode to show you size, permissions, and so on.

This separation is the whole reason the rest of this lesson works the way it does.

docs.title: Worked example: watching inode numbers and link counts
docs.text:
$ echo "hello" > original.txt
$ ls -i original.txt
135 original.txt

$ ln original.txt hardlink.txt
$ ls -i original.txt hardlink.txt
135 hardlink.txt
135 original.txt

$ stat original.txt | grep Links
Device: 0,39    Inode: 135         Links: 2

$ ln -s original.txt symlink.txt
$ ls -i symlink.txt
136 symlink.txt

$ ls -l symlink.txt
lrwxrwxrwx 1 vinodkumarsigilipelli vinodkumarsigilipelli 12 Oct 22 23:30 symlink.txt -> original.txt

$ rm original.txt
$ cat hardlink.txt
hello
$ cat symlink.txt
cat: symlink.txt: No such file or directory

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) ln original.txt hardlink.txt (no -s) creates a hard link: a brand new directory entry, hardlink.txt, pointing at the exact same inode number (135) as original.txt. They are not two copies of a file — they are two names for one file, and stat confirms it by reporting Links: 2, the inode's reference count. ln -s instead creates a symlink: a genuinely separate, tiny file (with its own inode, 136) whose content is just the text original.txt — a path for the kernel to follow. That's why deleting original.txt leaves hardlink.txt completely intact (the inode and its data blocks are still referenced, so nothing is freed) but breaks symlink.txt, which now points at a path that no longer resolves to anything.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
rm doesn't "delete a file" in the sense of erasing its content. What unlink() (the syscall rm makes) actually does is remove one directory entry and decrement the target inode's link count by one. The data blocks, and the inode itself, are only actually freed when that link count reaches zero — and even then, only if no process still has the file open. This is why a classic trick works: a long-running process can hold a file open, you can rm it from the filesystem's directory listing (making it invisible to ls), and the process keeps reading and writing it fine, because the kernel keeps an inode alive as long as either a directory entry or an open file descriptor references it. The space is only reclaimed when the last reference — of either kind — goes away; this is also exactly why disk space sometimes doesn't free up after you delete a huge log file: a service still has it open, and lsof | grep deleted is the standard way to find and fix it (restart the service, or truncate the file in place with : > /path/to/file).

It also explains two real constraints people run into. Hard links can't cross filesystems (a different mounted device has an entirely separate inode table, so an inode number from one has no meaning on another — ln will refuse with "Invalid cross-device link"), while symlinks can, because a symlink is just a path string, resolved fresh every time something follows it. And hard links can't point at directories (in practice; . and .. are the only hard links the kernel itself makes for you) because allowing arbitrary directory hard links would make it possible to build a directory tree that contains itself, which breaks the basic recursive assumption nearly every tool relies on when walking the filesystem.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming cp preserves hard links. Plain cp of two hard-linked files produces two independent copies with separate inodes; cp -a (or --preserve=links with GNU cp's -l-aware mode) is what you need to keep them linked, which matters for backup tools where double-counting hard-linked data can silently inflate size estimates.
  • Deleting a symlink's target and being surprised the symlink "still exists." ls -l on a broken symlink will still show an entry (often highlighted in red by default shell colors) — the symlink file itself is fine; it's only resolving the link (opening, cat-ing, cd-ing into it) that fails.
  • Expecting du and df to agree after deleting a large file a process still holds open. df reports space as the kernel sees it (still allocated, because the inode's link count or open-file reference hasn't hit zero); du, which walks the visible directory tree, won't even see the deleted file anymore. The size discrepancy is real and is the single most common "where did my disk space go" support ticket on long-running servers.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a file, note its inode number with ls -i, then make one hard link and one symlink to it. Delete the original filename. Predict, then verify: which of the two remaining names still lets you read the content? Then open the hard-linked file with tail -f in one terminal, delete it with rm from another, and run df -h . followed by du -sh . in the directory — explain the numbers you see using the link-count model from this lesson.

docs.title: 05 · Users, Groups & the Permission Model
docs.text: rwxr-xr-x is one of the first things every new Linux user memorizes without necessarily understanding, and the gap between memorizing and understanding shows up the first time someone has execute permission on a directory but can't list its contents, or read permission on a file but can't open it in an editor they expect to work.

docs.title: UIDs, GIDs and the three permission classes
docs.text:
Every process and every file is tagged with a UID (user ID) and one primary GID (group ID), plus — for a user — any number of supplementary groups. The kernel doesn't actually know usernames like alice; /etc/passwd and /etc/group are just lookup tables mapping numbers to names for humans' benefit, and everything the kernel checks is numeric. You can see this directly: delete a user from /etc/passwd while their UID still owns files, and ls -l will print the bare number instead of a name, because the mapping is gone but the ownership tag on disk never changed.

Permissions are checked against three classes relative to the process making the request, not the file: owner (does the process's UID match the file's owner UID?), group (does any of the process's GIDs match the file's group?), and other (neither of the above). The kernel checks these in that exact order and stops at the first match — which has a real, sometimes-surprising consequence: if you own a file but your group permissions happen to be more restrictive than "other," you still get the owner row's permissions, not whichever row is most generous.

docs.title: Worked example: rwx means something different on directories
docs.text:
$ mkdir project && echo "secret content" > project/notes.txt
$ chmod 750 project
$ ls -ld project
drwxr-x--- 2 vinodkumarsigilipelli vinodkumarsigilipelli 60 Oct 22 23:31 project

$ ls project
notes.txt

$ chmod 311 project
$ ls -ld project
d-wx--x--x 2 vinodkumarsigilipelli vinodkumarsigilipelli 60 Oct 22 23:31 project

$ ls project
ls: cannot open directory 'project': Permission denied

$ cat project/notes.txt
secret content

(Real output from this course's lab VM, run as the directory's own owner throughout — there is no root bypass here.) At 750 (owner rwx, group r-x, other nothing), the owner can both list and traverse — unsurprising, since the owner's bits grant everything. The genuinely sharp case is 311 (-wx--x--x): no class has the read bit, not even the owner, so ls project fails for everyone, including the file's own owner — read permission on a directory is what lets getdents() (what ls/readdir() use) enumerate the names inside it, and losing it blocks that regardless of who you are. And yet cat project/notes.txt, naming the file directly rather than asking the directory to list its contents, succeeds — because reading a file's content is governed by that file's own permission bits, not its parent directory's, and the directory's execute bit alone is enough to resolve a known path through it. (Note that a tool like find project -name notes.txt would not work here — find has to enumerate the directory's entries to search by name, which needs the same read bit ls was missing; only a path you already know by name, typed directly, skips the enumeration step.)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The reason r and x mean such different things on a directory than on a regular file traces back to what a directory's content actually is: a list of (filename, inode-number) pairs (Lesson 4). Read permission on a directory lets a process call getdents() (what readdir()/ls ultimately use) and see that list. Execute permission on a directory is really "search" permission: it lets the kernel resolve a specific filename inside that directory into an inode, as one step of resolving a longer path like /home/vinod/project/notes.txt. These are genuinely independent capabilities — "see what's here" versus "look something specific up by name" — and the 311 example above is the clean demonstration: without read, ls has nothing to enumerate; without needing to enumerate, knowing the name and having execute/search permission on every directory in the path is enough to reach the file, whose own permission bits then decide whether you can actually read it.

umask is the other half of the model people memorize without internalizing: it's not a permission itself but a mask — a bitmask of permissions to strip from whatever a program requests when creating a new file. A typical default umask of 022 strips the group and other write bits: a program that calls open() asking for 0666 (read/write for everyone, the traditional default for new files) ends up with 0644 once the umask is applied, because 022 subtracted the write bits from group and other. This is why new files and new directories you create interactively usually come out 644/755 without you ever running chmod — the shell's inherited umask is doing it silently, and changing umask (in ~/.bashrc or system-wide in /etc/login.defs) changes the default for every file created afterward, not retroactively.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running chmod -R 777 to "fix" a permission problem. This doesn't just overshoot — it removes the execute bit's actual meaning on files (giving every file "execute" regardless of whether it's a script) and opens every file and directory to world write, which on a shared or internet-facing system is a real security hole, not just an untidiness.
  • Confusing "I own the file" with "I have the most permissive applicable bits." As shown above, the kernel checks owner/group/other in order and stops at the first match — a file you own but whose owner-bits are r-- will be read-only for you even if "other" on that same file happens to be rwx.
  • Forgetting that execute-without-read on a directory is a legitimate, intentional pattern (sometimes called a "blind" directory) — used so a process can reach a specific, known file path without being able to enumerate siblings. Seeing --x--x--x on a directory during an audit isn't automatically a misconfiguration.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create a directory containing three files. Set the directory to rwxr-x--- and change its group to one you're not a member of (or simulate by predicting). Predict, then verify with a second user account (or sudo -u) whether that second user can: (a) list the directory, (b) read a file inside it by exact name, (c) read a file inside it by tab-completing the name. Then check your own umask with umask -S, create a new file and a new directory, and explain their resulting permissions from the umask value alone.

docs.title: 06 · Advanced Permissions: SUID, SGID, Sticky Bit & ACLs
docs.text: The standard rwx × owner/group/other model (Lesson 5) can't express "let any user run this program with the file owner's privileges" or "let everyone create files here, but only the creator can delete their own" — both are common, real requirements, and both are handled by three special bits plus an extension mechanism that goes beyond the classic nine permission bits entirely.

docs.title: The three special bits
docs.text: SUID (set-user-ID, shown as s in the owner's execute position) makes a program run with the file owner's UID, not the invoking user's UID, for as long as that process runs. SGID (set-group-ID, same idea in the group execute position) does the equivalent for the group; on a directory specifically, SGID means something extra: new files created inside inherit the directory's group rather than the creating user's primary group — the standard way to make a shared team directory where everyone's files end up in the same group automatically. The sticky bit (shown as t in the other execute position) means something different again, and only matters on directories: it restricts deletion — inside a sticky directory, you can only delete or rename files you own, regardless of write permission on the directory itself.

docs.title: Worked example: passwd, a shared directory, and /tmp
docs.text:
$ ls -l /usr/bin/passwd
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 142552 Feb  3  2026 /usr/bin/passwd

$ ls -ld /tmp
drwxrwxrwt 12 root root 240 Oct 22 23:30 /tmp

$ mkdir team-shared && chmod 2775 team-shared
$ sudo chgrp testeng team-shared
$ ls -ld team-shared
drwxrwsr-x 2 vinodkumarsigilipelli testeng 40 Oct 22 23:32 team-shared

$ id
uid=501(vinodkumarsigilipelli) gid=1000(vinodkumarsigilipelli) groups=1000(vinodkumarsigilipelli),999(systemd-journal)

$ touch team-shared/report2.txt
$ ls -l team-shared/report2.txt
-rw-rw-r-- 1 vinodkumarsigilipelli testeng 0 Oct 22 23:32 team-shared/report2.txt

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) passwd is owned by root and carries the SUID bit (the s where you'd expect x) — which is why an unprivileged user running passwd can update /etc/shadow, a file only root can normally write. Without SUID, every user would need root access just to change their own password, which defeats the point of having unprivileged accounts at all; SUID lets the program temporarily act with elevated privilege while still being invoked by a normal user, and the program itself is responsible for only doing the one narrow, safe thing it was written to do (update the calling user's own password entry, nothing else). /tmp's permissions (rwxrwxrwt, that trailing t) show the sticky bit in the wild: everyone can create files in /tmp, but the sticky bit stops one user from deleting another user's temp files even though the directory itself is world-writable. chmod 2775 on team-shared sets SGID (the leading 2); id confirms this shell's primary group is still vinodkumarsigilipelli (gid 1000) — yet the file it creates, report2.txt, comes out owned by group testeng, the directory's group, not the creating process's primary group. That's SGID-on-a-directory working exactly as specified: inheritance happens regardless of what group the creating process would otherwise have used.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The kernel implements SUID/SGID by checking, at execve() time (the syscall that actually replaces a process's code with a new program), whether the target file has the SUID or SGID bit set. If so, instead of the new process keeping the calling process's real UID/GID as its effective UID/GID (the normal case — effective IDs are what permission checks actually use), the kernel sets the new process's effective UID/GID to the file's owner/group. The process's real UID (who actually invoked it) is preserved separately, which is how passwd and similar tools can tell "who is calling me" from "what privilege do I currently have" and behave accordingly rather than blindly trusting the elevated privilege for everything.

This mechanism is also exactly why SUID is treated as a security-sensitive feature rather than a convenience: any bug in a SUID-root binary is a potential privilege escalation path, because the bug now executes with root's effective UID regardless of who triggered it. This is why the Linux kernel, by default, refuses to honor the SUID bit on shell scripts (even though you can technically chmod u+s one) — a script's first line only names an interpreter, and there's a well-known race window between the kernel opening the script and the interpreter re-opening it, during which the file on disk could be swapped out from under the privilege check; compiled binaries don't have that two-step open. It's also why security audits specifically grep filesystems for unexpected SUID binaries (find / -perm -4000 -type f) — a SUID binary that shouldn't be there, or a legitimate one with a known vulnerable version, is one of the most direct routes from "a foothold as a normal user" to "root."

POSIX ACLs (setfacl/getfacl) exist for everything the owner/group/other model genuinely can't express at all: granting one specific additional user (not a whole group) read access to a file, for instance, without changing its owner or creating a new group just for that one grant. getfacl on a file with ACLs set shows the extra entries, and ls -l signals their presence with a trailing + after the permission string — a detail that's easy to miss and a common source of "why can this person read a file whose ls -l bits say they shouldn't be able to" confusion during audits.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Setting SUID on a shell script and being confused when it "doesn't work." As explained above, the kernel deliberately ignores SUID on interpreted scripts on most systems; if you need SUID behavior for a script's logic, the standard fix is a small compiled wrapper binary that is itself SUID and that execs the script non-SUID.
  • Confusing the sticky bit with SGID. They occupy similar-looking positions in ls -l output (t vs s in the "other" vs "group" execute slot) but do unrelated things — sticky restricts deletion, SGID affects group ownership inheritance (on directories) or effective GID (on executables).
  • Forgetting that chmod -R on a directory tree with SGID set recalculates the special bits per-file, often stripping them from regular files (which don't need SGID at all) while potentially leaving directories correct — always re-check with find dir -type d -perm -2000 after a bulk chmod if SGID inheritance matters.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Find every SUID and SGID binary on a Linux machine you control with find / -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null, pick three, and for each one explain in one sentence why it plausibly needs elevated privilege (or flag it as suspicious if you can't justify it). Then create a shared-group directory with SGID set, have two different users (or simulate with sudo -u) create files in it, and confirm both files end up in the same group despite the users having different primary groups.

docs.title: 07 · Processes 101: PIDs, fork/exec & the Process Tree
docs.text: Every running program on Linux is a process, and every process except one was created by exactly one other process calling fork(). Understanding that one mechanism — fork, then usually exec — explains where processes come from, why every process has a parent, and what "PID 1" means and why it matters so much that systems treat losing it as fatal.

docs.title: fork() and exec(): two different jobs, often used together
docs.text: fork() makes an almost-exact copy of the calling process: same memory contents, same open file descriptors, same environment — but a new PID, and a return value that tells the two now-separate processes apart (the child gets 0, the parent gets the new child's PID). Right after a fork, you have two processes running the same program. That's rarely what you actually want, which is why fork is almost always followed immediately by exec(): exec doesn't create a new process at all — it replaces the calling process's program code and memory with a different program, keeping the same PID. The combination — fork to get a new process, exec to make it run something else — is literally how your shell starts every command you type.

docs.title: Worked example: watching PIDs, PPIDs, and the process tree
docs.text:
$ ps -ef --forest | head -n5
UID          PID    PPID  C STIME TTY          TIME CMD
root           2       0  0 23:26 ?        00:00:00 [kthreadd]
root           3       2  0 23:26 ?        00:00:00  \_ [pool_workqueue_release]
root           4       2  0 23:26 ?        00:00:00  \_ [kworker/R-rcu_gp]
...

$ ps -p 1 -o pid,ppid,comm
    PID    PPID COMMAND
      1       0 systemd

$ echo "parent pid via \$\$: $$"
parent pid via $$: 10457

$ (echo "subshell BASHPID: $BASHPID"; ps -o pid,ppid,comm -p $BASHPID)
subshell BASHPID: 10472
    PID    PPID COMMAND
  10472   10457 ps

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) ps -ef --forest draws the tree by PPID: kthreadd (PID 2) is the kernel's own thread-spawning helper, parent to a long list of kernel worker threads — these aren't started by fork()/exec() from userspace at all, which is why they show up in brackets and have no real command line. ps -p 1 shows systemd as PID 1, with PPID 0 — the only process on the whole system whose parent is "the kernel itself" rather than another process, because PID 1 is the one process the kernel starts directly during boot (Lesson 2), and every other process traces its ancestry back to it through a chain of fork calls. The last two commands show something subtler and genuinely easy to get wrong: the subshell's own PID, read via $BASHPID (10472), correctly reports its parent as 10457 — the outer shell's $$ — when asked through ps, which queries the kernel's live process table directly. ($PPID as a bash variable, by contrast, is set once when a shell starts and is not guaranteed to update inside subshells the way you'd expect — a good reason to trust ps//proc over shell variables when the exact parent matters.) Also notice ps itself is reported as the COMMAND running under PID 10472, the subshell's own PID — bash optimized away a second fork for that trailing external command and had the subshell process exec directly into ps, reusing the same PID rather than forking yet again.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
fork() is implemented using copy-on-write: the kernel doesn't actually duplicate the parent's memory pages the instant you call fork. Instead, both parent and child start out sharing the exact same physical memory pages, marked read-only. Only when either process tries to write to a shared page does the kernel step in, actually copy that one page, and let the write proceed against the private copy. This is why fork() is cheap even for a process using gigabytes of memory — a classic use case (a database doing a fork()-based backup snapshot) relies on this directly: the child gets what's effectively an instant, consistent point-in-time view of the parent's memory, without the kernel physically copying anything unless and until something changes.

PID 1 is special for a reason that goes beyond just "it started first." The kernel gives PID 1 reaping responsibility for one case other processes can't opt out of: when any process's parent dies before the child does, the child is reparented to PID 1 (historically; on modern Linux, to the nearest surviving ancestor marked as a "subreaper," which is usually still PID 1 in practice). This matters because every process, when it exits, leaves behind an exit status that its parent is expected to collect with wait() — a process that has exited but hasn't been "waited for" yet is a zombie (state Z in ps), and it stays a zombie, consuming a slot in the process table, until its parent collects it. If the original parent is gone, PID 1 inherits the job of eventually reaping that orphan. This is also exactly why container images that run a single application directly as PID 1, without a real init system, can leak zombie processes under load — the application was never written to reap children it didn't directly spawn, and nothing else in the container is positioned to do it; it's the standard justification for tools like tini or dumb-init as a container's actual PID 1.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting $PPID inside a subshell or pipeline for exact process relationships. As shown above, it's a shell variable set at shell-start time, not a live kernel query — ps -o ppid= -p $BASHPID or reading /proc/self/status's PPid: field gives you the real, current answer.
  • Assuming kernel threads (shown in [brackets] by ps) are "processes" in the same sense as your shell or a web server. They share the kernel's address space, were never fork()ed from userspace, and don't have a command line — tools and monitoring that assume every PID has an argv will misbehave on them.
  • Running an application directly as PID 1 inside a container without reaping logic, then being confused by slowly accumulating zombie processes (visible as Z state in ps) that never get collected because nothing with reaping responsibility is watching for them.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run ps -ef --forest on any Linux machine and find the longest unbroken parent-child chain from PID 1 down to a leaf process you recognize (your own shell is a good target). Then run ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm | awk '$4 ~ /Z/' to check for zombies (there usually aren't any on a healthy desktop/server — if you find one, look up its parent with ps -o comm= -p <ppid> and consider why that parent might not be reaping it).

docs.title: 08 · Standard Streams, File Descriptors & Pipes
docs.text: command > file 2>&1 works for almost everyone almost immediately after seeing it once, and command 2>&1 > file quietly does something different — redirecting stderr to the terminal, not the file — which only makes sense once you know what a file descriptor actually is and what > and 2>&1 each really do to it.

docs.title: File descriptors: numbers, not files
docs.text: Every open file, socket, or pipe a process has is tracked by the kernel in a small per-process table, and the process refers to each entry by a small integer: the file descriptor. By convention, every process starts with three already open: 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout), and 2 (stderr). These aren't special in any way the kernel enforces — a program could write its normal output to fd 2 and nobody would stop it — they're a convention that shells, terminals, and virtually all Unix tools agree to honor: read input from 0, write normal output to 1, write errors/diagnostics to 2 so they can be told apart from the data even when both are flowing to the same terminal.

docs.title: Worked example: inspecting real file descriptors and a redirection-order gotcha
docs.text:
$ sleep 30 < /dev/null > /tmp/fdtest/out.log 2>&1 &
$ ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd
lr-x------ 1 vinodkumarsigilipelli vinodkumarsigilipelli 64 Oct 24 16:10 0 -> /dev/null
l-wx------ 1 vinodkumarsigilipelli vinodkumarsigilipelli 64 Oct 24 16:10 1 -> /tmp/fdtest/out.log
l-wx------ 1 vinodkumarsigilipelli vinodkumarsigilipelli 64 Oct 24 16:10 2 -> /tmp/fdtest/out.log

$ ls /nonexistent > cmd.log 2>&1
$ cat cmd.log
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': No such file or directory

$ ls /nonexistent 2>&1 > cmd2.log
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': No such file or directory
$ cat cmd2.log
$

(Real output from this course's lab VM; PID substituted for readability.) The /proc/<pid>/fd listing is not a metaphor — it's a literal, inspectable directory of symlinks, one per open file descriptor, showing exactly what each number currently points at: fd 0 to /dev/null (because the command redirected stdin there explicitly), and both fd 1 and fd 2 pointing at the same log file, because > file 2>&1 means "point fd 1 at file, then point fd 2 at whatever fd 1 is now pointing at." The two ls /nonexistent runs show why order matters: in the first, > cmd.log runs first (fd 1 now points at the file), then 2>&1 makes fd 2 point there too — so the error, which ls writes to fd 2, ends up in cmd.log. In the second, 2>&1 runs first, while fd 1 still points at the original terminal — so fd 2 is pointed at the terminal, and then > cmd2.log repoints fd 1 (and only fd 1) at the file. The error goes to fd 2, which is still the terminal, so it prints live and cmd2.log ends up empty. Redirections are processed strictly left to right, each one only affecting the descriptor named at that moment — there's no "redirect everything" shortcut hiding behind 2>&1.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A pipe (|) is the kernel creating an in-memory buffer with two file descriptor ends: one open for writing (wired to the left command's stdout) and one open for reading (wired to the right command's stdin). It's not a temporary file, and it's not line-buffered text sitting in a shell variable — it's a genuine kernel object with a fixed-size buffer (commonly 64 KiB on Linux). This has a real, sometimes-surprising consequence: if the writing end fills that buffer faster than the reading end drains it, the writer blocks — the write() syscall simply doesn't return until there's room — which is how yes | head -n1 can run yes (which would otherwise loop forever generating text) and still finish almost instantly: once head reads one line and exits, the pipe's read end closes, and the next time yes tries to write, it receives SIGPIPE and is killed by the kernel rather than spinning forever into a pipe nobody is reading.

2>&1 is implemented with the dup2() syscall: it doesn't make fd 2 an alias that tracks fd 1 forever, it makes fd 2, at that instant, point at whatever underlying open file fd 1 currently references — after which the two are independent again (closing one doesn't affect the other, and later redirecting fd 1 again doesn't move fd 2). That one-time-copy semantic, more than anything else, is what makes redirection order something you have to reason about left-to-right rather than treat as a single declarative block.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing 2>&1 > file when you meant > file 2>&1. As shown above, these are not equivalent, and the bug is silent — the command still runs, output still appears somewhere, just not all in the file you expected.
  • Treating a pipe as having unlimited buffering. A producer that writes much faster than a slow consumer reads will block on write() once the kernel pipe buffer fills — this is normal, correct backpressure, not a hang, but it surprises people debugging a "stuck" process that's actually just waiting for a slow reader downstream.
  • Assuming closing a shell variable or unsetting something closes a file descriptor. Descriptors are closed by explicit close() calls (or a process exiting, or exec without the close-on-exec flag being overridden) — they are kernel table entries, not shell-level state, which is exactly why /proc/<pid>/fd can inspect them from outside the process entirely.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Start any long-running command in the background (sleep 120 &), find its PID with $!, and inspect /proc/<pid>/fd to see its open descriptors. Then predict, then verify, the difference between command > out.log 2>&1 and command 2>&1 > out.log using a command that writes to both stdout and stderr (ls on one existing and one nonexistent path works well: ls /tmp /nonexistent).

docs.title: 09 · Package Management Internals: dpkg/APT vs RPM/DNF
docs.text: "Install this package" sounds like one action, but on Linux it's really at least three: unpack files to disk, record exactly which files belong to which package (so a later uninstall knows what to remove and nothing more), and verify the package's declared dependencies are satisfiable. Two package-management lineages dominate Linux: the Debian/Ubuntu family (dpkg + APT) and the Red Hat/Fedora family (rpm + DNF). They differ in file formats and tooling but solve the identical underlying problem the same structural way.

docs.title: The low-level tool vs the dependency-solving tool
docs.text: dpkg is the low-level tool that actually installs .deb files and maintains the on-disk database of what's installed — but it has no concept of fetching anything from the internet and will flatly refuse to install a package whose dependencies aren't already present. APT (apt/apt-get) sits above dpkg: it manages repository lists (/etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/), downloads .deb files, and crucially resolves dependency graphs — figuring out the full set of packages (and compatible versions) needed to satisfy what you asked for, then handing the actual installation work down to dpkg. The Red Hat lineage has the exact same split: rpm is the low-level installer/database tool (directly analogous to dpkg), and DNF (the successor to yum) is the repository-aware dependency resolver sitting above it (directly analogous to APT).

docs.title: Worked example: what a package really leaves on disk
docs.text:
$ dpkg -L curl | head -n10
/.
/usr
/usr/bin
/usr/bin/curl
/usr/bin/wcurl
/usr/share
/usr/share/doc
/usr/share/doc/curl
/usr/share/doc/curl/NEWS.Debian.gz
/usr/share/doc/curl/README.Debian

$ dpkg -S /usr/bin/curl
curl: /usr/bin/curl

$ dpkg -s curl | head -n8
Package: curl
Status: install ok installed
Priority: optional
Section: web
Installed-Size: 508
Maintainer: Ubuntu Developers <ubuntu-devel-discuss@lists.ubuntu.com>
Architecture: arm64
Multi-Arch: foreign

$ apt-cache depends curl | head -n4
curl
  Depends: libcurl4t64
  Depends: libc6
  Depends: zlib1g

(Real output from this course's Ubuntu 26.04 lab VM.) dpkg -L curl is the package's exact file manifest — every path dpkg will remove if you later run apt remove curl, and nothing more; this manifest, not a guess based on install location, is how uninstalling a package doesn't accidentally sweep up files some other package also happens to keep nearby. dpkg -S runs that lookup in reverse: given a path, which installed package owns it — indispensable when you find a file and need to know what put it there. dpkg -s is the package's status record: its declared metadata and, critically, the literal string install ok installed, which is dpkg's own state machine value, not just "yes/no installed" (a half-finished install, interrupted mid-way, shows a different status like install reinstreq, which is exactly what dpkg --configure -a is built to detect and fix). apt-cache depends shows the dependency graph edges APT has to satisfy — libcurl4t64, libc6, zlib1g — each of which has its own dependencies in turn, and APT's actual job is finding one consistent, available version of every package in that whole transitive closure.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Both dpkg and rpm maintain their installed-package records as flat local databases — dpkg's live under /var/lib/dpkg/ (the status file and info/ directory of per-package file lists and maintainer scripts); rpm's live in /var/lib/rpm/ (historically Berkeley DB, now commonly SQLite on modern Fedora/RHEL). An "install" isn't really one atomic operation from the kernel's point of view: it's unpacking an archive to disk and appending/updating rows in this local database, plus running any package-supplied maintainer scripts (postinst, preinst for .deb; %post, %pre scriptlets for .rpm) that do extra setup a plain file copy can't — creating a system user, enabling a systemd service, migrating a config file format. This is exactly why interrupting a package manager mid-operation (a killed apt process, a lost SSH session during dnf update) can leave a system in a genuinely inconsistent state: the database might record a package as installed while its maintainer script never finished running, which is what commands like dpkg --configure -a (replay unfinished maintainer scripts) and rpm --rebuilddb exist to repair.

Dependency resolution is, in the general case, an NP-hard constraint-satisfaction problem: given a universe of packages each with version-ranged dependencies and conflicts, find a consistent set that satisfies everything requested. Both APT (via its internal solver, or the newer libsolv-based backends some distros use) and DNF (via libsolv directly, shared with other distros including openSUSE's Zypper) solve this with SAT-style solvers rather than naive recursive descent, because naive dependency-chasing can get stuck in situations a real solver resolves cleanly: package A needs B >= 2.0, package C needs B < 2.0, and the solver has to recognize that A and C simply can't both be installed rather than install a broken partial result. The packaging format difference (.deb being ar archives of compressed tarballs plus metadata; .rpm being cpio archives with an RPM-specific header) is almost incidental compared to this shared solver architecture underneath both ecosystems.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Deleting files a package installed, by hand, instead of removing the package. This desyncs the package database from reality — dpkg/rpm still believe the file exists and "belongs" to that package, which can cause confusing failures on the next upgrade or a false sense that removing the package later cleaned everything up (it won't try to delete a file it can already see is gone, but anything you added in that location stays).
  • Assuming a package being "installed" means its setup fully completed. As covered above, maintainer scripts can fail or be interrupted independently of the file unpacking step — always check actual service state (Level 2) after installing something that's supposed to start a daemon, rather than trusting install exit code alone.
  • Mixing APT/dpkg repositories of different Ubuntu/Debian releases on one system ("Frankendebian") expecting it to "just work" because the package format is the same — the solver will often find a technically consistent combination, but one that mixes library ABI versions never tested together, which is a common cause of mysterious crashes that package-format compatibility alone doesn't protect against.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Pick a small package you have installed (or install one you don't need long-term, like curl or jq), and run dpkg -L <package> (or rpm -ql <package> on an RPM-based system) to see its full file manifest. Then run apt-cache depends <package> (or dnf repoquery --requires <package>) and, for just the first two dependencies listed, look up their dependencies in turn — by hand, you'll feel exactly why this needs an automated solver once a real application with dozens of transitive dependencies is involved.

docs.title: 10 · Project: Build and Boot a Minimal Root Filesystem
docs.text: Every lesson in this level talked about the filesystem hierarchy, permissions, and processes as properties of the system you're logged into. This project builds a second, completely independent root filesystem from nothing but a package tool and a network connection, and uses chroot to run commands inside it — which forces "what does an OS actually need before it's usable" to stop being abstract.

docs.title: What debootstrap actually does
docs.text: debootstrap is the tool Debian/Ubuntu installers use internally: given a target directory, a release codename, and a package mirror, it downloads and unpacks just enough .deb packages to produce a minimal, bootable-in-spirit root filesystem — without needing to actually boot anything. It runs in two stages: an initial unpack of core packages, then a second stage that runs inside the new filesystem via chroot, so that package postinst scripts (Lesson 9) execute in the correct environment rather than against the host.

docs.title: Building it
docs.text:
$ sudo debootstrap --variant=minbase --arch=arm64 noble /tmp/minirootfs http://ports.ubuntu.com/ubuntu-ports
I: Configuring libstdc++6:arm64...
...
I: Configuring apt...
I: Configuring libc-bin...
I: Base system installed successfully.

(Real output from this course's lab VM — this command genuinely downloads and assembles a working minimal Ubuntu 24.04 "Noble" filesystem; expect it to take a few minutes depending on your network.) --variant=minbase asks for the smallest useful set of packages rather than a full default install; --arch=arm64 matches this course's lab VM (use your own machine's architecture, or cross-build a different one, which is exactly how you'd prepare a root filesystem for, say, a Raspberry Pi from an x86 desktop).

docs.title: Entering it
docs.text:
$ sudo mount --bind /dev /tmp/minirootfs/dev
$ sudo mount -t proc proc /tmp/minirootfs/proc
$ sudo mount -t sysfs sys /tmp/minirootfs/sys

$ sudo chroot /tmp/minirootfs /bin/bash -c "
    cat /etc/os-release
    echo hostname-in-chroot: \$(hostname)
    echo whoami: \$(whoami)
    ls /bin | wc -l
    apt list --installed 2>/dev/null | wc -l
"
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04 LTS"
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="24.04"
VERSION="24.04 LTS (Noble Numbat)"
ID=ubuntu
hostname-in-chroot: lima-linuxlab
whoami: root
293
91

(Real output.) cat /etc/os-release reports Noble 24.04 — a different, self-contained distro release from the 26.04 LTS host VM this project is running on — proving the new root filesystem really is independent, not a view into the host's own files. hostname reports the host's hostname, lima-linuxlab — because plain chroot changes only which directory a process treats as /; it does not create a new UTS namespace (the kernel mechanism that isolates hostname), so the chrooted shell still sees the real machine's hostname. 293 binaries and 91 packages is the entire footprint of a "minimal" Debian-family Linux system — small enough to read through dpkg -l in a few minutes, which is itself worth doing once, just to see what's actually considered load-bearing.

docs.title: What breaks without the bind mounts, and why that's the lesson
docs.text:
$ sudo umount /tmp/minirootfs/proc /tmp/minirootfs/sys /tmp/minirootfs/dev
$ sudo chroot /tmp/minirootfs /bin/bash -c "ps aux"
Error, do this: mount -t proc proc /proc

$ sudo chroot /tmp/minirootfs /bin/bash -c "uname -a"
Linux lima-linuxlab 7.0.0-34-generic ... aarch64 aarch64 aarch64 GNU/Linux
$ uname -a
Linux lima-linuxlab 7.0.0-34-generic ... aarch64 GNU/Linux

(Real output.) Unmounting /proc and re-running ps inside the chroot fails outright — ps has nothing to read, because /proc isn't automatically present inside a chroot; it has to be deliberately mounted there, which is exactly why the earlier bind-mount step exists at all and why debootstrap's own second stage does the same thing internally. The second pair of commands is the project's real payoff: uname -a inside the chroot and on the host report the identical kernel release, 7.0.0-34-generic. chroot did not boot a new kernel, did not boot anything at all — the minimal root filesystem is running entirely on the one kernel the host machine was already running, with a different / underneath it. That's the whole mechanism behind chroot, and it's also most of the mechanism behind how container runtimes work before you add namespaces and cgroups on top (Level 3's namespaces lesson builds exactly that on top of this same foundation).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A chroot() syscall records a new "root directory" pointer in the calling process's kernel-level process descriptor; every subsequent path resolution that starts from / for that process (and, after fork(), its descendants) resolves relative to that recorded directory instead of the real filesystem root. Nothing about memory, networking, process visibility, users, or the kernel itself changes — which is precisely why plain chroot is not a security boundary (a well-known escape technique for a process running as root inside a chroot is to open a file descriptor to a directory outside it before the chroot call, then use that descriptor afterward) and why modern container tooling layers PID, network, mount, and user namespaces (Level 3) on top of the same chroot-style root-swapping to get real isolation.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting the bind mounts and assuming the rootfs is "broken." ps, df, networking tools, and anything reading /proc or /sys will fail or behave strangely without those filesystems explicitly mounted inside the chroot — this is expected, not a sign the build failed.
  • Treating chroot as a security sandbox. As covered above, it isolates the filesystem view only; a privileged process can escape it, and an unprivileged one can still see and potentially signal processes outside it, since there's no PID namespace involved.
  • Not cleaning up bind mounts before deleting the rootfs directory. rm -rf on a directory with /proc, /sys, or /dev still bind-mounted inside it can delete far more than intended (or fail oddly) — always umount each bind mount first.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Build your own minimal root filesystem with debootstrap (or pacstrap on Arch, or a manual rpm --root bootstrap on Fedora, if you'd rather use a different family). Chroot into it, confirm uname -a matches your host kernel exactly, then try running a statically-linked binary you copy in from outside versus a dynamically-linked one — the dynamic one will fail unless its required shared libraries also exist inside the chroot, which is a direct, hands-on demonstration of what "dependency" really means at the binary level, not just the package level from Lesson 9.

docs.title: Level 2 · Processes, Memory & Storage
docs.text:
Level 2 is about a system that's running, not just installed. You'll send real signals and watch processes change state, read /proc/<pid>/status to see what the kernel actually tracks about a process, trigger an OOM kill on purpose, partition and mount a disk with LVM, and write your own systemd unit files instead of only reading ones someone else wrote.

What was run, and what wasn't

Process, memory, disk and systemd examples in this level were run on a real Linux VM. Memory-pressure and OOM-killer behaviour depends on the kernel's overcommit settings and available RAM, so exact numbers (how much memory before the kill, which process is chosen) will differ on your machine — the mechanism shown is real, the specific numbers are this lab's, and the lessons say so.

Prerequisites: Level 1 (processes, permissions, the filesystem). You do not need root for most of this level; the lessons that do (LVM, OOM provocation) say so and suggest doing them in a disposable VM.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Process States, Signals & Job Control: running/sleeping/zombie/stopped, SIGTERM vs SIGKILL vs SIGSTOP, and why a zombie can't be killed.
  2. Scheduling: Nice, Priorities & the CFS: niceness vs real priority, how the Completely Fair Scheduler picks the next process to run.
  3. Memory Management: virtual address space, paging, page cache vs "free" memory, and provoking the OOM killer on purpose.
  4. Disks & Block Devices: partitions, LVM physical/volume/logical groups, and creating an ext4 vs xfs filesystem.
  5. Mounting, fstab & Network Filesystems: mount namespaces at a glance, /etc/fstab fields, bind mounts, and NFS basics.
  6. systemd Deep Dive: units, targets, the dependency graph, and systemd-analyze.
  7. Writing systemd Services & Timers: a real unit file, Restart=, and a timer that replaces a cron job.
  8. Logging & journald: structured logs, journalctl filters, and persistent vs volatile journals.
  9. Device Files, udev & /dev: character vs block devices, major/minor numbers, and how udev names a new device.
  10. Project: Diagnose a Resource-Starved System: a script that eats memory and CPU on purpose, and the diagnostic pass that finds and explains it.

docs.title: After Level 2
docs.text: Level 3 goes outward: how Linux resolves a name and routes a packet, firewalls old and new, SSH's actual protocol, SELinux/AppArmor, and the namespaces and cgroups that containers are built from.

docs.title: 01 · Process States, Signals & Job Control
docs.text: "Just kill it" is the standard troubleshooting reflex, and it works often enough that people rarely stop to ask why kill -9 sometimes does nothing to a process that's clearly still showing up in ps. The answer is in the process's state, and in what a signal actually is: not a forceful interrupt in the way the name suggests, but a flag the kernel sets that the target process (if it's even in a position to) gets a chance to act on.

docs.title: The states ps shows you
docs.text: ps -o stat reports a single letter (sometimes with modifiers) for each process: R (running or runnable — on a CPU or waiting for one), S (sleeping, waiting on some event — I/O, a timer, a lock — and not consuming CPU meanwhile), D (uninterruptible sleep, almost always waiting on disk I/O — notoriously cannot be killed, not even with SIGKILL, until the I/O completes, because the kernel considers the operation in a state too delicate to abort safely), T (stopped, by a job-control or SIGSTOP-family signal), and Z (zombie — the process has exited, but its parent hasn't yet collected its exit status).

docs.title: Worked example: stopping, continuing, and a real zombie
docs.text:
$ sleep 60 &
$ ps -o pid,stat,comm -p $!
    PID STAT COMMAND
 242322 S    sleep

$ kill -STOP $!
$ ps -o pid,stat,comm -p $!
    PID STAT COMMAND
 242322 T    sleep

$ kill -CONT $!
$ ps -o pid,stat,comm -p $!
    PID STAT COMMAND
 242322 S    sleep

$ ps -p 2181 -o pid,ppid,stat,comm
    PID    PPID STAT COMMAND
   2181       1 Ss   sshd-session

$ ps -p 2188 -o pid,ppid,stat,comm
    PID    PPID STAT COMMAND
   2188    2181 Z    sshd

$ cat /proc/2188/status | grep -E "^(Name|State|PPid)"
Name:   sshd
State:  Z (zombie)
PPid:   2181

(Real output from this course's lab VM — the zombie above wasn't staged; it's a genuine leftover sshd child from an earlier SSH session on this machine, caught in the act.) kill -STOP/-CONT flip the target between S and T directly and observably — this is exactly what shell job control's Ctrl-Z (stop) and fg/bg (continue) do under the hood. The zombie is the more interesting case: PID 2188's state is unambiguously Z (zombie), its parent (2181, sshd-session) is still alive and well, and yet nothing you run against PID 2188 itself — kill -9 2188 included — will make it disappear. A zombie has no running code left to signal; it's a corpse of accounting information (exit status, resource usage) that the kernel is required to keep until something calls wait() on it. The only way to clear a zombie is for its parent to reap it (call wait()/waitpid()) — or for the parent itself to die, which reparents the zombie to PID 1 (Lesson 7, Level 1), whose entire job includes reaping orphans like this one.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Signals are, at the implementation level, bits set in a per-process pending-signal bitmask, checked by the kernel at specific points (returning from a syscall, returning from an interrupt) rather than delivered instantly the moment kill() is called. A process can block a signal (defer its delivery), ignore it, or install a handler (a function the kernel calls instead of taking the default action) — for every signal except two: SIGKILL (9) and SIGSTOP (19) are deliberately unblockable and unhandleable, which is exactly why they're the reliable "last resort" signals; every other signal's behavior, including the supposedly-polite SIGTERM (15), is only a request that a well-behaved process chooses to honor by exiting cleanly, and a process that's hung, ignoring signals, or stuck in uninterruptible sleep (D state, usually deep in a kernel-level I/O wait) can simply not respond to SIGTERM or even SIGKILL until the kernel operation it's blocked on completes on its own.

This is also why kill -9 has a reputation as "the nuclear option" rather than the correct default: because the process gets no chance to run its own exit handler, open files aren't necessarily flushed cleanly, temp files aren't cleaned up, and locks aren't released gracefully — SIGTERM first, giving the application a chance to shut down in an orderly way, with SIGKILL only as the fallback when SIGTERM is ignored, is the standard and correct escalation (and is literally what systemd does to a service that won't stop, after TimeoutStopSec expires — Level 2's systemd lessons return to this).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming kill -9 always works immediately.
