It does not against a zombie (there's no process left to kill) and does not against a process stuck in D state (uninterruptible sleep) until the underlying I/O resolves — in both cases the process will appear to "ignore" SIGKILL, which is a real and diagnosable state, not a bug in kill.
  • Confusing a zombie process with a resource leak you need to urgently fix by force. A few short-lived zombies awaiting reaping are completely normal; what matters is whether the parent eventually reaps them. A large, growing number of permanent zombies under one parent is the real signal of a bug — that parent isn't calling wait() at all.
  • Sending SIGSTOP to a process and forgetting about it. A stopped process holds onto any resources it had (memory, open files, locks) indefinitely, invisible in top's CPU column (it's not consuming any), until someone remembers to SIGCONT it or kills it outright.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Start a sleep 120 & job, and in order: check its STAT with ps, stop it with kill -STOP, confirm the state changed, continue it with kill -CONT, confirm it changed back, then let it finish naturally or kill it. Separately, search your own system for zombies with ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm | awk '$3 ~ /Z/'; if you find one, identify its parent and form a hypothesis for why that parent hasn't reaped it yet.

docs.title: 02 · Scheduling: Nice, Priorities & the CFS
docs.text: "Nice" is a strange name for a number that goes from -20 to 19, until you learn where it comes from: a higher value means you're being more generous — more "nice" — to everyone else on the system, by asking for a smaller share of the CPU. It's one knob, among several the kernel actually uses, and the gap between what you set and what the kernel does with it is where most of the confusion about process scheduling lives.

docs.title: nice and real priority are not the same number
docs.text: nice is the number you set, from -20 (most aggressive, highest claim on the CPU) to 19 (most accommodating, lowest claim). It is not what the kernel schedules against directly — the scheduler works with an internal, kernel-level priority derived from nice (and, for Linux's default scheduler, from a weight table used to compute how much virtual runtime a process accumulates). ps -o ni,pri shows both: ni is the number you set, pri is procps's view of the resulting kernel-level priority.

docs.title: Worked example: setting and changing niceness on real processes
docs.text:
$ nice -n 10 sleep 5 &
$ ps -o pid,ni,pri,comm -p $!
    PID  NI PRI COMMAND
 244284  10   9 sleep

$ sleep 5 &
$ ps -o pid,ni,pri,comm -p $!
    PID  NI PRI COMMAND
 244287   0  19 sleep

$ renice -n 15 -p 244287
244287 (process ID) old priority 0, new priority 15
$ ps -o pid,ni,pri,comm -p 244287
    PID  NI PRI COMMAND
 244287  15   4 sleep

$ chrt -p $$
pid 244269's current scheduling policy: SCHED_OTHER
pid 244269's current scheduling priority: 0

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) Default niceness is 0, reported here as PRI 19; asking for nice -n 10 dropped the reported priority to 9, and renice-ing a running process from 0 to 15 dropped its priority further to 4 — in this ps output, lower PRI consistently tracks higher (less favorable) nice. renice is the proof that niceness isn't a one-time launch-time setting: you can lower (be nicer) or, as root, raise the priority of any already-running process at any time, which is exactly what you'd reach for to deprioritize a batch job that's already hogging CPU without having to restart it. chrt -p shows the scheduling policy for the current shell: SCHED_OTHER, the default time-shared policy almost every normal process uses — Linux also supports real-time policies (SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR) for processes that need deterministic, priority-based preemption instead of fair time-sharing, used by things like audio processing or industrial control software where "fair" isn't the goal, "on time" is.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The default Linux scheduler for SCHED_OTHER processes is the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) (as of recent kernels, CFS's accounting has been reworked under the "EEVDF" scheduling class, but the fairness goal and the nice-to-weight relationship described here still hold). CFS doesn't use fixed time slices doled out round-robin; it tracks each process's virtual runtime — accumulated CPU time, scaled by a weight derived from its nice value — and always picks the process with the smallest virtual runtime to run next. A process with a less favorable (higher) nice value accumulates virtual runtime faster for the same real CPU time, which means it gets picked less often relative to others — nice values map onto actual CPU share through a fixed weight table where each nice-value step is roughly a 10% change in CPU share relative to its neighbor, not a linear "nice 10 gets 10% less" relationship.

This design is also why CFS is called "completely fair" with a straight face even though it's constantly making processes wait: fairness here means "no process accumulates a disproportionate share of actual CPU time relative to its weight," enforced continuously via a red-black tree keyed by virtual runtime (so "find the process with the least runtime so far" is an efficient tree lookup, not a linear scan) — not "every process gets an equal, fixed timeslice" the way older round-robin schedulers worked. Real-time policies (SCHED_FIFO/SCHED_RR) sit entirely outside this fairness model: any runnable real-time-scheduled process will always preempt any SCHED_OTHER process, regardless of nice value, which is exactly the point — and exactly why a buggy real-time process that never blocks or yields can starve an entire system, a well-known hazard that's part of why real-time scheduling privileges are normally restricted to root.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting a precise, linear relationship between nice value and CPU percentage. The actual effect depends on what else is runnable at the same time and the weight table's (roughly multiplicative, not linear) scaling — nice is a relative claim on CPU among competing processes, not an absolute percentage guarantee, and a nice-19 process with the CPU all to itself still gets 100% of it.
  • Setting real-time priority (chrt -f/chrt -r) on a process "to make it faster" without understanding starvation risk. A real-time process that spins without yielding can lock out everything else on that CPU, including, in bad cases, the kernel's own housekeeping work — this is a sharp tool, not a faster version of nice.
  • Forgetting that lowering niceness (toward -20, a higher CPU claim) requires root, while raising it (toward 19, being "nicer") doesn't — an unprivileged user can deprioritize their own processes freely but can't grab a bigger CPU share without elevated privilege, which is a deliberate anti-abuse design, not an arbitrary limitation.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Launch two CPU-bound loops at the same time (yes > /dev/null & twice, or any busy-loop you like) on a single-core-limited cgroup or VM so they actually compete for the same CPU. Renice one of them to 19 and watch top's CPU% column for both over the next several seconds — predict the rough proportion before you look.

docs.title: 03 · Memory Management: Virtual Memory, Paging & the OOM Killer
docs.text: free -h's "free" column being tiny while "available" stays large confuses nearly everyone the first time they look closely, and "why did the OOM killer pick that process" is one of the most common real incident-review questions on any team running Linux in production. Both come from the same underlying model: virtual memory, the page cache, and what the kernel does when physical memory genuinely runs out.

docs.title: Virtual memory, in one paragraph
docs.text: Every process sees its own private virtual address space — a process's pointers are addresses in that private space, not physical RAM addresses. The kernel's page tables map chunks of that virtual space (pages, 4 KiB on most Linux systems) to physical memory pages, translated by the CPU's memory-management unit on every access. This indirection is what makes multiple processes safely share one machine without being able to read each other's memory by accident, what makes fork()'s copy-on-write trick (Lesson 7, Level 1) possible, and what lets the kernel page infrequently-used memory out to swap (if configured) without any program needing to know.

docs.title: Worked example: a real, deliberate, cgroup-scoped OOM kill
docs.text:
$ free -h
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           3.8Gi       552Mi       1.0Gi       1.1Mi       2.5Gi       3.3Gi
Swap:             0B          0B          0B

$ sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=100M --unit=memtest python3 /tmp/eatmem.py
Running as unit: memtest.scope; invocation ID: 71182bc0a74847d699c6e9d720e28170
allocated 10 MB
allocated 60 MB
(scope terminated)

$ sudo dmesg | tail -n4
[21467.552821] python3 invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0xcc0(GFP_KERNEL), order=0, oom_score_adj=0
[21467.556631]  oom_kill_process+0x2a4/0x350
[21467.558380] oom-kill:constraint=CONSTRAINT_MEMCG,...,task_memcg=/system.slice/memtest.scope,task=python3,pid=246692,uid=0
[21467.558406] Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 246692 (python3) total-vm:121648kB, anon-rss:102100kB, file-rss:6084kB, shmem-rss:0kB, UID:0 pgtables:272kB oom_score_adj:0

(Real output from this course's lab VM — this is a genuine OOM kill, not a simulated log line.) free -h on this VM shows 3.8 GiB total but no swap configured at all, which is itself common on cloud VMs and containers. systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=100M runs the Python script inside a fresh cgroup (Level 3 covers cgroups properly) capped at 100 MB — the script logs successful allocations up to 60 MB and then simply stops, because somewhere past that point it crossed the 100 MB limit and was killed outright, with no MemoryError exception ever reached in Python (SIGKILL doesn't give a process a chance to catch anything). dmesg shows the kernel's own account: constraint=CONSTRAINT_MEMCG says explicitly this was a cgroup-level OOM kill, scoped to memtest.scope, not a whole-system OOM event — and this distinction matters in practice: on a modern systemd-managed Linux system, almost every "OOM killed my process" incident you'll actually investigate is this cgroup-scoped kind, because systemd puts every service in its own cgroup and most services set (or inherit) a memory limit, rather than the rarer, more dramatic system-wide OOM kill that happens when the entire machine runs out of memory.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The gap between free's "free" and "available" columns is the page cache: the kernel keeps recently-read file data cached in RAM (shown in buff/cache) because reusing cached pages is far faster than re-reading from disk. Critically, this cached memory is not wasted and is not unavailable — it's reclaimable on demand the moment something actually needs it, which is exactly what available reports: free memory plus cache the kernel could drop immediately without hurting anything. A system reporting tiny "free" and large "available" is behaving completely normally; a system where both are small is the one actually worth worrying about.

The OOM killer is the kernel's response when it genuinely cannot satisfy a memory request — not when memory usage is merely high, but when reclaiming cache, compacting memory, and (if configured) swapping still aren't enough. Rather than letting the whole system deadlock or crash, it picks a process to sacrifice using a computed oom_score (readable per-process at /proc/<pid>/oom_score) that weighs memory usage heavily, and can be nudged with /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj (a critical system service might set this very negative to make itself a last resort; a known-disposable batch job might set it positive to volunteer first). Since Linux 4.19, the kernel ships oomd-style PSI (Pressure Stall Information, in /proc/pressure/) that lets userspace intervene before the kernel OOM killer has to act at all — reclaiming memory, pausing or killing lower-priority cgroups proactively — which is increasingly how systems avoid the kernel OOM killer's necessarily blunt, late, last-resort decision in the first place.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reading free's "free" column as "how much memory do I have left." It almost always understates real headroom, because it doesn't credit reclaimable cache — "available" is the number that answers that question.
  • Assuming the OOM killer always targets the process that's "obviously" using the most memory. The score also factors in oom_score_adj and some kernel heuristics around a process's own children — a cgroup-scoped kill, as shown above, can also take out a process that's well within the system's overall memory budget but has exceeded its own cgroup's specific limit, which is a completely different trigger from whole-system pressure.
  • Treating "no swap configured" as automatically bad or automatically fine. No swap means memory pressure turns into OOM kills faster (less room to relieve pressure), which is sometimes a deliberate choice (predictable latency, no swap thrashing) and sometimes an oversight — know which one is true for your system.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run free -h and explain, in your own words, why available is larger than free on your system right now using the page-cache model from this lesson. Then — only inside a disposable VM or container, never on a machine you care about — reproduce a scoped OOM kill with systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=50M -- python3 -c "[bytearray(10_000_000) for _ in range(100)]" and find the resulting kill in dmesg; identify whether dmesg reports CONSTRAINT_MEMCG (cgroup-scoped, like this lesson's example) or a whole-system constraint, and explain the difference.

docs.title: 04 · Disks & Block Devices: Partitions, LVM & Filesystems
docs.text: A disk, a partition, and a filesystem are three different layers that get flattened into "my C: drive" thinking if you've never had to grow storage past what a single physical disk gives you. LVM exists specifically to break the assumption that a filesystem has to live on one unresizable chunk of one physical disk, and the clearest way to understand it is to build one from nothing but a couple of plain files.

docs.title: Partitions, then LVM, on top of raw block devices
docs.text: A block device (/dev/vda, /dev/sda, /dev/nvme0n1...) is the kernel's name for something that can be read and written in fixed-size blocks — a real disk, but also, as this lesson demonstrates, a loopback-mounted plain file. A partition divides one block device into fixed regions (/dev/vda1, /dev/vda2...) at creation time; resizing later means shuffling data to make room, which is exactly the rigidity LVM (Logical Volume Manager) exists to remove. LVM inserts a layer of indirection: one or more physical volumes (PVs — a partition or whole disk) are pooled into a volume group (VG), and logical volumes (LVs) are carved out of that pool's total space, not tied to any one underlying PV. An LV can span multiple physical disks, and growing it later is a software operation against the VG's free space, not a disk-geometry problem.

docs.title: Worked example: building LVM across two disks from scratch
docs.text:
$ sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=disk1.img bs=1M count=512
$ sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=disk2.img bs=1M count=512
$ LOOP1=$(sudo losetup -f --show disk1.img)
$ LOOP2=$(sudo losetup -f --show disk2.img)
$ echo "$LOOP1 $LOOP2"
/dev/loop0 /dev/loop1

$ sudo pvcreate $LOOP1 $LOOP2
  Physical volume "/dev/loop0" successfully created.
  Physical volume "/dev/loop1" successfully created.

$ sudo vgcreate demovg $LOOP1 $LOOP2
  Volume group "demovg" successfully created
$ sudo vgs
  VG     #PV #LV #SN Attr   VSize    VFree
  demovg   2   0   0 wz--n- 1016.00m 1016.00m

$ sudo lvcreate -n demolv -L 800M demovg
  Logical volume "demolv" created.

$ sudo mkfs.ext4 -q /dev/demovg/demolv
$ sudo mount /dev/demovg/demolv /mnt/demolv
$ df -h /mnt/demolv
Filesystem                 Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/demovg-demolv  770M  224K  714M   1% /mnt/demolv

(Real output from this course's lab VM — two 512 MB loopback-mounted plain files were made to behave exactly like two physical disks.) vgs shows the pool's total usable size, 1016.00m — slightly less than the raw 1024 MB (2×512 MB) because LVM reserves metadata space on each PV. The logical volume, demolv, was created at 800M — larger than either individual loop device (512 MB each), which is only possible because the VG pools both PVs' space together; an ordinary partition could never do this. The resulting device, /dev/mapper/demovg- demolv, is what gets formatted and mounted exactly like any normal block device — mkfs.ext4 and mount have no idea (and don't need to know) that the space underneath is actually spread across two separate files.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
LVM is implemented on top of the kernel's device-mapper framework: /dev/mapper/demovg-demolv is not a "real" block device backed by one contiguous span of disk — it's a virtual device whose I/O requests the kernel remaps, according to a mapping table lvcreate wrote, onto specific extents on the underlying physical volumes. This is the same device-mapper machinery that implements LVM snapshots (copy-on-write extent tracking), disk encryption (dm-crypt, which Level 3's namespaces-and-security material touches indirectly), and software RAID (dm-raid) — LVM is one consumer of a general-purpose block-remapping layer, not a special case bolted directly into the filesystem code.

The filesystem (ext4 here) sits entirely above this and is, by design, unaware of any of it: mkfs.ext4 just sees a block device of a given size and lays out its own structures (superblock, inode tables, block groups) onto it, exactly as it would onto a plain partition. This separation of concerns — device-mapper handles "where do these logical blocks actually live," the filesystem handles "how are files organized within this block range" — is what makes LVM snapshots, online resizing (lvextend followed by resize2fs or xfs_growfs), and moving a live logical volume between physical disks (pvmove) all possible without the filesystem driver needing to know anything changed underneath it, beyond a resize notification.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Resizing the logical volume and forgetting to resize the filesystem on top of it. lvextend only changes how much block space the LV occupies; the filesystem still thinks it's the old size until you also run resize2fs (ext4) or xfs_growfs (XFS, which only grows, never shrinks) — a very common "I grew my disk but df still shows the old size" support question.
  • Removing a physical volume that still has extents in use. vgreduce/pvremove on a PV that's still backing live data will fail safely (LVM checks this), but assuming you can freely detach any PV from a VG without first migrating its data (pvmove) is a common and avoidable mistake.
  • Confusing "online" resize capability with filesystem shrink capability. Most filesystems can be grown online without unmounting; shrinking is far more restrictive (ext4 can shrink but usually needs to be unmounted first; XFS cannot shrink at all) — plan storage layouts assuming shrinking will be hard or impossible.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Repeat this lesson's loopback LVM setup yourself (it's entirely safe — nothing touches real disks), then grow the logical volume with lvextend -L +200M demovg/demolv followed by resize2fs /dev/demovg/demolv, and confirm with df -h that the mounted filesystem actually grew. Clean up afterward with umount, lvremove, vgremove, pvremove, and losetup -d on both loop devices, in that order, and explain why that order matters.

docs.title: 05 · Mounting, fstab & Network Filesystems
docs.text: "Mounting" a filesystem is the operation that connects a block device's (or network share's, or bind-mounted directory's) contents into the single tree rooted at / (Level 1, Lesson 3) at some chosen point. /etc/fstab is just a declarative list of mounts to perform automatically at boot, and once you've seen its fields and one non-obvious mount type (a bind mount) done by hand, the file stops being a wall of cryptic options.

docs.title: Reading /etc/fstab
docs.text:
$ cat /etc/fstab
LABEL=cloudimg-rootfs   /    ext4   discard,commit=30,errors=remount-ro 0 1
LABEL=BOOT  /boot   ext4    defaults    0 2
LABEL=UEFI  /boot/efi   vfat    umask=0077  0 1

(Real /etc/fstab from this course's lab VM.) Each line has six fields: the device (here identified by filesystem label, which survives a device renumbering /dev/vda1 → /dev/vda2 in a way a hardcoded path wouldn't), the mount point, the filesystem type, a comma-separated options list, a legacy dump flag (almost always 0 now — most systems don't use the old dump backup utility), and an fsck pass number (0 = never check; 1 for the root filesystem, checked first; 2 for everything else, checked after root). findmnt shows the live, currently-active view of the same information, which can differ from fstab if something was mounted by hand after boot rather than declared there:

$ findmnt /
TARGET SOURCE    FSTYPE OPTIONS
/      /dev/vda1 ext4   rw,relatime,discard,errors=remount-ro,commit=30

docs.title: Worked example: a real bind mount
docs.text:
$ sudo mkdir -p /srv/source /srv/target
$ sudo bash -c "echo original-content > /srv/source/file.txt"
$ sudo mount --bind /srv/source /srv/target
$ cat /srv/target/file.txt
original-content
$ mount | grep "srv/target"
/dev/vda1 on /srv/target type ext4 (rw,relatime,discard,errors=remount-ro,commit=30)

(Real output.) A bind mount doesn't involve a different filesystem or device at all — it makes the same directory's contents visible at a second path simultaneously. Notice mount's own output: it still reports the source as /dev/vda1, the same device root lives on, because a bind mount isn't a new filesystem instance, it's an additional mount-table entry pointing the kernel's path resolution at an existing directory's inode from a second location. Writes through either path affect the same underlying files — this is exactly the mechanism container runtimes use to expose a host directory inside a container's filesystem namespace, and it's what Level 2's package-management and Level 1's filesystem lessons both assumed was happening "underneath" without naming it.

docs.title: Worked example: a real NFS export and mount, loopback
docs.text:
$ sudo mkdir -p /srv/nfsshare
$ echo shared-via-nfs | sudo tee /srv/nfsshare/greeting.txt
$ echo "/srv/nfsshare 127.0.0.1(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,no_root_squash)" | sudo tee /etc/exports
$ sudo exportfs -ra
$ sudo systemctl restart nfs-kernel-server

$ sudo mount -t nfs 127.0.0.1:/srv/nfsshare /mnt/nfsclient
$ cat /mnt/nfsclient/greeting.txt
shared-via-nfs
$ mount | grep nfsclient
127.0.0.1:/srv/nfsshare on /mnt/nfsclient type nfs4 (rw,relatime,vers=4.2,rsize=524288,wsize=524288,
  proto=tcp,sec=sys,clientaddr=127.0.0.1,...)

(Real output — an actual NFS server and client, running against each other over loopback on this course's lab VM.) /etc/exports is the NFS server's own version of a declarative mount list — one line per shared directory, naming which clients may mount it (127.0.0.1 here, but normally a subnet or hostname) and with what options: rw (read-write), sync (acknowledge writes only once actually committed, the safe default), no_subtree_check (skip an expensive consistency check most modern setups don't need), no_root_squash (don't remap the client's root user to an unprivileged one — fine for this loopback demo, a real security consideration on a real network). mount's output on the client side shows it negotiated NFSv4.2 automatically and reports real protocol-level details — read/write buffer sizes, the TCP transport, the security mode — that only exist because this is a real network filesystem conversation, not a local block device.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: All three mount types in this lesson — a normal disk mount, a bind mount, and NFS — go through the same kernel entry point, the VFS (Virtual Filesystem Switch): a common interface every filesystem driver implements (open, read, write, readdir...), which is exactly why cat and ls work identically whether the path underneath happens to be ext4, a bind-mounted directory, or a remote NFS export. The VFS keeps a tree of mount structures, and mounting is fundamentally the operation of grafting one filesystem's root (or, for a bind mount, an arbitrary existing directory) onto a path in that tree. A bind mount is the simplest possible case — the "filesystem" being grafted in is just another part of the same already-mounted filesystem, reached by inode rather than by a new block device. NFS is the most elaborate case: the NFS client driver, instead of talking to a local block device, serializes each VFS operation into an RPC call sent over the network to the NFS server, which performs the real read()/write() against its own local filesystem and returns the result — the client-side application code calling read() has no idea its request just went over a network at all.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting that a bind mount of a directory doesn't automatically propagate newly-created mounts inside it (in the default private-mount mode) — nested mounts created after the bind mount was established may not be visible on the other side unless shared/mount-propagation options are explicitly set.
  • Editing /etc/fstab with a typo and rebooting without testing first. A broken fstab entry for a non-root filesystem can leave the system booting into an emergency shell rather than finishing boot — mount -a (which reads and attempts every fstab entry without rebooting) is the safe way to test a new line before trusting it to a reboot.
  • Using no_root_squash on a real, multi-host NFS export without understanding the exposure. It means any client machine's root user can act as root on the server's exported files — reasonable on an isolated loopback demo like this lesson's, a real risk on an actual multi-tenant network.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Create your own bind mount of any directory onto an empty one, write a file through the new mount point, and confirm (via the original path) that it's the same underlying storage, not a copy. Then, if you have a second machine or VM available, repeat this lesson's NFS export against it instead of loopback, and compare mount's reported protocol version and options to what you saw here.

docs.title: 06 · systemd Deep Dive: Units, Targets & Dependencies
docs.text: systemctl status and systemctl restart get most people through a normal day, but "why won't this service start," "what is it actually waiting on," and "what does multi-user.target even mean" all need the model underneath those two commands: units, targets, and the dependency graph systemd resolves to decide what starts, in what order, and when.

docs.title: Units and targets
docs.text: A unit is systemd's generic word for "a thing it manages" — a .service (a daemon or one-shot command), a .mount (a filesystem mount point), a .socket (a listening socket, which can start its service lazily on first connection), a .timer (Lesson 7's scheduled-trigger mechanism), and several other types. A target is a special unit that exists purely to group other units as a synchronization point — multi-user.target doesn't "do" anything itself; it's the named milestone that "normal multi-user operation is ready" maps onto, and other units declare WantedBy=multi-user.target to say "start me as part of reaching that milestone," which is the mechanism behind systemctl enable.

docs.title: Worked example: a real unit file and its real dependency tree
docs.text:
$ systemctl get-default
graphical.target

$ systemctl cat ssh.service
# /usr/lib/systemd/system/ssh.service
[Unit]
Description=OpenBSD Secure Shell server
Documentation=man:sshd(8) man:sshd_config(5)
After=network.target nss-user-lookup.target auditd.service
ConditionPathExists=!/etc/ssh/sshd_not_to_be_run

[Service]
ExecStartPre=/usr/sbin/sshd -t
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/sshd -D $SSHD_OPTS
ExecReload=/usr/sbin/sshd -t
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID
KillMode=process
Restart=on-failure
Type=notify

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Alias=sshd.service

$ systemctl list-dependencies ssh.service --no-pager | head -n8
ssh.service
● ├─-.mount
● ├─ssh.socket
○ ├─sshd-keygen.service
● ├─system.slice
● └─sysinit.target
●   ├─apparmor.service
●   ├─blk-availability.service

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) The [Unit] section's After= line is an ordering constraint, not a dependency by itself: it says "if both of us are going to run, start network-related units first," but says nothing about whether ssh.service actually needs them — that's what Wants=/Requires= (not present here, because SSH is deliberately tolerant of starting without a fully-ready network) would express. ConditionPathExists=!... is a runtime gate that can skip starting the unit entirely without that counting as a failure. [Install]'s WantedBy=multi-user.target is the line systemctl enable acts on: enabling creates a symlink so that reaching multi-user.target pulls this service in. list-dependencies walks the actual resolved graph for this unit — notice ssh.socket appears (systemd's socket-activation companion unit) and sysinit.target pulls in a long list of early-boot units this service transitively depends on reaching first.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
systemd starts units in parallel wherever the dependency graph allows it, which is the single biggest reason it boots faster than older sequential init systems — if two units have no ordering relationship to each other, there's no reason to make one wait for the other. After=/Before= express pure ordering; Wants=/Requires= express the actual pull-in relationship (whether reaching the target should bring the other unit along at all), and Requires= additionally propagates failure (if a strictly required unit fails, the dependent unit is stopped too) while Wants= doesn't. systemd computes a full directed graph from all of this across every loaded unit and runs a topological-ish parallel scheduler over it — which is also exactly why a cyclic dependency (A Requires= B, B Requires= A) is a real, specific failure systemd detects and reports, rather than something that just hangs silently.

Type= in [Service] tells systemd how to know the service actually finished starting, which is more subtle than "the process exists." Type=simple (the default) considers the service started the instant ExecStart's process is forked — fine for a process that's immediately ready, wrong for one with real startup work to do. Type=notify (used by ssh.service above) requires the program to explicitly call sd_notify(READY=1) via the systemd notification protocol once it's genuinely ready to serve, which is why services using it can be relied on not to have clients connect to them a half-second too early — something Type=simple can't guarantee at all.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating After= as if it implies a dependency. As shown above, it's pure ordering — a unit can be ordered After= something that never even runs, and will still start fine (just without waiting for it, since it never appears).
  • Editing a vendor-shipped unit file directly under /usr/lib/systemd/system/. Package updates overwrite it (the same fragility as grub.cfg and files under /usr, Level 1); the correct approach is systemctl edit <unit>, which creates an override file under /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/ that survives upgrades.
  • Forgetting systemctl daemon-reload after hand-editing a unit file. systemd caches parsed unit definitions; without a reload, systemctl restart on the changed unit will apply the old configuration, which looks exactly like the edit "didn't work."

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Pick any running service on a Linux system you control and run systemctl cat <service> followed by systemctl list-dependencies <service>. Identify one After= relationship and one Wants=/Requires= relationship in its unit file (or its drop-ins, if it has none directly), and explain in your own words what would actually change in startup behavior if each were removed.

docs.title: 07 · Writing systemd Services & Timers
docs.text: Reading unit files is one skill; writing one that actually does what you intend, restarts the right way when it fails, and runs on the schedule you meant, is another. This lesson writes, enables, and watches run a real service-and-timer pair — the modern systemd-native replacement for a cron job.

docs.title: Why a timer instead of cron
docs.text: A .timer unit paired with a .service unit gets you everything cron never had for free: the service's output goes through the normal journald pipeline (Lesson 8) instead of needing its own mail/logging setup, you can express dependencies (After=network-online.target if the job needs network), you get systemctl status showing you exactly when it last ran and whether it succeeded, and OnUnitActiveSec= (run N seconds after the previous run finished) avoids the classic cron problem of a 5-minute job scheduled every 5 minutes quietly overlapping itself if one run happens to take 6 minutes.

docs.title: Worked example: a real service and timer, running on a real schedule
docs.text:
$ cat /etc/systemd/system/heartbeat.service
[Unit]
Description=Course demo heartbeat

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/bin/bash -c "echo heartbeat at $(date -Is) >> /tmp/heartbeat.log"

$ cat /etc/systemd/system/heartbeat.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run heartbeat.service every 5 seconds

[Timer]
OnBootSec=2s
OnUnitActiveSec=5s
AccuracySec=1s

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

$ sudo systemctl enable --now heartbeat.timer
Created symlink '/etc/systemd/system/timers.target.wants/heartbeat.timer' → '/etc/systemd/system/heartbeat.timer'.

$ systemctl list-timers heartbeat.timer --no-pager
NEXT                        LEFT LAST                           PASSED UNIT            ACTIVATES
Sat 2026-10-24 16:20:13 IST   4s Sat 2026-10-24 16:20:08 IST 172ms ago heartbeat.timer heartbeat.service

$ cat /tmp/heartbeat.log
heartbeat at 2026-10-24T16:19:57+05:30
heartbeat at 2026-10-24T16:20:02+05:30
heartbeat at 2026-10-24T16:20:08+05:30

$ systemctl status heartbeat.service --no-pager
○ heartbeat.service - Course demo heartbeat
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/heartbeat.service; static)
     Active: inactive (dead) since Sat 2026-10-24 16:20:08 IST; 160ms ago
TriggeredBy: ● heartbeat.timer
    Process: 257214 ExecStart=/bin/bash -c ... (code=exited, status=0/SUCCESS)

(Real output — this timer genuinely fired three times, 5 seconds apart, over a 12-second observation window on this course's lab VM.) Type=oneshot tells systemd this service is meant to run to completion and exit, not stay running — the correct type for anything that does a unit of work and finishes, as opposed to a long-lived daemon. heartbeat.service's status after a run is inactive (dead) with status=0/SUCCESS — that's the expected, healthy end state for a oneshot, not a failure. OnBootSec=2s fired the first run 2 seconds after the timer was enabled; OnUnitActiveSec=5s fired every run after exactly 5 seconds from the previous run's completion — the log timestamps, 16:19:57, 16:20:02, 16:20:08, confirm the real 5-second cadence, not an approximation.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Timers are themselves ordinary systemd units with their own lifecycle, which is why systemctl list-timers, systemctl status <timer>, and the normal enable/disable/start/stop verbs all work on them exactly like any other unit — there's no separate "cron daemon" subsystem running in parallel; it's the same unit-and-dependency machinery from Lesson 6. OnCalendar= (not used in this example, but common for "every day at 3am"-style schedules) is parsed by systemd-analyze calendar, which is worth running against any calendar expression before trusting it, because the syntax, while powerful, is genuinely easy to get subtly wrong on the first attempt.

Restart= (used on the real ssh.service in Lesson 6 as Restart=on-failure) only applies to units systemd expects to keep running (Type=simple, notify, etc.) — it tells systemd what to do when the main process exits unexpectedly: on-failure restarts only on a non-zero exit or signal death, always restarts even on a clean exit, and no (the default) never restarts automatically. Combined with RestartSec= (how long to wait before retrying) and StartLimitBurst=/StartLimitIntervalSec= (how many restarts to allow within what window before giving up entirely), this is systemd's built-in crash-loop protection — without a start limit, a service that fails instantly on every start would otherwise restart in an unbounded, CPU-burning loop forever.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using Type=simple for a oneshot job. systemd will consider the unit "started" the instant the process forks, then immediately see it exit and may report it as failed or flapping, depending on Restart= settings — Type=oneshot exists specifically so "ran once and exited 0" reads as success, not as a crash.
  • Scheduling a frequent timer with OnCalendar= instead of OnUnitActiveSec= when you actually want "N seconds after the last run finished." OnCalendar= schedules by wall-clock time regardless of whether the previous run is still going, which can reintroduce the exact cron-overlap problem timers are meant to avoid.
  • Forgetting systemctl daemon-reload after creating or editing a unit file (the same mistake as Lesson 6) — a brand-new unit file won't even be visible to systemctl start/enable until systemd reloads its unit cache.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write your own .service/.timer pair that appends a timestamp to a log file every 10 seconds, enable it, watch it fire at least three times with journalctl -u <your-service> -f, then change OnUnitActiveSec= to a different interval, run daemon-reload, and confirm the new interval takes effect without needing to disable and re-enable the timer.

docs.title: 08 · Logging & journald: Structured Logs at the OS Level
docs.text: Grepping a text log file for a timestamp and a process name is something every Linux user eventually does, and journalctl can replace almost all of that grepping — because unlike a traditional syslog text file, each journal entry isn't a line of text at all; it's a structured record with named fields, several of which the kernel or systemd attached automatically, with no help from the program that logged the message.

docs.title: Worked example: one real log entry's actual structure
docs.text:
$ journalctl -u ssh.service -o json-pretty -n 1 --no-pager
{
    "MESSAGE" : "Stopped ssh.service - OpenBSD Secure Shell server.",
    "UNIT" : "ssh.service",
    "SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER" : "systemd",
    "_COMM" : "systemd",
    "_EXE" : "/usr/lib/systemd/systemd",
    "_UID" : "0",
    "_GID" : "0",
    "_BOOT_ID" : "1e8b72759fec45ccae08682c99b4d38f",
    "_SYSTEMD_UNIT" : "init.scope",
    "_SYSTEMD_CGROUP" : "/init.scope",
    "_TRANSPORT" : "journal",
    "__MONOTONIC_TIMESTAMP" : "2081453838",
    "_SOURCE_REALTIME_TIMESTAMP" : "1792718432683583",
    "CODE_FILE" : "src/core/job.c",
    "CODE_FUNC" : "job_emit_done_message",
    "CODE_LINE" : "815"
}

$ journalctl --disk-usage
Archived and active journals take up 8M in the file system.

$ ls -la /var/log/journal
drwxr-sr-x+  3 root systemd-journal 4096 Oct 22 23:26 .

(Real output from this course's lab VM — one genuine log entry, with nothing trimmed from its field list except a few internal sequence-number fields.) Notice how much of this record was not written by ssh.service or even by the message's apparent author: _UID, _GID, _BOOT_ID, _SYSTEMD_CGROUP, _SOURCE_REALTIME_TIMESTAMP were all stamped on by the journal itself at the moment the message was received, straight from kernel/process metadata — which is exactly why journalctl -u <unit> can filter perfectly by unit even for programs that never call any systemd-specific logging API: the filtering key comes from the environment the message was logged in, not from parsing the text of the message. CODE_FILE/CODE_FUNC/CODE_LINE show that this particular message came from a program using sd_journal_print()-family calls directly (which can tag source location), while a plain program writing to stdout/stderr under a service unit still gets the unit, UID, GID, cgroup and boot-ID fields for free, just not the source-location ones. /var/log/journal existing at all (as opposed to being absent) is this system's signal that journald is configured for persistent storage — logs survive a reboot — rather than the volatile-by-default /run/log/journal, which is wiped on every reboot.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
journald stores entries in its own binary, indexed file format (not plain text), which is what makes rich filtering (journalctl _UID=1000, journalctl _SYSTEMD_CGROUP=/system.slice/ssh.service, time-range queries) fast without re-parsing gigabytes of text on every query — closer to a lightweight structured database than a .log file. It still interoperates with traditional syslog: journald can forward everything to a classic rsyslog/syslog-ng daemon (common on systems that need, e.g., centralized log shipping with tooling that expects flat syslog), and it accepts input not just from sd_journal_print()-aware programs but from anything writing to stdout/stderr under a systemd unit, from the kernel's own ring buffer (journalctl -k, replacing dmesg for most interactive use), and from the traditional /dev/log socket for programs that only know how to speak classic syslog.

The persistent vs. volatile storage choice (Storage= in /etc/systemd/journald.conf, default auto, which persists if /var/log/journal exists and is volatile otherwise) matters more than it looks like it should: a volatile-only journal means every log from before the last reboot is simply gone — fine for a stateless container that ships logs elsewhere immediately, a real problem if you're trying to post-mortem a crash on a server that just restarted. journalctl --disk-usage and the SystemMaxUse=/RuntimeMaxUse= settings control how large the journal is allowed to grow before journald starts rotating out old entries — unlike unbounded flat text logs that can, in the worst case, fill a disk, journald is size-capped by design.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming journalctl without filters shows "everything" usefully. On a busy system it's an overwhelming firehose; -u <unit>, -b (this boot only, or -b -1 for the previous boot), --since/--until, and -p err (priority filter) are what make it actually usable day to day.
  • Not checking whether the journal is persistent before relying on post-incident logs. If /var/log/journal doesn't exist and Storage=auto, logs from before the crash that caused the reboot may already be gone by the time you go looking for them.
  • Forgetting that a service's own stdout/stderr go to the journal by default, so grepping an old-style /var/log/<app>.log file for an application that was migrated to run under systemd can turn up nothing, not because logging stopped, but because it moved to journalctl -u <that-service>.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run journalctl -u ssh.service -o json-pretty -n 1 (or any service you have) on a Linux machine you control, and identify at least three fields in the output that the journal attached automatically rather than the program itself. Then check whether your system's journal is persistent (ls /var/log/journal) and, if it's volatile-only, make it persistent by creating that directory with the correct ownership (systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix=/var/log/journal) and restarting systemd-journald.

docs.title: 09 · Device Files, udev & /dev
docs.text: /dev/vda, /dev/null, /dev/sda1 — these look like ordinary files, sit in an ordinary-looking directory, and yet none of them have any real content on disk the way /etc/fstab does. They're device files: a userspace handle onto a kernel driver, identified by a pair of numbers you can see with a plain ls -l.

docs.title: Character vs block, and the two numbers that identify a driver
docs.text: ls -l on a device file shows a leading c or b instead of the usual -/d/l: c for a character device (data transferred as an unstructured stream — a terminal, /dev/null, /dev/zero), b for a block device (data accessed in fixed-size blocks, addressable by position — a disk or disk partition). Where a regular file's ls -l shows a size, a device file shows two numbers instead: major, identifying which driver handles this device, and minor, identifying which specific instance that driver should talk to.

docs.title: Worked example: real device files and real udev-assigned names
docs.text:
$ ls -l /dev/null /dev/zero /dev/vda /dev/vda1
crw-rw-rw- 1 root root   1, 3 Oct 22 23:26 /dev/null
crw-rw-rw- 1 root root   1, 5 Oct 22 23:26 /dev/zero
brw-rw---- 1 root disk 253, 0 Oct 22 23:28 /dev/vda
brw-rw---- 1 root disk 253, 1 Oct 22 23:28 /dev/vda1

$ udevadm info --query=all --name=/dev/vda
P: /devices/pci0000:00/0000:00:06.0/virtio2/block/vda
M: vda
N: vda
S: disk/by-diskseq/9
S: disk/by-path/pci-0000:00:06.0
S: disk/by-path/virtio-pci-0000:00:06.0
E: DEVNAME=/dev/vda
E: DEVTYPE=disk
E: DISKSEQ=9
E: MAJOR=253
E: MINOR=0
E: SUBSYSTEM=block

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) /dev/null and /dev/zero are both character devices (c) sharing major 1 — the kernel's generic memory-backed "pseudo-device" driver — distinguished from each other only by minor (3 vs 5); the driver code uses the minor number to decide "this open is /dev/null, discard everything" versus "this open is /dev/zero, return infinite zero bytes" without needing separate drivers at all. /dev/vda is a block device (b), major 253, the virtio_blk driver (this is a virtual machine, so its disk is a paravirtualized virtio device, not a real SATA/NVMe controller — a real machine would show a different major tied to its actual disk driver). udevadm info reveals that /dev/vda isn't the only name pointing at this device: S: lines list symlinks udev created — disk/by-diskseq/9, disk/by-path/pci-0000:00:06.0 — stable alternate names under /dev/disk/ that keep working even if /dev/vda were renumbered to /dev/vdb on a different boot (which genuinely happens when disk detection order changes).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Device files don't contain driver code — they're just a (type, major, minor) tuple the kernel's VFS layer uses to look up which driver's file_operations table to call when a program open()s them. The driver, whether built into the kernel or loaded as a module (Level 4), is what actually does something when read()/write()/ ioctl() happens on an open device file. This is why creating a device file by hand with mknod (rarely needed today, but instructive) can point at a major/minor pair with no corresponding driver loaded — the file exists, ls -l shows it, but opening it fails, because the number-to-driver mapping only means something once the kernel side is actually present.

/dev itself is almost always devtmpfs — a kernel-populated, RAM-backed virtual filesystem (similar in spirit to /proc//sys, Level 1 Lesson 3) that the kernel fills in automatically as devices are detected, before udev even starts. udev, a userspace daemon, listens for the kernel's device-detection events (via a netlink socket) and does the work the kernel's own devtmpfs population doesn't: running the matching rules from /lib/udev/rules.d/ and /etc/udev/rules.d/ to set correct permissions and ownership, trigger device-specific setup (loading firmware, setting up a USB device's driver-specific quirks), and create the extra, human- and automation-friendly symlinks shown above. This two-stage split — kernel creates the raw node immediately, userspace enriches it slightly after — is exactly why a device can briefly exist as /dev/sdb with default, possibly-wrong permissions for a moment right after a hotplug, before udev's rules finish applying.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Hardcoding /dev/sda (or similar plain device names) in scripts or fstab entries for anything other than the most disposable, single-disk scenario. Device enumeration order (sda vs sdb) can change across reboots, especially with multiple disks or hot-swappable storage — the by-uuid, by-label, or by-path symlinks under /dev/disk/ are the stable alternative udev exists partly to provide.
  • Assuming every device file under /dev currently works. As explained above, the file can exist (created by devtmpfs or a stale mknod) with no corresponding driver loaded or hardware present — ls -l showing the entry isn't proof the device is usable.
  • Writing custom udev rules without testing them with udevadm test first. A rule with a typo'd match condition can silently fail to apply (leaving default permissions) or, worse, match more devices than intended — udevadm test /sys/class/.../<device> runs the rule-matching logic without actually triggering real device changes, which is the safe way to iterate.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run ls -l /dev/null /dev/zero /dev/random /dev/urandom and note which major/minor pairs are shared and which differ. Then run udevadm info --query=all --name=<your root disk device> and list every stable symlink udev created for it under /dev/disk/ — explain, for at least one of them, a scenario where using that symlink instead of the raw device name would have avoided a real problem.

docs.title: 10 · Project: Diagnose a Resource-Starved System
docs.text: Every lesson in this level gave you one piece of the diagnostic toolkit — process state, scheduling, memory, storage, systemd, logs, devices. This project puts the first three together: create a real CPU-starved system on purpose, then diagnose it from the outside using exactly the tools and numbers you'd reach for on a real incident, with nothing invented or simulated.

docs.title: Building the problem
docs.text:
cat > cpu_hog.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
while true; do :; done
EOF
chmod +x cpu_hog.sh
./cpu_hog.sh &
./cpu_hog.sh &

This is deliberately the simplest possible CPU hog: an infinite loop doing nothing but checking its own condition over and over, which the kernel schedules exactly like any other runnable, CPU-bound process (Lesson 2's CFS model) — a pathological but completely realistic stand-in for "a process stuck in a bad loop" or "a worker that's spinning instead of blocking on I/O," both real incident patterns.

docs.title: Diagnosing it with real output
docs.text:
$ ps -eo pid,ppid,pcpu,pmem,stat,comm --sort=-pcpu | head -n6
    PID    PPID %CPU %MEM STAT COMMAND
 257439  257422  100  0.0 R    cpu_hog.sh
 257440  257422  100  0.0 R    cpu_hog.sh
   2057       1  0.3  0.8 Ssl  lima-guestagent
   9408    9371  0.2  0.9 Sl   containerd
      1       0  0.0  0.4 Ss   systemd

$ uptime
 16:22:38 up  6:04,  1 user,  load average: 0.00, 0.05, 0.04

$ vmstat 1 3
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- -------cpu-------
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st gu
 3  0      0 1044928  39724 2509912    0    0    59   202  266    0  0  0 99  0  0  0
 2  0      0 1045776  39724 2510048    0    0     0     0 2410  281 50  0 50  0  0  0
 2  0      0 1045836  39724 2510048    0    0     0     0 2212  105 50  0 50  0  0  0

(Real output from this course's lab VM, with two cpu_hog.sh processes genuinely running.) ps --sort=-pcpu immediately names the two offenders: STAT R (runnable, actually on CPU or waiting for it — not sleeping) at a flat 100 %CPU each, dwarfing every other process on the box. uptime's load average — 0.00, 0.05, 0.04 — is the one number here that's genuinely surprising if you expect it to reflect the hogs: these samples were taken in the first couple of seconds after starting the loops, and load average is an exponentially-decaying moving average over 1/5/15 minutes, so it takes real wall-clock time to climb and reflect a sudden CPU spike — a system can be pegged at 100% CPU right now while uptime still shows a low number, purely because not enough time has passed for the average to catch up. vmstat's r column (processes runnable, not just running) jumping to 2–3 on a VM with more cores available, alongside us (user-mode CPU%) sitting at 50 with id (idle) also at 50, is the real, immediate signal: roughly half this machine's CPU capacity is consumed by user-mode work that never blocks, which uptime's lagging average hadn't caught up to yet.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The reason ps's %CPU and vmstat's us/sy/id percentages are trustworthy immediately, while uptime's load average is not, comes down to what each one actually measures. ps and vmstat report recent, short-window CPU accounting pulled straight from /proc counters the kernel updates continuously — closer to an instantaneous snapshot. Load average, by contrast, is explicitly defined as a smoothed, historical figure (the classic Unix CPU scheduler load metric, counting both running and runnable-but-waiting processes, which on Linux also counts processes blocked in uninterruptible I/O — D state from Lesson 1 of this level — which is why a disk-bound system can show high load with idle CPU, a completely different root cause from this project's CPU-bound example despite looking similar in a single uptime number). Reading load average correctly means treating it as "how busy has this system been recently," not "how busy is it right now" — the two diverge exactly in scenarios like this project's first few seconds.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a single uptime reading as sufficient evidence a system is fine. As this project shows directly, load average lags real CPU pressure by design; always cross-check with vmstat's immediate r/us/sy/id columns or ps --sort=-pcpu before concluding "nothing's wrong."
  • Assuming high load average always means CPU contention. Because Linux's load average also counts processes in uninterruptible I/O wait (D state), a load spike with low CPU usage and high wa (I/O wait) in vmstat points at disk or network storage, not the CPU scheduler — a materially different fix.
  • Killing the first high-%CPU process you see without checking STAT. A process at high %CPU in R state doing real, intended work (a legitimate batch job) looks identical in that one column to a runaway loop — ps's longer history (etime, time) and whether the workload is expected are what actually distinguish them.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this project's CPU hog yourself (two infinite-loop background processes), then within the first 5 seconds run uptime, vmstat 1 3, and ps --sort=-pcpu. Confirm for yourself that load average hasn't caught up yet while the other two already show the real picture. Then let the hogs keep running for at least a full minute and re-check uptime — watch the 1-minute figure finally climb to reflect what the other tools showed you immediately.

docs.title: Level 3 · Networking & Security Internals
docs.text:
Level 3 follows a request from a hostname to a byte on the wire and back, then looks at the kernel mechanisms that keep processes from stepping on each other: firewalls, mandatory access control, and the namespaces/cgroups pair that containers are actually built from (no Docker required — you'll build the isolation yourself).

What was run, and what wasn't

Networking commands (ip, ss, dig/resolvectl, nft), SSH key generation, and namespace/cgroup commands were run on a real Linux VM. SELinux examples are noted as not run in this lab — the VM's distribution ships AppArmor, not SELinux, which is itself a real and common situation (Ubuntu/Debian default to AppArmor, RHEL/Fedora default to SELinux); the SELinux lesson is built from current Red Hat and selinux-project.org documentation and says so plainly. AppArmor examples are run and real.

Prerequisites: Level 1 and 2. Root access inside a disposable VM is assumed for the firewall and namespace exercises — never run unfamiliar firewall rules on a machine you can't afford to lock yourself out of.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. The Linux Network Stack: interfaces, IP addresses, the routing table, and ip route get tracing a real route decision.
  2. DNS Resolution on Linux: /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/nsswitch.conf, and how systemd-resolved changed the picture.
  3. Netfilter & Firewalls: the netfilter hooks, iptables's chains/tables, and why nftables replaced it.
  4. Sockets, Ports & the ss/netstat Toolset: TCP state machine as seen in ss -tan, and what a listening socket actually is.
  5. SSH Internals: host keys vs user keys, ssh-agent, and the handshake at a conceptual level.
  6. Linux Security Modules: SELinux vs AppArmor: mandatory access control, labels vs path-based profiles, and when each is used.
  7. Namespaces & Cgroups: the seven-ish namespace types and the two cgroup hierarchies (v1 and v2) that isolate and limit processes.
  8. Kernel Tuning: sysctl & /proc Parameters: /proc/sys, sysctl, and a few parameters worth actually knowing.
  9. Auditing & Hardening: auditd rules, fail2ban jails, and reading a CIS benchmark without treating it as gospel.
  10. Project: Build a Container From Namespaces and Cgroups: unshare + chroot
    • a cgroup memory limit, assembled by hand into something that behaves like a (very small) container.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: Level 4 is tools and judgment: tracing and profiling a real process, I/O scheduling, kernel modules, reading /proc and /sys as a debugging surface, recovering from a bad boot, and a capstone that builds, hardens and diagnoses a server from nothing.

docs.title: 01 · The Linux Network Stack: Interfaces, IP & Routing
docs.text: ping either works or it doesn't, and when it doesn't, "is it DNS, is it routing, is it a firewall, is it the remote host" is the standard troubleshooting ladder — one this lesson and the next few build, starting from the bottom: what an interface actually is, and how the kernel decides, for any destination address, which interface and which next hop to send a packet through.

docs.title: Interfaces and addresses
docs.text: A network interface (eth0, lo, wlan0...) is the kernel's representation of something that can send and receive packets — a real NIC, a virtual/paravirtualized device (as in this course's VM), or lo, the loopback interface that exists purely so a machine can talk to itself without touching real hardware. An interface can carry multiple IP addresses, each with a scope (global — routable beyond this machine; link — only valid on this local network segment, like IPv6 link-local addresses) and, when address assignment comes from DHCP, a lease duration you can see directly.

docs.title: Worked example: a real interface, a real routing table, two real route decisions
docs.text:
$ ip addr show eth0
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc pfifo_fast state UP group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 52:55:55:78:ba:7d brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 192.168.5.15/24 metric 200 brd 192.168.5.255 scope global dynamic eth0
       valid_lft 2021sec preferred_lft 2021sec
    inet6 fe80::5055:55ff:fe78:ba7d/64 scope link proto kernel_ll

$ ip route show
default via 192.168.5.2 dev eth0 proto dhcp src 192.168.5.15 metric 200
192.168.5.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.5.15 metric 200
192.168.5.2 dev eth0 proto dhcp scope link src 192.168.5.15 metric 200

$ ip route get 8.8.8.8
8.8.8.8 via 192.168.5.2 dev eth0 src 192.168.5.15 uid 501
    cache

$ ip route get 1.1.1.1
1.1.1.1 via 192.168.5.2 dev eth0 src 192.168.5.15 uid 501
    cache

(Real output from this course's lab VM — a Lima-managed VM, which is why the address range and MAC prefix look VM-typical rather than like real cloud infrastructure.) inet 192.168.5.15/24 ... dynamic: dynamic confirms this address came from DHCP, not static configuration, and the valid_lft/preferred_lft lease timers are the real reason a DHCP-assigned address can change later — nothing on this system "owns" this IP permanently. The routing table has exactly three entries: a route to the local subnet (192.168.5.0/24, directly reachable, no gateway needed), a host route to the gateway itself, and a default route (0.0.0.0/0, shown as default) via 192.168.5.2 for everything else. ip route get shows the kernel's actual routing decision for a specific destination rather than making you read the whole table and reason it out by hand: both 8.8.8.8 (Google's public DNS) and 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare's) resolve to the exact same decision — out eth0, via the same gateway — because neither matches the more specific 192.168.5.0/24 route, so both fall through to the default route, which is exactly what a default route is for.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Routing table lookup is a longest-prefix match: the kernel doesn't scan routes in file order, it picks the route whose destination prefix is the most specific match for the packet's destination address, and only falls back to a less specific (eventually the default, /0) route when nothing more specific matches. This is why 192.168.5.0/24 (a /24, matching 256 addresses) correctly takes priority over the /0 default route for any address starting 192.168.5., even though both are present in the same table — specificity, not order of insertion, decides.

ip route get doesn't just print a table row back at you — it genuinely runs the kernel's route resolution logic for that one destination (through the same code path an actual outgoing packet would use) and shows you the result, including the source address the kernel would select (src 192.168.5.15 here) if you didn't specify one yourself; on a machine with multiple addresses or interfaces, this source-selection step is itself a real decision, not an arbitrary pick, and ip route get <dst> from <specific-src> lets you ask "what if I wanted to send from this particular address instead." The cache line in the output is a reminder that Linux historically cached routing decisions for reuse (a performance optimization removed and reworked more than once across kernel versions); don't read too much into its exact presence or absence across different kernel releases — the authoritative routing decision is always the via .../dev ... line above it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming ping failing means "the network is down." ping tests ICMP reachability specifically, which many networks and hosts deliberately block while TCP/UDP traffic flows fine — a failed ping with working curl/ssh to the same host usually means a firewall rule (Lesson 3), not a routing or connectivity problem.
  • Confusing scope link addresses (like the fe80::... IPv6 address above) with globally routable ones. Link-local addresses are only meaningful on the directly-attached network segment and will never appear in a routing table as a path to anywhere beyond it.
  • Reading a routing table top-to-bottom and assuming the first matching line wins. As covered above, the kernel selects by most-specific prefix match, not list order — a /32 host route listed after a /0 default route in ip route show's output still wins for its one specific address.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run ip addr show and ip route show on any Linux machine, and identify: your default gateway, whether your main address is static or DHCP-assigned (look for the dynamic flag), and your subnet's prefix length. Then run ip route get against three different destinations — one on your local subnet, one well-known public IP, and one made-up address outside any configured range — and confirm which routing table entry each one actually uses.

docs.title: 02 · DNS Resolution on Linux: resolv.conf, nsswitch & systemd-resolved
docs.text: "DNS" is often blamed as a single thing that either works or doesn't, but name resolution on a modern Linux system actually passes through at least two configuration layers before a single DNS packet goes anywhere — and on most current distros, /etc/resolv.conf doesn't even point at a real DNS server anymore.

docs.title: The two layers: nsswitch, then resolv.conf
docs.text: /etc/nsswitch.conf's hosts: line decides, for any program calling the standard getaddrinfo()/gethostbyname() C library functions, which sources to check and in what order — typically files dns, meaning check /etc/hosts first, then fall through to actual DNS. This is why adding an entry to /etc/hosts reliably overrides DNS for that name on a correctly-configured system: it's not a special case, it's nsswitch.conf's literal, documented order. Only once resolution falls through to the dns source does /etc/resolv.conf — the traditional file naming actual nameservers — come into play at all.

docs.title: Worked example: a real resolv.conf, nsswitch, and a traced DNS query
docs.text:
$ cat /etc/resolv.conf
# This is /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf managed by man:systemd-resolved(8).
# Do not edit.
nameserver 127.0.0.53
options edns0 trust-ad
search .

$ grep ^hosts /etc/nsswitch.conf
hosts:          files dns

$ resolvectl status
Global
         Protocols: -LLMNR +mDNS -DNSOverTLS DNSSEC=no/unsupported
  resolv.conf mode: stub

Link 2 (eth0)
    Current Scopes: DNS
Current DNS Server: 192.168.5.2
       DNS Servers: 192.168.5.2

$ resolvectl query github.com
github.com: 20.207.73.82                                    -- link: eth0
-- Information acquired via protocol DNS in 22.2ms.
-- Data is authenticated: no; Data was acquired via local or encrypted transport: no
-- Data from: network

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) The nameserver in /etc/resolv.conf is 127.0.0.53 — localhost, not the network's actual DNS server — and the file's own comments explain why: this is systemd-resolved's stub resolver, a tiny local DNS server every program's getaddrinfo() call actually talks to. resolvectl status reveals the real upstream server, 192.168.5.2 (this network's DHCP-provided gateway/resolver), which systemd-resolved learned automatically and queries on the stub's behalf. resolvectl query traces one real resolution end to end: github.com resolved to a real IP in 22.2ms, over plain DNS (not encrypted — DNSSEC=no and "Data is authenticated: no" tell you this network path isn't validating or encrypting DNS responses, worth knowing before trusting a DNS answer in a hostile network context).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Before systemd-resolved became the default on most major distros, /etc/resolv.conf really was a flat, directly-edited file naming real upstream nameservers, and DHCP clients or VPN software would rewrite it directly whenever network configuration changed — a frequent source of races and clobbered settings when multiple tools tried to manage the same file. The stub-resolver model fixes this by introducing one stable local point of contact (127.0.0.53, always present, never changes) that every application and library continues to query exactly as before, while the actual upstream server list, DNSSEC validation, DNS-over-TLS, and per-interface DNS configuration (useful for VPNs that should only resolve their own internal names, not hijack all DNS) are all managed centrally by the systemd-resolved daemon behind that stable stub — resolvectl status is how you see past the stub to what's actually configured.

Crucially, nsswitch.conf's lookup order applies above all of this: a program never talks to DNS directly without first consulting /etc/hosts (per the files source), and nsswitch.conf can name other sources entirely — mdns4 for mDNS/".local" name resolution on a LAN, ldap in some enterprise directory setups — all through the exact same pluggable Name Service Switch mechanism, which is why changing how a program resolves names at the system level never requires touching that program's own code; it's a system-wide, centrally configured hook every properly-written networked program goes through.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Editing /etc/resolv.conf directly on a systemd-resolved-managed system and expecting it to persist. The file's own header warns about this: it's regenerated, and a direct edit is lost on the next network event — the supported ways to change DNS servers are resolvectl commands, or your network manager's own configuration.
  • Assuming a DNS failure is a DNS server problem without checking /etc/hosts and nsswitch.conf first. A stale or incorrect /etc/hosts entry overrides real DNS silently, by design, per the files dns order — it's one of the most common "but DNS is clearly working for everyone else" bugs.
  • Trusting plain DNS answers as authenticated. As resolvectl query's own output shows plainly (Data is authenticated: no), standard DNS has no built-in integrity guarantee unless DNSSEC validation is actually enabled and the response says so — a spoofed answer on an untrusted network is a real risk this output format is specifically designed to surface rather than hide.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run resolvectl status on a Linux machine and identify the actual upstream DNS server(s) in use versus the stub address in /etc/resolv.conf. Then add a made-up hostname to /etc/hosts pointing at 127.0.0.1, and confirm with getent hosts <that-name> (which goes through the real nsswitch.conf-configured lookup path, unlike resolvectl query, which talks to DNS directly) that it resolves to your override rather than hitting DNS at all.

docs.title: 03 · Netfilter & Firewalls: iptables vs nftables
docs.text: "Is iptables dead?" comes up constantly, and the honest, slightly surprising answer — provable on your own machine in one command — is that on most current distros, the iptables command still works exactly as always, but it isn't talking to the old kernel subsystem anymore. It's a compatibility layer over something newer.

docs.title: Netfilter: the hooks underneath both tools
docs.text: Netfilter is the kernel subsystem that actually filters, modifies, and routes packets — a set of defined hook points a packet passes through on its journey (prerouting, input, forward, output, postrouting), each of which userspace rules can attach to. Neither iptables nor nftables is netfilter; both are userspace tools that configure netfilter's hooks, just with different rule languages and, for the older tool, an important recent change in what's actually running underneath.

docs.title: Worked example: proving iptables is now an nftables frontend
docs.text:
$ iptables -V
iptables v1.8.11 (nf_tables)

$ sudo nft list ruleset
table ip nat {
    chain LIMADNS {
    }

    chain PREROUTING {
        type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept;
        counter packets 0 bytes 0 jump LIMADNS
    }
    ...
}

$ sudo nft add table inet demo
$ sudo nft add chain inet demo input '{ type filter hook input priority 0 ; }'
$ sudo nft add rule inet demo input ip saddr 10.99.99.99 drop
$ sudo nft list table inet demo
table inet demo {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority filter; policy accept;
        ip saddr 10.99.99.99 drop
    }
}

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) iptables -V literally reports (nf_tables) in parentheses — that's the tool telling you, in its own version string, which kernel backend it's using. On this system, running iptables commands doesn't touch the legacy x_tables/ipt_* kernel modules at all; it translates your iptables-syntax rule into an equivalent nftables rule behind the scenes. nft list ruleset shows this VM's actual firewall/NAT configuration already contains an nftables table named nat with a chain called LIMADNS — created not by anything in this lesson, but by Lima's own networking setup, intercepting and redirecting DNS traffic for the VM. The add table/add chain/add rule sequence then builds a trivial custom rule directly in nftables's native syntax: a chain attached to the input hook, dropping any packet whose source address is 10.99.99.99 — demonstrating the same hook-attachment model iptables itself now compiles down to.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The original iptables worked against x_tables, a kernel framework with a fixed structure: packets flow through fixed built-in chains (INPUT, OUTPUT, FORWARD...) grouped into fixed tables (filter, nat, mangle...), and every rule is evaluated by the kernel in sequence for every matching packet — simple, but inflexible, and increasingly slow on rulesets with thousands of entries because there's no efficient lookup structure, just a list to walk. nftables, introduced as x_tables's eventual successor, replaced this with a small, generic in-kernel virtual machine: rules are compiled into bytecode-like instructions, tables and chains are entirely user-defined (not fixed names the kernel hardcodes), and set/map data structures allow genuinely fast matching (checking a packet's source IP against ten thousand addresses in a set is a fast hash lookup, not ten thousand sequential rule comparisons). The iptables-nft compatibility binary (what current distros ship as plain iptables) translates classic iptables syntax into equivalent nftables rules at the moment you run it, specifically so existing scripts, firewall management tools, and institutional muscle memory didn't all have to be rewritten the day nftables became the default backend.

This matters practically because mixing legacy (iptables-legacy, still available on most distros as a separate binary, talking to the old x_tables backend directly) and nft-backed (iptables-nft) rules on the same machine can produce a genuinely confusing, partially-inconsistent ruleset — two tools, two different kernel paths, both claiming to manage "the firewall." update-alternatives --list iptables (Debian/Ubuntu) or checking which binary iptables actually resolves to is the way to confirm, with certainty, which backend a given system is really using before debugging a rule that "should" be working.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing firewall rules in both iptables and nft syntax on the same machine without checking they're using the same backend. If one is legacy and one is nft-backed, you can end up with two independent, overlapping rule sets that don't see or interact with each other at all, each only showing half the picture.
  • Assuming "I don't use nft directly, so my firewall doesn't use nftables." As demonstrated above, that's often simply false on a modern distro — checking iptables -V's backend annotation takes one command and removes the guesswork.
  • Forgetting that policy order matters within a chain, under both tools. The first matching rule's action (accept/drop/jump) typically takes effect immediately — a broad accept rule placed before a more specific drop rule silently makes the drop rule unreachable for traffic the earlier rule already matched.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run iptables -V on a Linux machine you control and check whether it reports an nf_tables or legacy backend. Then, in a disposable VM (never on a machine you rely on for connectivity, including over SSH), create a simple nft table/chain/rule that drops traffic from one IP address you don't use, verify it with nft list ruleset, then remove it with nft delete table.

docs.title: 04 · Sockets, Ports & the ss/netstat Toolset
docs.text: "Is anything listening on port 8080" and "who is this connection to" are two of the most common first questions in any networking investigation, and ss (the modern replacement for the older netstat) answers both directly from the kernel's live socket table — no packet capture needed, because the kernel already knows exactly what every socket on the machine is doing.

docs.title: What a socket is, and what "listening" means
docs.text: A socket is the kernel's handle for one endpoint of a network conversation — bound to a protocol (TCP/UDP), a local address and port, and, once connected, a remote address and port too. A socket in LISTEN state isn't connected to anyone; it's a server announcing "I will accept new connections arriving on this port," with the kernel maintaining a queue of connections that have completed the TCP handshake but haven't yet been accept()ed by the application. A socket in ESTABLISHED state is an actual, active, two-way conversation — the pairing of a specific local address:port with a specific remote address:port is what uniquely identifies it.

docs.title: Worked example: real listening sockets and a real established connection
docs.text:
$ sudo ss -tlnp
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
LISTEN 0      4096         0.0.0.0:22         0.0.0.0:*    users:(("systemd",pid=1,fd=277))
LISTEN 0      4096         0.0.0.0:111        0.0.0.0:*    users:(("rpcbind",pid=247297,fd=4))
LISTEN 0      4096   127.0.0.53%lo:53         0.0.0.0:*    users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=231833,fd=21))
LISTEN 0      4096      127.0.0.54:53         0.0.0.0:*    users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=231833,fd=23))

$ python3 -m http.server 8899 --bind 127.0.0.1 &
$ ss -tln | grep 8899
LISTEN 0      5          127.0.0.1:8899       0.0.0.0:*

$ ss -tn state established
Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
0      0          127.0.0.1:8899     127.0.0.1:38698
0      0          127.0.0.1:38698    127.0.0.1:8899

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) The first listing shows real listening sockets and exactly which process owns each: sshd on port 22 bound to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces), rpcbind on 111 (NFS's portmapper, left over from Lesson 5 of the previous level), and — worth noticing specifically — systemd-resolve listening on 127.0.0.53 and 127.0.0.54, two different loopback addresses, both port 53: this is the DNS stub resolver from Lesson 2, and the second address is a secondary stub used for a specific resolved feature (per-link DNS scoping) that doesn't matter for this lesson except as proof that "localhost" isn't just one address — 127.0.0.0/8 is an entire reserved range, and binding different services to different addresses within it is a legitimate way to keep them from colliding on the same port. The last two lines show one TCP connection from both sides at once: 127.0.0.1:8899 (the server) paired with 127.0.0.1:38698 (the client's ephemeral port, picked by the kernel automatically since the client didn't ask for a specific one) — and the same pairing, reversed, as seen from the client's own socket. One connection, two socket entries, one on each end, both ESTABLISHED.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A TCP connection is uniquely identified by a 4-tuple: (local IP, local port, remote IP, remote port) — not by port number alone. This is why a server can hold thousands of simultaneous connections on one listening port 443: each client connection gets a different remote IP and/or ephemeral port, so the 4-tuple stays unique even though the local half of every one of them is identical (<server-ip>:443). The ephemeral port range (client-side ports the kernel assigns automatically, typically somewhere in 32768–60999 on Linux, tunable via /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range) is what let 38698 appear above without anyone requesting it — the kernel picked the first available port in that range when the client's socket connected.
