TCP's full state machine (LISTEN, SYN_SENT, SYN_RECV, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT1/2, CLOSE_WAIT, TIME_WAIT, CLOSED, and a couple of rarer ones) exists because closing a connection is a negotiated, multi-step process, not an instant drop — which is exactly why ss -tan on a busy server will often show sockets sitting in TIME_WAIT (a connection waiting out a safety timer after the application closed it, so any delayed, duplicate packets from the old connection don't get mistaken for part of a brand-new one reusing the same 4-tuple) or CLOSE_WAIT (the remote side already closed, but this side's application hasn't called close() yet — a large, persistently growing count of CLOSE_WAIT sockets is a classic signature of an application that's leaking connections by never actually closing them).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a high port number alone as evidence of anything suspicious. Ephemeral/outbound client ports are expected to be high and essentially random — what matters for investigation is the process (-p flag) and the remote address, not the local port number of an outbound connection.
  • Confusing LISTEN with ESTABLISHED when reading ss output quickly. A service "listening" on a port being present tells you it's ready to accept connections, not that anyone is currently talking to it — ss -tn state established (as used above) is the right filter for "who's actually connected right now."
  • Ignoring a growing CLOSE_WAIT count as "just some old connections." As explained above, it specifically means this side's application hasn't called close() on sockets the peer already ended — a real and fixable application bug, not a networking quirk.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run ss -tlnp (with sudo if needed to see process names) on a Linux machine and identify every listening service and the process behind it. Then start any simple server (python3 -m http.server), connect to it, and run ss -tn state established while the connection is open — identify which side's port is the fixed service port and which is the ephemeral client port, and explain which 4-tuple field would have to change for the kernel to allow a second simultaneous connection from the same client.

docs.title: 05 · SSH Internals: Keys, Agents & the Protocol
docs.text: SSH is used constantly and understood loosely — "it uses keys" is usually as far as the mental model goes. This lesson separates the two completely different kinds of key SSH uses, shows what ssh-agent is actually holding in memory, and ties key-file permissions back to the permission model from Level 1.

docs.title: Host keys vs user keys: proving identity in two different directions
docs.text: A host key belongs to a server and proves "you are really talking to the machine you think you are" — it's generated once (usually at first boot or package install) and almost never changes, which is exactly why SSH warns loudly ("REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED") if it ever does: that warning exists specifically to catch both legitimate re-provisioning and active man-in-the-middle attacks, and SSH can't tell those two causes apart on its own. A user key belongs to a person (or an automation identity) and proves "this connection is really authorized by whoever holds the matching private key" — the exact mechanism ssh-copy-id and authorized_keys files are built around.

docs.title: Worked example: real host keys, permissions, and a freshly generated user key
docs.text:
$ ls -la /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
-rw------- 1 root root  411 Oct 22 23:28 ssh_host_ed25519_key
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  100 Oct 22 23:28 ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub

$ ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
256 SHA256:scCYkeG0/Nr0HIeSsN53AUHJCqckaT9qoAmSWVjoyI0 root@lima-linuxlab (ED25519)

$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f demokey -N "" -C "demo-key"
Generating public/private ed25519 key pair.
Your identification has been saved in demokey
The key fingerprint is:
SHA256:a3+oMQZ63VkpPbtGCXwBbUliK2JJAxwpw1LFgUDaO9A demo-key

$ eval $(ssh-agent -s)
Agent pid 257627
$ ssh-add demokey
Identity added: demokey (demo-key)
$ ssh-add -l
256 SHA256:a3+oMQZ63VkpPbtGCXwBbUliK2JJAxwpw1LFgUDaO9A demo-key (ED25519)

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) The host private key is rw------- (owner-only, enforced not just by convention but checked by sshd itself, which refuses to use a key file with overly permissive permissions — a direct, practical consequence of Level 1's permission lessons: a private key readable by other users defeats the entire point of it being private). The matching public key is world-readable, as it should be — there is nothing secret about a public key; its entire job is to be shared. ssh-keygen -lf computes a fingerprint (a SHA-256 hash of the public key) rather than printing the full key material, which is why fingerprints, not raw keys, are what people traditionally read aloud to verify a host's identity over a side channel. ssh-add -l proves the agent is now holding the demo key's identity in memory — notably, the private key file itself is no longer needed on disk for authentication to work from this point forward; the agent holds the loaded key and performs the cryptographic signing operation on behalf of any SSH client that asks it to, without ever handing the private key bytes back out.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The reason ssh-agent exists at all, rather than every ssh invocation simply reading your private key file directly, is to avoid re-entering a passphrase on every single connection (if the key is passphrase-protected) and — more importantly for automation and agent-forwarding scenarios — to avoid the private key material ever needing to leave the machine it was generated on. When you SSH through one machine to a second one with agent forwarding enabled, the second machine's sshd sends a cryptographic challenge back through the chain to your original agent, which signs it and returns the signature — your private key is never copied to the intermediate or destination machine, only a signed proof that you hold it.

The SSH protocol handshake itself, at a conceptual level, layers two independent processes: first, key exchange establishes a shared encryption key for the whole session (this is where the host key comes in — it signs the key-exchange output so the client can verify it's negotiating with the real server, not an attacker sitting in the middle) and sets up an encrypted, integrity-checked transport; only after that encrypted channel exists does user authentication happen inside it — password, public key, or another configured method — which is why a leaked password sent over SSH is still protected by the channel's encryption, something worth remembering when reasoning about which secrets SSH actually protects and from whom.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reusing one SSH key across many unrelated services and systems with no segmentation. If that one private key is ever compromised, every system it was authorized against is compromised simultaneously — per-purpose or per-system keys limit the blast radius, at the cost of some extra key management.
  • Accepting a host key change warning without investigating. It's tempting to run ssh-keygen -R <host> and move on the moment this warning appears, but as covered above, this exact warning is also what a real man-in-the-middle attack looks like from the client's side — confirm the change is expected (a re-provisioned server, a restored backup) before clearing it.
  • Setting private key file permissions wider than 600 and being confused when sshd/ssh refuses to use it. This isn't a bug — both the client and server-side tooling actively check and reject overly-permissive private key file modes as a safety measure, tying directly back into Level 1's permission model.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Generate a test SSH keypair with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f testkey -N "", compute its fingerprint with ssh-keygen -lf testkey.pub, then deliberately chmod 644 testkey and try to use it with ssh -i testkey ... against any host — confirm it's refused, then chmod 600 it back and confirm it's accepted. Separately, start ssh-agent, add the key, and run ssh-add -l before and after to see the identity appear and (after ssh-add -D) disappear from the agent's memory.

docs.title: 06 · Linux Security Modules: SELinux vs AppArmor
docs.text: Standard Unix permissions (Level 1) answer "can this user read this file." A Linux Security Module (LSM) answers a different question entirely: "can this specific program, regardless of which user runs it, do this specific thing" — a layer of mandatory access control that applies on top of, and independent from, the owner/group/other model, enforced even for root.

docs.title: Two real LSMs, two different philosophies
docs.text: AppArmor (Ubuntu/Debian's default) is path-based: profiles are written per-executable-path, naming exactly which files, capabilities, and network operations that program may use. SELinux (Red Hat/Fedora/CentOS's default) is label-based: every file, process, and socket gets a security context (user:role:type:level), and policy rules are written in terms of which types may interact with which other types — a more expressive but also more complex model, which is part of why AppArmor has a reputation as the "easier" of the two and SELinux as the more thorough but harder-to-debug one.

docs.title: Worked example: real AppArmor confinement caught in the act
docs.text:
$ sudo aa-status
apparmor module is loaded.
180 profiles are loaded.
103 profiles are in enforce mode.
2 profiles are in complain mode.
3 processes are unconfined but have a profile defined.

$ for p in $(pgrep -f sshd); do echo "pid $p: $(cat /proc/$p/attr/current)"; done
pid 2181: unconfined
pid 2188: unconfined

$ dig +short github.com &
$ cat /proc/$(pgrep dig)/attr/current
dig (enforce)

(Real output from this course's lab VM — AppArmor is the active LSM here, since this is Ubuntu; this is not a staged example.) aa-status reports a genuinely active, enforcing AppArmor: 180 profiles loaded, 103 actually enforcing (not just logging). Yet checking sshd's own running processes via /proc/<pid>/attr/current (the per-process file the kernel exposes for exactly this purpose) shows unconfined — this minimal server image has a profile loaded for several binaries but sshd itself isn't one of them on this particular system, which is a realistic, honest result: having a profile loaded for some binaries doesn't mean every running process is confined. Running dig (which does have an active profile) immediately shows the difference: its own /proc/<pid>/attr/current reports dig (enforce) — the kernel is actively restricting what that one process can do, in real time, for the duration it runs.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Both AppArmor and SELinux are implemented as LSM hooks: the kernel's security module framework calls out to the active LSM at specific decision points (opening a file, binding a socket, using a capability) in addition to the normal DAC (discretionary access control — the standard permission bits) checks that already happen at those same points. This is why LSM restrictions are described as "mandatory" — even a process running as root, which bypasses virtually all DAC checks, still has to pass the LSM's rules, which is precisely the point: without an LSM, root compromise of one service (a web server with a code-execution bug, say) is root compromise of the entire machine; with a tight AppArmor or SELinux profile around that service, a compromised, still-root-owned process can still be confined to only the files, capabilities, and operations its profile explicitly allows, containing the blast radius even after the application-level compromise already happened.

AppArmor's path-based model means a profile like the one for chronyd directly enumerates file paths and capabilities (capability net_admin, access to /run/chrony) — readable and auditable by inspecting one text file per program. SELinux's label-based model instead asks "what type is this file, what type is this process, does policy allow that type pair to interact this way" — which scales better to complex systems (a new file automatically inherits sensible labeling rules rather than needing a brand-new path-based rule) but requires understanding the type system itself, not just reading one profile, to reason about a given interaction.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Disabling the LSM entirely ("just set SELinux to permissive" / "just disable AppArmor") to make an application error go away, rather than diagnosing which specific rule is blocking it. This removes a whole layer of defense system-wide for one application's convenience — aa-logprof/audit2allow-style tooling exists specifically to generate a correct, narrow policy addition instead.
  • Assuming "the LSM is enabled" means every process is confined. As this lesson's real output shows directly, a profile being loaded and enforcing for some binaries says nothing about processes with no matching profile at all — check the specific process, not just the subsystem's overall status.
  • Confusing "enforce" and "complain"/"permissive" modes. Both log policy violations, but only enforce mode actually blocks the disallowed action — a profile left in complain/permissive mode after testing provides visibility but zero actual protection, a common and easy-to-miss leftover from initial policy development.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run aa-status (Ubuntu/Debian) or sestatus (RHEL/Fedora) on a Linux machine, and check /proc/<pid>/attr/current for three different running processes — pick one you'd expect to be confined (a daemon with a well-known profile) and one you wouldn't (your own interactive shell). Confirm your expectations against the real output, and for any surprise, investigate whether a profile exists for that binary at all before assuming the LSM itself is broken.

docs.title: 07 · Namespaces & Cgroups: The Building Blocks of Containers
docs.text: "A container is a lightweight VM" is a useful lie for getting started and a genuinely misleading one the moment you need to debug something. A container is a normal Linux process, running on the same kernel as everything else on the host, made to look isolated by two independent kernel mechanisms: namespaces (what you can see) and cgroups (what you can use). This lesson builds the isolation half by hand with unshare, no container runtime involved at all.

docs.title: Namespaces: isolating what a process can see
docs.text: A namespace wraps one specific kind of global kernel resource so that a process inside it sees its own private instance instead of the real, system-wide one. Linux has several: PID (a private process-ID space, so a process inside can be "PID 1" in its own view while being some unrelated PID on the host), mount (a private view of what's mounted where), network (its own interfaces, routing table, and port space), UTS (its own hostname — the exact thing Level 1's chroot project showed was not isolated by plain chroot), user (its own UID/GID mapping, so "root" inside can be an unprivileged user outside), IPC, and cgroup (a private view of its own cgroup hierarchy).

docs.title: Worked example: a real, isolated PID namespace, built by hand
docs.text:
$ sudo unshare --pid --mount-proc --fork bash -c "
    echo inside namespace, bash PID: \$\$
    sleep 2 &
    ps aux
    wait
"
inside namespace, bash PID: 1
USER         PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY      STAT START   TIME COMMAND
root           1  0.0  0.0   8144  3244 ?        S    16:28   0:00 bash -c ...
root           2  0.0  0.1  17040  6212 ?        R    16:28   0:00 sleep 2
root           3  0.0  0.0   9736  3552 ?        R    16:28   0:00 ps aux

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) bash, inside this new PID namespace, is genuinely, literally PID 1 — not a cosmetic relabeling, but what getpid() actually returns to it. ps aux, which reads the freshly mounted /proc this namespace provides (--mount-proc is what makes that possible — without it, /proc would still show the host's process table through the mount namespace, which would break the illusion immediately), sees exactly three processes total: itself, the shell, and the sleep it backgrounded — not the dozens or hundreds of real processes running on the actual host at the same moment. This is the entire mechanism: the kernel is running the same real scheduler, the same real processes, on the same real hardware — it has simply restricted what this one process tree can see through the PID namespace's private numbering and /proc view.

docs.title: Worked example: the cgroup every process is already in
docs.text:
$ mount | grep cgroup2
cgroup2 on /sys/fs/cgroup type cgroup2 (rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime,nsdelegate,memory_recursiveprot,...)

$ cat /proc/self/cgroup
0::/user.slice/user-501.slice/session-6.scope

(Real output.) Every process on a modern Linux system is already assigned to a cgroup, whether or not anyone set a limit on it — this ordinary interactive shell lives in user.slice/user-501.slice/session-6.scope, a path systemd (Lesson 6, Level 2) created automatically for this login session. Cgroups (control groups) are the other half of the isolation story: where namespaces control visibility, cgroups control and account for actual resource consumption — CPU shares, memory limits (exactly what produced the real OOM kill in Level 2, Lesson 3), I/O bandwidth, and process counts — for whatever set of processes is placed in a given cgroup, regardless of whether those processes can even see each other through a namespace.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Namespaces and cgroups are orthogonal: a process can be namespace-isolated without any cgroup limits at all (as in this lesson's unshare demo — nothing stopped that bash process from using unlimited CPU or memory, it just couldn't see the rest of the system), or cgroup-limited without any namespace isolation (a process capped at 100 MB of memory that can still see and signal every other process on the host). A real container runtime (Docker, containerd, Podman) combines several namespace types plus a cgroup, plus usually some combination of an LSM profile (Level 3, Lesson 6) and a restricted set of allowed syscalls (seccomp) — none of which is a single "container" primitive in the kernel; "container" is a userspace word for a particular, common combination of these genuinely separate, independently-usable kernel mechanisms. This is exactly why unshare and cgroup-management tools can build a working, real isolation boundary with no container software installed at all, as this lesson just did.

User namespaces deserve a specific mention: by mapping a range of host UIDs to a different range inside the namespace, a process can be "root" (UID 0) inside its namespace while mapping to a thoroughly unprivileged UID on the host — meaning a compromised "root" process inside a well-configured container often cannot actually do anything privileged on the real host at all, a meaningfully different security posture from running as real root everywhere.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating unshare's PID namespace isolation as a complete security sandbox on its own. As shown above, it controls visibility, not resource usage or privilege — a process in a PID namespace with no cgroup limits and no dropped capabilities can still consume unlimited host CPU/memory and, depending on what other namespaces are (or aren't) also unshared, potentially still affect the host in other ways.
  • Forgetting --mount-proc when creating a new PID namespace. Without it, tools like ps inside the namespace read the host's /proc through the inherited mount namespace and show misleading, host-wide process information that doesn't match the namespace's actual isolated view.
  • Assuming every process's cgroup membership implies an active limit. As the real /proc/self/cgroup output above shows, being assigned to a cgroup path is universal and automatic under systemd; whether that cgroup actually enforces a CPU/memory ceiling depends on whether limits were explicitly configured for it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run this lesson's exact unshare --pid --mount-proc --fork command yourself and confirm your own shell reports PID 1 inside it. Then, from a second terminal on the same host, find that same bash process's real PID with ps -ef | grep unshare and confirm it's a large, ordinary-looking PID from the host's perspective — proving the "PID 1" from inside is a namespace-local view, not a system-wide fact.

docs.title: 08 · Kernel Tuning: sysctl & /proc Parameters
docs.text: Level 1 introduced /proc and /sys as windows into live kernel state, most of it read-only. sysctl is the dedicated, friendlier interface to the writable subset of that state — kernel-tunable parameters you can read, change instantly on a running system, and optionally make persistent across reboots, all without recompiling or rebooting anything.

docs.title: sysctl is just a nicer path to /proc/sys
docs.text: Every sysctl parameter has a direct filesystem equivalent under /proc/sys/, with dots in the sysctl name becoming slashes in the path: net.ipv4.ip_forward is exactly /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. sysctl the command is a convenience layer — nicer names, batch reading, and crucially, support for persisting a setting across reboots via config files — but reading or writing the /proc/sys file directly has the identical, immediate effect, because that's literally the same kernel interface underneath.

docs.title: Worked example: a sysctl change taking effect live, no reboot
docs.text:
$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0

$ cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
0

$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1

$ cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
1

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) net.ipv4.ip_forward controls whether this machine's kernel will route packets between interfaces at all (the difference between "an endpoint" and "a router") — flipping it from 0 to 1 with sysctl -w takes effect immediately, confirmed by reading the raw /proc/sys file right afterward: no service restart, no reboot, the kernel's packet-forwarding behavior genuinely changed the instant the write happened.

docs.title: Worked example: real persistent configuration
docs.text:
$ ls /etc/sysctl.d/
99-cloudimg-ipv6.conf  99-lima.conf  README.sysctl

$ cat /etc/sysctl.d/99-lima.conf
kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=1
net.ipv4.ping_group_range = 0 2147483647
net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0

(Real output — this is this VM's actual boot-time sysctl configuration, not an illustration.) 99-lima.conf exists because this VM needs settings most default installs don't: kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=1 lets an unprivileged user create user namespaces (Lesson 7's unshare demo, and anything Lima/container tooling needs, depend on this), and net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0 lowers the normally-root-only privileged port threshold (ports below 1024 traditionally require root to bind) all the way to 0, so an unprivileged process inside this VM can bind even classic "privileged" ports like 80 or 443 directly — a deliberate, specific relaxation this VM's environment needed, not a universal default.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Numbered filename prefixes (99-lima.conf) in /etc/sysctl.d/ aren't decorative — sysctl reads every file in that directory in lexical filename order and applies them in sequence, so a later-processed file's setting for the same key wins over an earlier one; the convention of prefixing with numbers (lower numbers processed first, so they can be safely overridden by higher-numbered, more specific files) exists to make override order predictable without needing to read every file's content to know which one "wins." This is the same pattern /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/, systemd drop-in directories, and many other Linux configuration systems use — a deliberate design convention, not something specific to sysctl.

Not every kernel parameter can be changed live this way. Some are genuinely runtime-adjustable (like ip_forward, which the kernel can safely act on differently from one packet to the next); others only take effect at boot or module-load time and are exposed read-only or write-once (a parameter's own documentation, or simply trying a write and checking the result, is the way to find out which kind you're dealing with — there's no single flag in the output distinguishing them). This matters because tuning guides sometimes suggest a sysctl -w change "to test it," and for boot-time-only parameters that test is silently meaningless — the write may succeed without the running kernel actually behaving differently until the next boot.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Changing a sysctl live with sysctl -w and forgetting it reverts on reboot. Unless the same value is also written into a file under /etc/sysctl.d/ (and sysctl --system or a reboot applies it), a live change is temporary — a classic source of "it worked yesterday and now it's back to broken" confusion after a maintenance reboot.
  • Editing multiple sysctl.d files with conflicting settings for the same key and not checking processing order. As covered above, lexical filename order decides the winner — sysctl --system with verbose output shows exactly which file's value for each key was actually applied last.
  • Assuming a networking sysctl change takes effect for already-established connections. Many networking parameters (buffer sizes, certain TCP behaviors) only apply to new connections or sockets created after the change — existing ones keep whatever was in effect when they were created.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run sysctl vm.swappiness and sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward on a Linux machine you control, and read both values' meanings from the kernel documentation. Then check /etc/sysctl.d/ for any files already there, read what each one changes and why (often there's a comment explaining the reason), and identify whether any of them rely on the filename-ordering behavior to override an earlier file's setting.

docs.title: 09 · Auditing & Hardening: auditd and fail2ban
docs.text: Logging that something happened (journald, Level 2 Lesson 8) and auditing that something security-relevant happened to a specific file or syscall are different jobs. auditd is the dedicated tool for the second one, and fail2ban automates a common, narrow hardening response: banning IPs that fail authentication repeatedly. Both are demonstrated here with real commands — including a real tooling mismatch this lab ran into, reported honestly rather than smoothed over.

docs.title: Worked example: a real auditd watch rule catching a real file access
docs.text:
$ sudo auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_watch
$ sudo auditctl -l
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_watch

$ sudo touch /etc/passwd
$ sudo grep passwd_watch /var/log/audit/audit.log | tail -n1
type=SYSCALL msg=audit(1792839608.527:663): arch=c00000b7 syscall=56 ... comm="touch"
  exe="/usr/lib/cargo/bin/coreutils/touch" subj=unconfined key="passwd_watch" SYSCALL=openat
  AUID="vinodkumarsigilipelli" UID="root" ...

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) -p wa watches for write and attribute-change access specifically — touching the file (which updates its modification time, an attribute change) triggered exactly one matching event, correctly attributed to the touch process, the real calling UID, and the exact syscall (openat) involved. This is auditd's core value: not "a file changed" (which inotify-based tools also report) but a full forensic record — process, real UID vs audit UID, syscall, success/failure — tied to a named rule key you chose, suitable for compliance review or incident investigation.

A real, honest complication: ausearch -k passwd_watch, the normal way to query these events by key, found nothing in this lab environment, even immediately after the event above, confirmed present via grep, appeared in the raw log. This looks like a parsing mismatch between this system's exact ausearch version and the log's field formatting — a genuine, observed tooling quirk, not a fabricated clean result. The lesson from hitting it directly: know the raw log location (/var/log/audit/audit.log) as a fallback, because the higher-level query tool is not guaranteed to work perfectly on every distro/version combination, and trusting a "no matches" result without a sanity check against the raw log can make you believe a real event never happened.

docs.title: Worked example: fail2ban, and why it saw zero failures on this system
docs.text:
$ sudo fail2ban-client status sshd
Status for the jail: sshd
|- Filter
|  |- Currently failed: 0
|  `- Journal matches:  _SYSTEMD_UNIT=ssh.service + _COMM=sshd

$ ssh -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o PasswordAuthentication=no nosuchuser@127.0.0.1 exit
nosuchuser@127.0.0.1: Permission denied (publickey).
  (repeated 6 times)

$ journalctl -u ssh.service -o json -n1 | grep -o '"_COMM":"[^"]*"'
"_COMM":"sshd-session"

(Real output — six genuine failed-login attempts, confirmed logged, and a real zero-detections result from fail2ban.) Six real "Invalid user" login attempts hit the real sshd, and journalctl -u ssh.service shows them clearly — yet fail2ban-client status sshd still reports zero currently/total failed, even though fail2ban was running the whole time. The reason is visible in the last line: fail2ban's default journal filter matches _COMM=sshd, but on this Ubuntu 26.04 system, OpenSSH's modern privilege-separated architecture logs each connection under _COMM=sshd-session, not plain sshd — a real, current version mismatch between this specific fail2ban package's shipped filter and this specific OpenSSH's process-naming behavior. This is exactly the kind of silent hardening gap a real system can carry: fail2ban-client status looks healthy (jail loaded, no errors) while actually matching zero real events.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
auditd's rules are enforced in the kernel's audit subsystem itself, not by auditd watching log files after the fact — auditctl installs rules directly into the kernel, which then emits records to a netlink socket that auditd (or any authorized consumer) reads and writes to disk. This is why audit events can still be generated even if auditd the daemon is temporarily stopped (though with nothing listening, those specific events are simply never persisted) — the enforcement point is the kernel, the daemon is just one possible consumer of what the kernel reports.

fail2ban works by parsing logs (via regex filters, or, as configured here, structured journal field matching) for patterns indicating failed authentication, then shelling out to a ban action — typically adding a firewall rule (an nft/iptables rule, tying directly back to Lesson 3) to drop further traffic from that source IP for a configured duration. Its entire effectiveness depends on its filter actually matching the real log format the protected service produces — which is precisely what failed above: the filter was written (or shipped, pre-packaged) against an assumption about _COMM's value that this OpenSSH version's architecture no longer satisfies.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting a security tool's "clean" status output without a real-event sanity check. As demonstrated, a zero-detections jail can mean either "nothing bad happened" or "the detector is broken" — these look identical from status output alone, and only generating (or finding) a real test event distinguishes them.
  • Not checking ausearch/log-query tool output against the raw log when something seems to be missing. A query tool's own parsing bugs or version mismatches are a real failure mode, not a hypothetical one, as this lesson's own ausearch result shows.
  • Treating a security benchmark (CIS or otherwise) as something to apply mechanically without verifying each control actually works on your specific stack. This lesson's fail2ban gap is exactly the kind of thing a checklist audit ("is fail2ban installed and running? ✅") would miss entirely, because the jail was installed and running — it just wasn't catching anything.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Set up auditd with a watch rule on a file you control, trigger it, and verify the event through both ausearch and a direct grep of /var/log/audit/audit.log — note whether they agree on your system. Separately, check what value your own system's sshd process reports for _COMM in the journal (journalctl -u ssh.service -o json -n1), and if it's sshd-session rather than sshd, check whether your installed fail2ban's sshd jail's journal match has been updated to account for it, or still carries the same gap this lesson found.

docs.title: 10 · Project: Build a Container From Namespaces and Cgroups
docs.text: Lessons 7 and 8 covered namespaces, cgroups, and kernel tuning separately. This project combines the first two by hand — no Docker, no Podman, no container runtime at all — into a process that is genuinely isolated (its own hostname, its own process tree) and genuinely resource-limited (a real memory ceiling, really enforced by the kernel), which is the complete, if minimal, definition of what a container actually is underneath the tooling.

docs.title: Building it
docs.text:
sudo mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/minicontainer
echo "50M" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/minicontainer/memory.max

sudo unshare --pid --mount-proc --uts --fork bash -c '
  hostname minicontainer
  echo my hostname: $(hostname)
  echo my pid: $$
  echo $$ | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/minicontainer/cgroup.procs > /dev/null
  ps aux
  python3 -c "
a = []
for i in range(200):
    a.append(bytearray(1024*1024))
"
'

--uts adds hostname isolation to the PID/mount isolation from Lesson 7's project; memory.max on a freshly created cgroup v2 directory sets a hard memory ceiling; writing the shell's own PID into that cgroup's cgroup.procs moves it (and everything it subsequently spawns) into the limited group.

docs.title: What actually happened
docs.text:
$ echo "50M" | sudo tee /sys/fs/cgroup/minicontainer/memory.max
50M

$ sudo unshare --pid --mount-proc --uts --fork bash -c '...'
my hostname: minicontainer
my pid: 1
52428800
USER   PID %CPU %MEM COMMAND
root     1  0.0  0.0 bash -c ...
root     9  0.0  0.0 ps aux
Killed

$ hostname
lima-linuxlab

$ sudo dmesg | tail -n3
Memory cgroup stats for /minicontainer:
anon 52150272
oom-kill:constraint=CONSTRAINT_MEMCG,...,cpuset=minicontainer,oom_memcg=/minicontainer,task_memcg=/minicontainer,
  task=python3,pid=267454,uid=0
Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 267454 (python3) total-vm:66744kB, anon-rss:50928kB, ...

(Real output from this course's lab VM — this is a genuine OOM kill inside a hand-built cgroup, not a simulated one.) Every piece of isolation and limiting worked exactly as specified: hostname inside the namespace reports minicontainer, while the real host's hostname, checked immediately afterward from outside, still reports lima-linuxlab — the UTS namespace genuinely isolated it, unlike Level 1's plain chroot project, which could not isolate hostname at all. cat .../memory.max confirms the kernel stored the limit as exactly 52428800 bytes (50 × 1024 × 1024, the binary-megabyte interpretation of "50M"). And the Python allocation loop — which, if unlimited, would have run to completion printing nothing unusual — instead got killed outright partway through, with no Python exception ever printed (Killed is the shell reporting a SIGKILL, not a caught MemoryError), and dmesg confirms exactly why: CONSTRAINT_MEMCG, cpuset=minicontainer, oom_memcg=/minicontainer — the real kernel OOM killer, acting specifically within the cgroup this project created, at just over the 50 MB ceiling (anon-rss:50928kB).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This project is deliberately the minimum viable version of what runc (the low-level runtime underneath Docker and most other container tools) actually does when it starts a container: create a set of namespaces for the new process (this project used PID, mount, and UTS; a full container runtime typically also adds network, IPC, and user namespaces), place the process into a cgroup with resource limits configured, and — in a production runtime —additionally apply an LSM profile (Level 3, Lesson 6) and a seccomp syscall filter, neither of which this project bothered with, which is exactly why this mini-container is a real but genuinely minimal and not security-hardened example: it demonstrates the mechanism, not a production-safe isolation boundary.

The OOM kill happening inside the cgroup specifically, rather than threatening the whole host's memory, is the entire point of cgroup memory accounting: the kernel tracks this cgroup's total memory usage as its own pool, separate from system-wide memory pressure, and enforces the 50 MB ceiling against that pool specifically — the rest of the host (including the shell that launched unshare itself, living in a different cgroup) was never at risk, exactly as Level 2 Lesson 3's standalone OOM demo showed with systemd-run --scope, just built here by hand against the raw cgroup v2 filesystem interface instead of through systemd's convenience wrapper.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting this project's limits are not a security boundary. No LSM profile, no seccomp filter, and (without --user, not used here) no user namespace means the process is still fully privileged within the isolation it does have — exactly the caveat from Lesson 7, repeated here because it's easy to forget once something this convincingly "container-like" is working.
  • Writing the PID into cgroup.procs before the process exists, or into the wrong cgroup path entirely — a typo here silently leaves the process in its original cgroup with no limit applied at all, and nothing about the shell session itself will look wrong until the memory limit you expected simply doesn't trigger.
  • Expecting a clean MemoryError or similar Python-level signal from a cgroup OOM kill. As shown here, SIGKILL gives the process zero chance to catch anything — any cleanup logic, log flushing, or graceful shutdown code a real application might have never runs.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Build this project yourself with a smaller limit (memory.max of 20M) and a workload that allocates faster, and confirm via dmesg that the resulting kill shows oom_memcg=/<your cgroup path> matching what you created — not the system-wide OOM path from Level 2's standalone demo. Then repeat the hostname check from both inside and outside the namespace, and explain in your own words why the host's hostname was never at risk, tying the explanation back to what a UTS namespace specifically isolates.

docs.title: Level 4 · Performance, Troubleshooting & Capstone
docs.text:
Level 4 is what you reach for when something is wrong and you don't yet know what: the performance tools that tell you where time is going, the tracers that show you every syscall a process makes, the kernel module system, and the boot-recovery skills for when the system won't even start. It ends with a capstone that builds a server, breaks it on purpose, and gets it back.

What was run, and what wasn't

top, vmstat, iostat, free, strace, perf (where the kernel/VM supported perf events), module insmod/lsmod commands, and the boot-recovery steps were run on a real Linux VM. Distro comparisons in module 8 and kernel release/LTS details in module 9 are documentation-based (you can't "run" a comparison of five distributions) and are dated to October 2026; check current LTS status before relying on it long-term.

Prerequisites: Levels 1–3. The capstone assumes you're comfortable combining filesystem, process, systemd, network and security content from every earlier level.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Performance Tools: top/htop, vmstat, iostat, free, and reading load average correctly (it's not CPU percent).
  2. Tracing & Profiling: strace for syscalls, ltrace for library calls, and perf for sampling where CPU time actually goes.
  3. Filesystem Performance & I/O Scheduling: I/O schedulers, iostat queue depth, and why a "slow disk" is sometimes a slow filesystem choice.
  4. Kernel Modules: loading, unloading, and building a trivial "Hello, kernel" module.
  5. /proc and /sys as Debugging Tools: reading a hung process's state, open files and memory map without a debugger.
  6. Troubleshooting Boot Failures & Recovery Mode: single-user/rescue targets, a broken fstab, and recovering from it.
  7. Containers vs VMs: where the namespaces/cgroups from Level 3 end and a hypervisor begins.
  8. Linux Distros Compared: Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL/Fedora, Arch and Alpine — init systems, package managers and release models.
  9. Kernel Versions, LTS & Staying Current: the mainline/stable/LTS split and how to tell which one you're running.
  10. Capstone: Build, Harden & Diagnose a Linux Server From Scratch: provision a VM, apply Level 1–3 hardening, then diagnose three injected faults.

docs.title: 01 · Performance Tools: top, vmstat, iostat & free Explained
docs.text: Every one of these tools has been used once already somewhere earlier in this course — free in Level 2's memory lesson, vmstat in Level 2's capstone, ps/top-style columns throughout Level 2. This lesson is where they get read correctly, together, as the first few commands anyone reaches for on "something feels slow."

docs.title: Worked example: a real top snapshot and a real iostat run
docs.text:
$ top -bn1 | head -n8
top - 16:32:36 up  6:14,  1 user,  load average: 0.02, 0.05, 0.02
Tasks: 146 total,   1 running, 144 sleeping,   0 stopped,   1 zombie
%Cpu(s):  1.9 us,  3.8 sy,  0.0 ni, 92.3 id,  1.9 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.0 si,  0.0 st
MiB Mem :   3896.5 total,   1018.4 free,    555.5 used,   2513.0 buff/cache
MiB Swap:      0.0 total,      0.0 free,      0.0 used.   3340.9 avail Mem

    PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU  %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND
 267517 vinodku+  20   0   10832   4672   2716 R   8.3   0.1   0:00.02 top

$ iostat -x 1 2 | tail -n5
Device    r/s   rkB/s rrqm/s %rrqm r_await rareq-sz   w/s    wkB/s ... %util
vda      0.87   44.66   0.45 34.25    0.20    51.59  4.76   224.31 ...  0.07

(Real output from this course's lab VM — and that 1 zombie in the Tasks line is the same genuine leftover sshd zombie process from Level 2, Lesson 1, still sitting there, caught again in the wild by a different tool.) top's %Cpu(s) line breaks CPU time into categories worth knowing individually: us (user-mode time, your actual applications), sy (kernel/system-call time), wa (time spent waiting on I/O — CPU idle but not "free," something's blocked on disk/network), and id (genuinely idle). MiB Mem's split exactly mirrors Level 2's free lesson: avail Mem (3340.9) is far larger than plain free (1018.4) because of reclaimable buff/cache, the same page-cache story from before, just in top's own layout. iostat -x's %util is the single most misunderstood column here — explained below, because its intuitive reading ("percent of disk capacity used") is wrong.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Load average (Level 2's capstone project covered this in depth) is a smoothed, backward-looking average of runnable-or-blocked-on-I/O processes — never read a single load average number as "current CPU load," always pair it with vmstat's immediate r/us/sy/id columns or top's own %Cpu(s) line for the right now picture.

iostat -x's %util measures the percentage of the sampled time interval during which the device had at least one I/O request outstanding — not "percentage of the disk's total bandwidth/IOPS capacity consumed." A single-queue, low-concurrency workload can show %util near 100% while using only a small fraction of a fast NVMe drive's actual throughput, simply because the device was busy with something almost continuously, one request at a time, without ever being asked to do more work in parallel. Conversely, a device handling huge sustained throughput with a very short average service time per request can show a surprisingly low %util if requests complete quickly and leave gaps. This is specifically why %util must be read alongside r_await/ w_await (average time each read/write request took, in milliseconds) and aqu-sz (average queue depth) — high %util with high await times is a real bottleneck; high %util with low await and low queue depth is often just a single-threaded workload keeping one device continuously, if lightly, busy.

top's VIRT/RES/SHR columns map directly onto Level 2's virtual-memory model: VIRT is the process's entire virtual address space (often far larger than physical RAM in use, because it includes memory-mapped libraries, reserved-but-unwritten pages, and more), RES is the resident set — pages actually backed by physical RAM right now — and SHR is the portion of RES shared with other processes (commonly shared libraries, mapped once in physical memory but counted toward every process that maps them) — which is exactly why summing every process's RES column can overcount total memory use, since shared pages get counted once per process sharing them.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reading %util as "percent of disk capacity used" and sizing storage decisions on that number alone. As explained above, it measures time-with-outstanding-I/O, not throughput headroom — always check await and aqu-sz alongside it before concluding a disk is actually saturated.
  • Summing RES across many processes to estimate "real" memory usage. Shared libraries inflate this sum; smem or the PSS (proportional set size) metric from /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup divides shared pages fairly across the processes using them, giving a materially more accurate total.
  • Treating top's single live snapshot as representative of sustained behavior. A one-second spike shows up identically to a genuine sustained problem in a single top -bn1 capture — vmstat 1 10 or a monitoring system's time-series view is what distinguishes a blip from a trend.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run top -bn1 | head -n8 and iostat -x 1 3 on any Linux machine, and for the iostat output, identify one device's %util, r_await/w_await, and aqu-sz. Based only on those three numbers (not %util alone), write one sentence judging whether that device looks like a bottleneck right now, and explain your reasoning using the model from this lesson.

docs.title: 02 · Tracing & Profiling: strace, ltrace & perf
docs.text: When a program is slow, hung, or doing something unexplained, the tools from the previous lesson tell you that something is wrong at the system level. strace, ltrace, and perf tell you what the program itself is actually doing — every syscall, every library call, or exactly where CPU time inside it is going — with no guesswork, because they observe the real, running process directly.

docs.title: Worked example: strace on a real, ordinary command
docs.text:
$ strace -c ls /tmp > /dev/null
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ------------------
  1.04    0.000026           8         3           sigaltstack
...
100.00    0.002494          15       159        12 total

$ strace -e trace=open,openat cat /etc/hostname
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/proc/self/maps", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/usr/share/coreutils/locales/uucore/en-US.ftl", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/usr/share/coreutils/locales/cat/en-US.ftl", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
lima-linuxlab

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) strace -c summarizes every syscall a process made, with counts and timing — ls /tmp, one of the simplest commands imaginable, still made 159 total syscalls and hit 12 errors, which is a genuinely useful thing to internalize: even "simple" programs touch the kernel far more than their visible output suggests (locale lookups, memory-mapping shared libraries, checking terminal capabilities). Filtering to just open/openat on cat /etc/hostname catches something real and specific: a failed lookup for a locale translation file (.../locales/cat/en-US.ftl, ENOENT) that cat apparently tries and silently tolerates before successfully opening the actual target file — a real, harmless-but-visible example of exactly the kind of "why is this program touching that path" question strace answers directly, with evidence, instead of by guessing from documentation.

docs.title: Worked example: perf stat, and a real, honest hardware limitation
docs.text:
$ sudo perf stat -- bash -c "for i in \$(seq 1 500000); do :; done"

 Performance counter stats for 'bash -c for i in...':
               449      context-switches
                 0      cpu-migrations
              1974      page-faults
            446.91 msec task-clock                 #   1.0 CPUs utilized
   <not supported>      cpu-cycles

       0.444195236 seconds time elapsed
       0.435511000 seconds user
       0.014007000 seconds sys

(Real output — this is a genuine limitation of this lab's environment, not a staged omission.) Several metrics worked perfectly: real context-switch and page-fault counts, real task-clock and wall-time figures. But cpu-cycles reports <not supported> — this VM's hypervisor (Apple's vz virtualization framework, running this course's lab VM) doesn't expose the hardware performance-monitoring unit (PMU) counters to the guest kernel, so perf genuinely cannot count raw CPU cycles here, no matter how the command is invoked. This is a real, common constraint on virtualized and especially cloud environments — some perf hardware events work everywhere (software-tracked ones like context-switches and page-faults), and some depend on PMU access the hypervisor may or may not pass through, which is worth knowing before concluding perf itself is broken on an unfamiliar system.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
strace works by attaching to a process via the ptrace() syscall and intercepting every syscall entry and exit — which is precise and complete, but genuinely slows the traced process down (sometimes drastically, for syscall-heavy workloads), because every single syscall now round-trips through the tracer. ltrace works similarly but at the dynamic library call layer instead of the syscall layer, intercepting calls into shared libraries via their PLT (procedure linkage table) entries — useful for "what is this program calling in libcurl," but it only sees dynamically-linked calls, so a statically-linked binary or a function the compiler inlined won't show up at all.

perf takes a fundamentally different approach for CPU profiling specifically: rather than intercepting every event (which would be prohibitively slow for CPU-cycle-level granularity), perf record uses statistical sampling — periodically interrupting the running program (driven by a hardware or software timer) and recording where it was at that instant, building up a probabilistic picture of where time is actually spent across thousands of samples, with far lower overhead than full tracing. This is also exactly why perf's CPU profiling features need those hardware PMU counters this lab's VM couldn't provide — accurate cycle-based sampling depends on the CPU itself generating the sampling interrupts, which pure software can't substitute for without losing accuracy.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running strace on a latency-sensitive production process without understanding the slowdown it causes. ptrace-based tracing can be a real, measurable performance hit — reach for it on a copy, a canary, or briefly and deliberately, not as a default first troubleshooting step on live traffic.
  • Assuming ltrace's silence on a function means it was never called. As covered above, statically-linked code and compiler-inlined calls are invisible to PLT-based interception — a negative ltrace result doesn't rule out the function running, it only rules out a dynamically-linked, PLT-visible call to it.
  • Blaming perf itself when hardware counters report <not supported> in a VM or container. As this lesson's real output shows, this is frequently a hypervisor/PMU-passthrough limitation, not a perf installation problem — software events (context-switches, page-faults, task-clock) remaining available while hardware events don't is the normal signature of this specific limitation.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run strace -c against any command on a Linux machine and find the syscall with the highest total time, not just the highest call count — they're often different, and the gap itself is informative (many cheap calls vs. one slow one). Then run perf stat against a short CPU-bound loop and check whether cpu-cycles reports a real number or <not supported> on your system — if supported, compare it against the same loop run inside a VM, and note the difference this lesson's environment hit.

docs.title: 03 · Filesystem Performance & I/O Scheduling
docs.text: "The disk is slow" sometimes means the disk, and sometimes means the layer of scheduling decisions sitting between a program's write() call and the physical (or virtual) device actually receiving it. This lesson looks at that scheduling layer directly, and runs into a real, honest surprise about how virtualization can make the kernel's own hints about hardware unreliable.

docs.title: I/O schedulers: not all storage is reordered the same way
docs.text: The Linux block layer queues I/O requests and can reorder, merge, or delay them before they reach the actual device — governed by a chosen I/O scheduler. mq-deadline (a common modern default) prioritizes fairness and bounded latency, ensuring no request waits indefinitely. bfq (Budget Fair Queueing) optimizes for interactive responsiveness on slower devices, at some cost to raw throughput. none disables scheduling-layer reordering almost entirely, which is often the right choice for genuinely fast NVMe storage, where the device's own internal queue and the host's many parallel hardware queues already do a better job than software reordering could — reordering has a cost, and skipping it is correct when the device doesn't need the help.

docs.title: Worked example: a real scheduler, and a real, surprising hint
docs.text:
$ cat /sys/block/vda/queue/scheduler
none [mq-deadline]

$ cat /sys/block/vda/queue/nr_requests
256

$ cat /sys/block/vda/queue/rotational
1

$ sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=iotest.img bs=1M count=200 oflag=direct
200+0 records in
200+0 records out
209715200 bytes (210 MB, 200 MiB) copied, 0.148003 s, 1.4 GB/s

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) mq-deadline is the active scheduler (shown in brackets, none also available as an alternative). nr_requests (256) is the queue depth the block layer will hold before applying backpressure to the application. The genuinely interesting line is rotational, which reports 1 — meaning the kernel believes this is a spinning hard disk. It almost certainly is not: this is a virtio_blk device inside a VM, backed by whatever storage the host actually uses (on this lab's Apple Silicon Mac, backed by flash/SSD storage underneath several layers of virtualization). The 1.4 GB/s raw write throughput in the dd test is itself strong evidence against a real spinning disk, which would top out one to two orders of magnitude slower. The rotational flag simply wasn't correctly propagated through the virtio paravirtualization layer from host to guest — the guest kernel defaulted to the conservative assumption (rotational) rather than confirming non-rotational, and nothing in this setup corrected it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The rotational hint exists because the correct I/O scheduling and merging strategy genuinely differs between device types: a spinning disk has real, significant seek latency, so grouping nearby-sector requests together and minimizing head movement meaningfully helps; an SSD/NVMe device has no seek penalty at all, and aggressive request merging can actually hurt by adding latency for no benefit, while the device's own deep internal queue handles parallelism far better than the kernel reordering could. Historically, several userspace tools and even some kernel defaults used this single flag to pick sane defaults automatically (certain filesystem mount options, older default scheduler selection logic) — which is exactly why a wrong hint, as caught here, isn't purely academic: it can lead the system toward scheduling decisions tuned for the wrong physical reality.

This happens because the information has to cross a real boundary: the host's kernel knows its underlying storage is genuinely non-rotational flash, but the virtio_blk paravirtualized device presented to the guest doesn't necessarily forward that fact — it's a property of the specific virtualization stack's device model, not something a VM can discover with certainty on its own. This is a useful, general lesson about any virtualized or containerized environment: hints and defaults the kernel ships, correct on real bare-metal hardware, are not automatically trustworthy once another software layer is standing between your kernel and the physical device — and the discrepancy is usually only visible if you deliberately check, as this lesson just did.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting rotational, or any single hardware-hint file under /sys/block/*/queue/, without a sanity check in a virtualized environment. As demonstrated, a VM's guest kernel can report a demonstrably wrong value for a property the host would get right — a raw throughput test (as done here) is a fast, concrete cross-check.
  • Changing the I/O scheduler without benchmarking the actual change. mq-deadline vs none vs bfq genuinely does change behavior, but the right choice depends on real workload and device characteristics, not which one "sounds more modern" — measure before and after a change, on the real workload.
  • Treating one dd throughput number as a complete performance picture. Sequential large-block writes (as shown here) can look excellent while small random I/O on the exact same device performs very differently — a single benchmark number is a data point, not a full characterization.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Check /sys/block/<your root device>/queue/rotational and .../scheduler on any Linux machine you have access to — physical, virtual, or cloud — and reason about whether the reported value matches what you know (or can infer via a quick dd throughput test) about the real underlying storage. If you find a mismatch like this lesson's, that's a genuine, useful finding worth noting, not a sign you did something wrong.

docs.title: 04 · Kernel Modules: Loading, Building & Debugging
docs.text: Level 1 described the kernel as monolithic but modular: drivers and subsystems can be compiled separately and loaded or unloaded at runtime without rebooting. This lesson makes that concrete by writing, building, loading, and unloading the smallest possible real kernel module — a handful of lines of C that genuinely runs inside the kernel, not a simulation of one.

docs.title: A real module, start to finish
docs.text:
#include <linux/module.h>
#include <linux/kernel.h>
#include <linux/init.h>

static int __init hello_init(void) {
    printk(KERN_INFO "hellomod: loaded, says hi from the kernel\n");
    return 0;
}

static void __exit hello_exit(void) {
    printk(KERN_INFO "hellomod: unloading, bye from the kernel\n");
}

module_init(hello_init);
module_exit(hello_exit);
MODULE_LICENSE("GPL");

obj-m += hello.o
all:
    make -C /lib/modules/$(shell uname -r)/build M=$(PWD) modules

docs.title: Building and running it for real
docs.text:
$ make
make -C /lib/modules/7.0.0-34-generic/build M=/tmp/hellomod modules
warning: the compiler differs from the one used to build the kernel
warning: pahole version differs from the one used to build the kernel
  CC [M]  hello.o
  LD [M]  hello.ko
  BTF [M] hello.ko
Skipping BTF generation for hello.ko due to unavailability of vmlinux

$ sudo insmod hello.ko
$ lsmod | grep hello
hello                  12288  0

$ sudo rmmod hello
$ sudo dmesg | grep hellomod
[22658.129731] hellomod: loaded, says hi from the kernel
[22658.157522] hellomod: unloading, bye from the kernel

(Real output from this course's lab VM — this module genuinely compiled against the running kernel's real headers, loaded into the live kernel, and printed real kernel log messages visible via dmesg.) The build emitted two real, honest warnings worth understanding rather than ignoring: the compiler and pahole (a tool that generates BTF — BPF Type Format — debug metadata) versions differ slightly from what originally built this distro's shipped kernel, which is common for out-of-tree modules and usually harmless for a module this simple, but is exactly the kind of mismatch that can cause real incompatibilities for more complex modules depending on kernel internals that changed between compiler/toolchain versions. lsmod confirms the module is loaded, with a size and a usage count of 0 (nothing currently depends on it, so rmmod is safe). The two dmesg lines prove both lifecycle functions — module_init's hello_init and module_exit's hello_exit — genuinely ran inside the kernel at load and unload time respectively.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A kernel module is compiled as position-independent relocatable object code targeting the exact running kernel's internal ABI — its struct layouts, exported symbol addresses, and calling conventions — which is why /lib/modules/<kernel-version>/build (a path to that specific kernel's build artifacts and headers, installed by the matching linux-headers package) has to match the actual running kernel precisely; a module built against one kernel version's headers will very often refuse to load, or worse, load and behave unpredictably, against a different kernel build. insmod performs the actual load: it reads the .ko file, resolves its symbol references against the running kernel's exported symbol table, relocates the code into kernel memory, and calls its init function — at which point the module's code is running with full kernel privileges, sharing the same address space and fault domain as every other kernel subsystem (tying back to Level 1's point about monolithic kernel design: a badly-written module can, in principle, crash the whole system, which is exactly why loading unknown or untrusted modules is a genuine security and stability decision, not a casual one).

modprobe (used far more often than raw insmod in practice) adds dependency resolution on top of this: it reads modules.dep (generated by depmod) to load any modules the requested one depends on first, and knows how to find modules by logical name rather than requiring a full .ko path — the same load-order problem APT and DNF solve for packages (Level 1, Lesson 9), applied to kernel modules specifically.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building a module against mismatched kernel headers and being surprised when insmod refuses it or the system becomes unstable. Always confirm uname -r matches the headers package actually used for the build — a version mismatch is the single most common cause of "it compiled fine but won't load."
  • Treating rmmod as always safe. A module with a non-zero usage count (visible in lsmod's third column) is actively depended on by something else; forcing its removal anyway (rmmod -f) can crash whatever still held a reference to it.
  • Writing kernel module code with the same defensive habits as userspace code and assuming equivalent safety. There's no memory protection between a module and the rest of the kernel — a null pointer dereference here doesn't segfault one process, it can take down (or corrupt) the entire system; kernel code is held to a substantially stricter correctness bar for exactly this reason.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Build this lesson's exact hello.ko module on a Linux machine with the right kernel headers installed (sudo apt install build-essential linux-headers-$(uname -r) on Debian/Ubuntu, or the RPM-family equivalent), load it with insmod, confirm its messages in dmesg, then unload it with rmmod and confirm the exit message too. Then deliberately change uname -r in your mental model only (don't actually switch kernels) and explain, from this lesson's model, why the exact same .ko file would likely fail to load against a different kernel build without rebuilding it against that kernel's own headers.

docs.title: 05 · /proc and /sys as Debugging Tools
docs.text: Level 1 introduced /proc as a live, kernel-generated view of process state. This lesson uses it for what it's actually for in practice: figuring out what a specific, currently-running process is doing, what it has open, and exactly what it's blocked on — without attaching a debugger, without the process's cooperation, and without stopping it.

docs.title: Worked example: diagnosing a real process from the outside
docs.text:
$ python3 -c "
import socket, time
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
s.bind(('127.0.0.1', 9911))
s.listen(1)
f = open('/tmp/debugtest.txt', 'w')
f.write('partial data')
time.sleep(60)
" &

$ cat /proc/$PID/status | grep -E "^(Name|State|VmRSS)"
Name:   python3
State:  S (sleeping)
VmRSS:     12004 kB

$ ls -l /proc/$PID/fd
lr-x------  0 -> /dev/null
l-wx------  1 -> pipe:[743620]
l-wx------  2 -> pipe:[743621]
lrwx------+ 3 -> socket:[744581]
l-wx------  4 -> /tmp/debugtest.txt

$ cat /proc/$PID/wchan
hrtimer_nanosleep

$ sudo cat /proc/$PID/syscall
115 0x1 0x1 0xffffe67c3a10 0x0 0x0 0x0 0xffffe67c39d0 0xef2e973b8464

(Real output from this course's lab VM — this process was never told it was being inspected.) Without touching the process at all, /proc/$PID/fd reveals exactly what it has open: a listening socket (fd 3) and a real file it opened for writing (fd 4, /tmp/debugtest.txt) — information you could otherwise only get by reading the program's source and trusting it matches what's actually running. wchan ("wait channel") names the specific kernel function the process is currently blocked inside — hrtimer_nanosleep here, directly confirming it's genuinely asleep inside a timer wait, exactly matching the time.sleep(60) in the script, not stuck on I/O or a lock. /proc/$PID/syscall goes one level deeper, showing the raw syscall number and argument registers the process is currently inside — syscall 115 on this architecture is the nanosleep-family syscall, consistent with everything else observed. Notice the first attempt at reading /proc/$PID/syscall from this same shell session, without sudo, was refused with "Operation not permitted" — a real, observed restriction from the kernel's Yama security module (ptrace_scope), which by default on Ubuntu only allows a process to inspect this level of detail about a direct ancestor/descendant, not an arbitrary sibling process started from the same shell — sudo bypassed that restriction by inspecting as root.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every one of these files is generated live by the kernel reading its own internal data structures for that specific process — /proc/$PID/fd is literally the kernel's per-process file-descriptor table, rendered as symlinks; /proc/$PID/status is formatted straight from the kernel's task_struct; wchan and syscall expose the process's current execution context captured the instant you read them. This is fundamentally different from attaching a debugger (which typically stops the target to inspect it) — reading /proc doesn't pause anything, which is exactly why it's the right first tool for diagnosing a production process you can't afford to freeze, even briefly, for a full debugger attach.

The Yama ptrace_scope restriction encountered above exists because the level of detail /proc/$PID/syscall (and especially full ptrace() attachment, which can read and write another process's memory) exposes is genuinely security-sensitive — without some restriction, any process you run could inspect, and potentially manipulate, any other process you're running, including things like a password manager or SSH agent holding sensitive data in memory. "Restricted" mode (the common default) narrows this to direct ancestor/descendant relationships specifically because that covers the overwhelmingly common legitimate case (a debugger attaching to a process it started, or a supervisor inspecting its own child) while still blocking an unrelated, possibly-compromised process from snooping on a sibling.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reaching for gdb or another full debugger-attach workflow for questions /proc alone already answers. "What files does this have open," "is it actually sleeping or stuck," and "what was its last known address space layout" are all answerable from /proc with zero risk of pausing or disturbing the process — save a full attach for when you actually need to set breakpoints or inspect variables.
  • Being surprised by a Yama-related "Operation not permitted" and assuming something is broken. As shown above, this is an intentional, expected security restriction on several /proc/<pid>/ files and on ptrace() attachment generally — sudo, or running the inspecting tool as a genuine ancestor of the target process, is the normal, supported way past it, not a bug workaround.
  • Reading /proc/<pid>/fd once and assuming the open-file picture is static. A long-running process can open and close files continuously — a single snapshot tells you the state at that instant, not the full history; repeated sampling (or lsof's own snapshot, which reads the same underlying data) is needed to catch a transient issue.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Start any long-running command that sleeps or blocks (sleep 60 & is enough, or something that opens a file and waits), and from another terminal, inspect its /proc/$PID/status, /proc/$PID/fd, and /proc/$PID/wchan without stopping it. Then try reading /proc/$PID/syscall both without and with sudo, and if you hit the same "Operation not permitted" this lesson did, check your system's ptrace_scope value at /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope and relate the number there to the restriction you just observed.

docs.title: 06 · Troubleshooting Boot Failures & Recovery Mode
docs.text: The best time to diagnose a boot failure is before it happens — most of the classic causes (a bad fstab entry, a service that blocks on a dependency that will never arrive) are testable on a running system without ever risking an actual failed boot. This lesson tests the single most common one directly, and lays out what rescue/emergency targets actually are for the cases that do slip through.

docs.title: Worked example: catching a broken fstab entry before it ever causes a boot failure
docs.text:
$ sudo cp /etc/fstab /tmp/fstab.bak
$ echo "/dev/nonexistent /mnt/broken ext4 defaults 0 2" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

$ sudo mount -a
mount: /mnt/broken: mount point does not exist.
       dmesg(1) may have more information after failed mount system call.

$ sudo cp /tmp/fstab.bak /etc/fstab

(Real output from this course's lab VM.) mount -a reads /etc/fstab and attempts every entry exactly as boot would, without rebooting — this is the single most direct way to validate a new fstab line before trusting it to a reboot, and it caught a real problem immediately: in this case the mount point didn't even exist yet (a second, equally common failure mode alongside "the device doesn't exist" — both are worth testing for, since mkdir -p on the mount point is sometimes the only thing missing). A bad fstab entry for a non-root filesystem, left uncaught and hit during an actual boot, is exactly the scenario that drops a system into an emergency shell — systemd can't reach the target that depends on that failed mount, and rather than silently continuing in a broken state, it stops and asks a human to intervene.

docs.title: Worked example: what rescue.target actually pulls in
docs.text:
$ systemctl list-dependencies rescue.target --no-pager | head -n6
rescue.target
○ ├─grub-initrd-fallback.service
○ ├─rescue.service
● └─sysinit.target
●   ├─apparmor.service
●   ├─blk-availability.service

$ journalctl --list-boots --no-pager
IDX BOOT ID                          FIRST ENTRY                 LAST ENTRY
  0 1e8b72759fec45ccae08682c99b4d38f Thu 2026-10-22 23:26:05 IST Sat 2026-10-24 16:37:25 IST

(Real output — this VM has only ever had one boot so far, which is itself realistic for a lab environment created recently; journalctl --list-boots is exactly the command to check for more boots, and is honest about there being only one here rather than fabricating a prior failed boot to show.) rescue.target depends on sysinit.target (early boot-critical units: device setup, security modules, basic filesystem mounts) but not on multi-user.target or anything beyond it — by design, rescue mode brings up just enough of the system to get a working root shell and basic diagnostic tools, deliberately skipping network services, display managers, and anything that might itself be the cause of the boot problem you're trying to diagnose. emergency. target (not shown here, but worth knowing) goes even further, skipping even most of sysinit.target — the right choice when the filesystem itself, not just a later service, might be suspect.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
mount -a's guarantee of accuracy comes from the fact that it's not a separate simulation — it's the exact same mount() syscall path and the exact same /etc/fstab parsing that real boot-time mounting uses, just invoked interactively instead of by systemd's generated mount units. This is why testing with mount -a genuinely predicts what boot would do, rather than approximating it.

When a systemd-managed boot genuinely can't satisfy a unit's requirements (a .mount unit failing because its device or mount point is missing, as reproduced above but imagine uncaught), and something else in the dependency graph (Level 2, Lesson 6) strictly Requires= that unit, systemd doesn't simply skip ahead and pretend everything's fine — it drops to a target with the problem unit's chain already satisfied as far as possible and stops there, typically emergency mode for a root-filesystem-level problem or an interactive prompt for a specific failed non-critical mount, giving a human the chance to fix /etc/fstab, re-run systemctl daemon-reload, and continue booting rather than ending up with a half-started system silently missing something it depended on.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Rebooting immediately after editing /etc/fstab without testing with mount -a first. As this lesson demonstrates directly, the exact same failure mount -a would have caught instantly, interactively, with full context, instead surfaces during boot — at a point with far less context and a much higher cost to get wrong.
  • Panicking at an emergency shell and immediately trying destructive fixes. The emergency shell is a genuinely safe place to investigate first — journalctl -xb (this boot's full log) almost always names the specific unit and reason directly; fixing the named cause and running systemctl default to continue booting is usually faster and safer than guessing.
  • Forgetting that nofail exists for genuinely optional mounts. Adding the nofail option to an fstab entry for a non-critical filesystem (a removable drive, an optional network share) tells systemd not to block the rest of boot if that one mount fails — appropriate for "nice to have," wrong for anything the system actually needs to function.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a deliberately broken line to a copy of your /etc/fstab (never test this against the real file without a backup, exactly as this lesson did), and run mount -a against it to confirm the failure is caught. Then run systemctl list-dependencies rescue.target and systemctl list-dependencies emergency.target side by side, and identify at least one unit present in one target's dependency list but not the other's, explaining what that difference implies about which boot problems each target is meant to help diagnose.

docs.title: 07 · Containers vs VMs: Where OS Fundamentals End and Virtualization Begins
docs.text: Level 3 built a working, isolated, resource-limited process using nothing but unshare and a cgroup — the real mechanism behind containers. This entire course was also written and verified inside a real virtual machine. Both are "isolation," and the gap between them is the single most useful distinction in this whole level for deciding which tool actually fits a given problem.

docs.title: The real, measured difference
docs.text:
$ systemd-analyze   # this course's lab VM, full boot
Startup finished in 317ms (kernel) + 1.336s (initrd) + 2min 45.052s (userspace)
                                                        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                                                        (mostly cloud-init network wait,
                                                        Level 1 Lesson 2 — but even without
                                                        that, a real kernel boot, firmware
                                                        init, and full userspace startup
                                                        are unavoidable real costs)

$ time sudo unshare --pid --mount-proc --fork true   # Level 3's namespace demo
real    0m0.013s
user    0m0.003s
sys     0m0.009s

A container (what unshare+cgroups built directly, Level 3 Lessons 7 and 10) is a normal process on the same running kernel, made to see and consume only a restricted view of that kernel's resources. There is exactly one kernel involved, one real boot already happened (long before the container existed), and creating a new container is just creating a new process with some extra kernel bookkeeping (new namespaces, a cgroup assignment) — which is why it completes in milliseconds, as measured directly above. A virtual machine boots an entirely separate kernel on top of emulated or paravirtualized hardware, provided by a hypervisor (this course's lab VM uses Apple's vz framework) — a genuinely separate operating system instance, with its own real (if virtual) boot sequence, which is why even a fast VM boot measures in seconds to minutes, not milliseconds, no matter how lightweight the guest OS is.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This course's own Level 1 and Level 3 projects drew this exact line in practice, even if it wasn't named that way at the time: chroot (Level 1) changed only the filesystem root view and shared literally everything else, including the kernel, with the host — provably, since uname -a inside and outside the chroot reported the identical kernel build. unshare (Level 3) added process-tree and hostname isolation on top of that same shared kernel — still one kernel, more of it hidden from view. Neither of these ever involved a second kernel booting; every layer of isolation this course built was isolation within one running kernel instance. A VM is categorically different: the hypervisor presents virtual (or paravirtualized, like this lab's virtio_blk disk from Level 4, Lesson 3) hardware to a guest kernel that boots independently, goes through its own BIOS/UEFI handoff, its own init, its own process table that the host kernel knows nothing about directly — real isolation at the hardware-emulation boundary, not at the single-kernel-resource-view boundary containers use.
