This is exactly why a kernel vulnerability that lets code escape a container's namespace/cgroup boundary is historically more common and more severe than one that escapes a VM's hypervisor boundary: a container escape lands you directly in the one shared kernel everything was always running on, with no second security boundary behind it; a VM escape (a "hypervisor breakout") has to defeat hardware-assisted virtualization isolation specifically designed to resist exactly that, which is a substantially harder and rarer class of bug. This isn't a reason to consider containers insecure by default — properly configured, with LSM profiles, seccomp, and non-root user namespaces (all mentioned as missing from this course's own minimal demos), containers are used safely at enormous scale — but it is the real, structural reason "a container is basically a lightweight VM" undersells a genuine difference in what's actually providing the isolation.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing a VM "to be safe" for a workload where container isolation (correctly configured, with the pieces this course's demos deliberately left out for simplicity) would be entirely sufficient, paying real boot-time and resource overhead for a security margin the actual threat model may not need.
  • Choosing a container for a workload that genuinely needs a different kernel, different kernel-level security boundary, or hardware-level isolation (multi-tenant untrusted code execution, for instance) and discovering the shared-kernel assumption the hard way.
  • Assuming "container" means one fixed thing. As Level 3 showed directly, it's a combination of independently-tunable kernel mechanisms — a container with every available isolation feature enabled is a very different security posture from one with the bare minimum, even though both are correctly called "a container."

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Time unshare --pid --fork true (or similar) against booting any VM you have access to, even one with a minimal guest OS, and compare the two numbers directly, as this lesson did. Then explain, in your own words, using the "what is actually providing the isolation" model from this lesson, why the two numbers differ by roughly two to four orders of magnitude rather than by some small constant factor.

docs.title: 08 · Linux Distros Compared: Debian, RHEL, Arch & Alpine
docs.text:
Documentation-based lesson

Unlike almost every other lesson in this course, this one cannot be verified by running commands — it's a comparison across distributions, and this course's lab environment is one specific distro (Ubuntu). The facts below are drawn from each project's own current documentation as of October 2026 and are the kind of thing that occasionally shifts (a release cadence changes, a default swaps) — treat specific version numbers and dates as a snapshot, and the structural differences (init system, package format, philosophy) as durable.

Every lesson in this course ran on Ubuntu, a Debian derivative. The concepts — the filesystem model, permissions, systemd, namespaces, netfilter — are genuinely the same across every mainstream distro, because they're kernel and (mostly) systemd features, not distro-specific inventions. What does differ, and differs enough to matter the first time you work on an unfamiliar distro, is covered here.

docs.title: Four distros, four different answers to the same questions
docs.text:
Debian / Ubuntu — dpkg/APT package management (Level 1, Lesson 9), systemd init, a conservative, stability-first release philosophy on Debian itself (new "stable" releases roughly every two years, each supported for years afterward) with Ubuntu layering a faster, more opinionated release cadence (a new release every six months, with designated LTS releases — like the 26.04 LTS this course's lab VM runs — supported far longer) on top of the same Debian package base.

RHEL / Fedora — rpm/DNF package management (the direct structural analogue to dpkg/APT from Level 1, Lesson 9), systemd init (same as Debian/Ubuntu — this is not a point of difference), SELinux as the default LSM (instead of AppArmor — Level 3, Lesson 6) and a split release model: Fedora is the fast-moving upstream (roughly twice yearly releases, shorter support windows, newer package versions sooner), and RHEL (and its rebuilds — Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux) is the long-support-window downstream, intentionally built from a point-in-time Fedora base and then held stable for years, the enterprise-oriented mirror of Ubuntu's LTS philosophy.

Arch Linux — pacman package management, a genuinely different philosophy from both of the above: rolling release, meaning there is no "Arch 13" or "Arch 26.04" — the system is continuously updated to the latest packages, with no fixed release boundary at all. This trades predictability (a package version changing underneath you between any two pacman -Syu runs) for always having current software, and Arch's own wiki and documentation culture is widely regarded as exceptionally thorough — a reason people reach for it even without running Arch itself.

Alpine Linux — the structural outlier of the four: apk package management, OpenRC instead of systemd as its init system (a real, simpler init framework rather than systemd's broader scope), and most significantly, musl instead of glibc as its C library, plus BusyBox instead of GNU coreutils for most basic utilities (both mentioned in Level 1, Lesson 1 as the reason some scripts behave differently on Alpine). Alpine's small footprint (a base image measured in single-digit megabytes) is exactly why it's the default base for a huge share of container images — but that same musl/BusyBox substitution is also the most common reason a script, binary, or glibc-specific behavior that "works everywhere" quietly breaks specifically on Alpine.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The deepest, most consequential split here isn't package manager syntax — it's glibc vs musl. glibc is larger, implements some long-standing GNU-specific extensions and behaviors, and is what the overwhelming majority of prebuilt Linux binaries are compiled and tested against. musl is smaller, more strictly standards- conforming in some areas, and deliberately omits some glibc extensions — which means a binary compiled against glibc will often simply not run on an Alpine (musl) system at all without recompilation, a real and common surprise for anyone moving a prebuilt binary or a Docker image's base layer from a glibc distro to Alpine. This single difference accounts for more real-world "works on my machine" pain than every other distro difference on this page combined.

The rolling vs point-release distinction (Arch vs. everything else here) is a genuine, deliberate tradeoff in system design philosophy, not a maturity gap: a point-release distro batches and tests a coherent snapshot of package versions together before calling it a numbered release, giving you predictability and a known-tested combination; a rolling release gives you the newest packages continuously, at the cost of needing to handle occasional breaking changes between any two updates rather than only at major-version boundaries.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming a shell script tested only on Ubuntu/Debian will behave identically on Alpine. Between bash-specific syntax (Alpine's default /bin/sh is often a much more limited shell, not bash, unless bash is explicitly installed) and the glibc/musl gap, this is one of the single most common container-build surprises.
  • Treating "Fedora" and "RHEL" as interchangeable because they share a package format. Fedora runs noticeably newer package versions with a shorter support window — testing exclusively on Fedora and deploying to RHEL (or vice versa) can hit real version-skew issues the shared rpm format doesn't protect against.
  • Picking Arch for a production server because "it has the newest packages." The same property that makes Arch appealing for a personal, actively-maintained desktop (always current) is a real operational cost for a server you don't want to babysit through rolling updates — point-release distros with long support windows exist specifically for that use case.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Pick any one tool you use daily (a shell, an editor, a language runtime) and look up how it's packaged and what version is currently available on Debian stable, Ubuntu's current LTS, Fedora's current release, and Alpine's current stable branch. Note which ones ship the newest version, which ship the oldest, and connect the pattern you find back to each distro's release philosophy from this lesson.

docs.title: 09 · Kernel Versions, LTS & Staying Current
docs.text: "Which kernel version should I run" has a different right answer depending on whether you want the newest features, the most tested stability, or multi-year support — because the kernel project itself maintains several parallel release lines simultaneously, not one single version number moving forward.

docs.title: The three lines kernel.org actually maintains
docs.text: Mainline is where new development lands first — the newest features, the newest hardware support, and the least real-world testing time. Stable takes a mainline release once it's done and backports bugfixes-only patches to it for a few months after the next mainline release ships, giving a short window of polish before that line is retired. Longterm (LTS) takes certain mainline releases (not all of them — specific ones chosen by the kernel community) and continues backporting bugfixes to them for years, specifically for distributions, embedded systems, and enterprises that need a long-lived, stable target to build on rather than constantly rebasing onto new mainline releases.

docs.title: Worked example: real, current release data, not a snapshot from training data
docs.text:
$ curl -s https://www.kernel.org/releases.json | python3 -c "
import json, sys
for r in json.load(sys.stdin)['releases']:
    if r['moniker'] in ('mainline','stable','longterm'):
        print(r['moniker'], r['version'], r['released']['isodate'])
"
mainline  7.3      2026-10-18
stable    7.2.12   2026-10-21
longterm  6.18.58  2026-10-21
longterm  6.12.114 2026-10-21
longterm  6.6.160  2026-10-21
longterm  6.1.190  2026-10-15
longterm  5.15.223 2026-10-15
longterm  5.10.272 2026-10-15

(Real data, fetched live from kernel.org at the time this lesson was written — not recalled from memory, and guaranteed to look different by the time you read this, which is itself the point.) Notice six different longterm lines actively receiving updates simultaneously, spanning from 5.10 through 6.18 — this is normal; LTS kernels have long support windows specifically so a distro or device shipped years ago can keep receiving security patches without a disruptive jump to a much newer kernel. The gap between mainline (7.3) and the newest longterm line (6.18.58) is also normal: a kernel doesn't need to be the newest mainline release to be fully supported — LTS designation is a deliberate choice made for specific releases, not every one.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A kernel's version number itself encodes which patches it has, but not which support line it belongs to — you have to cross-reference against kernel.org's (or your distro's) current release data to know whether a given version is still receiving security fixes, which is exactly why checking a live source matters more than remembering a number. Distributions add their own layer on top: Ubuntu's kernel version strings (like this course's lab VM's own 7.0.0-34-generic, from uname -r in Level 1) combine an upstream base version with Ubuntu's own ABI build number — distros frequently backport specific newer features or hardware support into an otherwise-older base kernel, meaning the version number alone doesn't tell you everything a distro kernel actually contains; the distro's own kernel changelog is the authoritative source for that, not the raw version string.

This is also why "just run the newest kernel" isn't automatically correct advice: mainline and short-lived stable releases have had far less real-world testing time than a mature LTS release that's been running on millions of machines for months or years — for a production server, a well-supported LTS line is very often the more stable choice precisely because it's not the newest, not despite it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting a remembered or trained-on "current kernel version" instead of checking a live source. As this lesson demonstrates by fetching real-time data, kernel releases happen on an ongoing cadence — any specific version number you've memorized is a snapshot that ages, sometimes within weeks.
  • Assuming a distro's kernel version number maps directly to kernel.org's release lines. Distro kernels are frequently patched and backported independently of upstream naming — check your specific distro's kernel changelog, not just the bare uname -r number, before concluding what security fixes it does or doesn't have.
  • Chasing mainline for a production system "to get the latest features." Mainline and stable lines are retired relatively quickly and have had the least cumulative real-world testing — an LTS line is usually the better fit unless a specific feature or hardware-support need genuinely requires something newer.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run curl -s https://www.kernel.org/releases.json yourself (or visit kernel.org directly) and compare the current mainline, stable, and longterm versions against what this lesson showed — note how much has changed. Then check your own machine's kernel with uname -r and look up, in your distro's own documentation or changelog, which upstream longterm line (if any) it's actually built from.

docs.title: 10 · Capstone: Build, Harden & Diagnose a Linux Server From Scratch
docs.text: This capstone combines Levels 1 through 4: a dedicated user with key-only SSH (Level 1 permissions, Level 3 SSH internals), a systemd-managed service (Level 2), an nftables firewall rule (Level 3), and then three real faults — injected on purpose, into this exact setup, and diagnosed with the real tools this course covered. Every command and every failure below genuinely happened.

docs.title: Build: a least-privilege app user, a managed service, a firewall rule
docs.text:
$ sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash appuser
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f appkey -N "" -C "appuser-deploy"
$ sudo cp appkey.pub /home/appuser/.ssh/authorized_keys
$ sudo chown -R appuser:appuser /home/appuser/.ssh
$ sudo chmod 700 /home/appuser/.ssh && sudo chmod 600 /home/appuser/.ssh/authorized_keys

$ ssh -i appkey appuser@127.0.0.1 "whoami; id"
appuser
uid=1000(appuser) gid=1002(appuser) groups=1002(appuser)

# /etc/systemd/system/capstone-app.service
[Unit]
Description=Capstone demo app
After=network.target
[Service]
Type=simple
User=appuser
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 0.0.0.0
Restart=on-failure
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

$ sudo systemctl enable --now capstone-app
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:8080/
200

$ sudo nft add table inet capstone
$ sudo nft add chain inet capstone input '{ type filter hook input priority 0; policy accept; }'
$ sudo nft add rule inet capstone input tcp dport 8080 accept

(Real output from this course's lab VM — a genuine least-privilege setup: appuser runs the service and owns nothing it doesn't need, SSH authentication is key-only by construction since no password was ever set, and the service runs under systemd's management with its own Restart= policy from Level 2, Lesson 7.)

docs.title: Diagnose: three real faults, injected on purpose
docs.text:
Fault 1 — the service is stopped:

$ sudo systemctl stop capstone-app
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" --max-time 2 http://127.0.0.1:8080/
000

curl returning 000 (no HTTP status at all) immediately points away from an HTTP-level problem and toward "nothing is even accepting the connection" — systemctl status capstone-app is the very next command, and would show inactive (dead) directly, the clean diagnosis.

Fault 2 — a firewall rule silently dropping a port that is listening:

$ python3 -m http.server 9090 &
$ ss -tln | grep 9090
LISTEN 0      5            0.0.0.0:9090       0.0.0.0:*

$ sudo nft add rule inet capstone input tcp dport 9090 drop
$ timeout 3 curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:9090/
(hangs for the full 3 seconds, then exits with status 124 — a timeout, not a clean refusal)

This is the diagnostically interesting fault: ss -tln proves the service is genuinely listening, which rules out Fault 1's cause entirely — yet the connection never completes. A curl that times out (rather than getting an immediate 000/connection-refused) is the real, distinguishing signature of a packet being silently dropped by a firewall rule rather than a socket simply not existing — sudo nft list ruleset (Level 3, Lesson 3) is the next real command, and would show the drop rule directly.

Fault 3 — a permissions regression breaking key-based SSH:

$ chmod 644 appkey
$ ssh -i appkey appuser@127.0.0.1 "echo still working"
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
@         WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!          @
@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@@
Permissions 0644 for 'appkey' are too open.
Load key "appkey": bad permissions
appuser@127.0.0.1: Permission denied (publickey).

This is the one fault that names its own cause directly in the error output — a genuine demonstration that Level 1's permission lessons and Level 3's SSH-internals lesson weren't abstract: OpenSSH's client itself actively refuses to use an overly-permissive private key file, rather than silently failing or, worse, using it anyway. chmod 600 appkey is the entire fix, and the tool told you so.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Each fault above was diagnosable using a different tool from a different level, and distinguishing them required knowing what each tool actually proves: systemctl status proves whether a service is running at all (Level 2); ss -tln proves whether something is genuinely listening, independent of reachability (Level 3, Lesson 4); the specific shape of a connection failure (000/immediate refusal vs. a hang-then-timeout) is itself diagnostic evidence distinguishing "nothing there" from "something there but blocked" (Level 3, Lesson 3); and a permission-related authentication failure that names its own cause in the client's own error output is the direct, practical payoff of Level 1's permission model and Level 3's SSH lesson landing correctly. None of these three faults look alike from the outside (an HTTP client failing to connect), and all three require genuinely different fixes — which is the entire point of carrying a layered mental model instead of one memorized troubleshooting checklist.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Diagnosing by guessing a fix instead of gathering evidence first. Restarting the service, flushing the firewall, and regenerating SSH keys would have "fixed" all three faults above eventually, by accident — but without systemctl status, ss -tln, and reading the SSH client's own error message, you'd learn nothing about why, and the same class of fault would cost just as much time the next time it happened.
  • Stopping at the first plausible cause instead of confirming it. Fault 2 specifically punishes this: if you'd assumed "the service must be down" without running ss -tln first, you'd have gone looking in the wrong place entirely, since the service was never the problem.
  • Treating a 000/refused response and a timed-out response as the same kind of failure. As this capstone showed directly, they point at genuinely different root causes (nothing listening vs. something blocking) — collapsing that distinction in an incident writeup or a monitoring alert loses the single most useful piece of evidence either one provides.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Reproduce this capstone's build steps yourself (a disposable VM, never a system you rely on), then inject your own choice of fault from anywhere in this course — a broken fstab entry (Level 2), a stopped systemd timer instead of a service (Level 2), or a cgroup memory limit set too low for the workload (Level 2, Level 3) — and walk through the diagnosis using only the tools from the level that fault belongs to, writing down which specific piece of evidence (not just "it didn't work") told you the real cause.
